Signal Adds Screenshot Restrictions to Limit Mobile AI Data Capture

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (893 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that meredith Whittaker confirmed on November 20, 2026 that the encrypted messaging app is restricting screenshots on iOS 27 and on Android when it detects an AI assistant trying to read the screen, seeking to prevent operating-system agents from capturing private chats.
  • On iOS 27, the announcement indicates an enabled Block Siri AI setting.
  • Signal’s concern is at the endpoint, where private content becomes visible on a screen.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that meredith Whittaker confirmed on November 20, 2026 that the encrypted messaging app is restricting screenshots on iOS 27 and on Android when it detects an AI assistant trying to read the screen, seeking to prevent operating-system agents from capturing private chats. The protections are incomplete, and Signal cannot reliably block screenshots on macOS.

On iOS 27, the announcement indicates an enabled Block Siri AI setting. Android uses a conditional approach: Signal automatically enables Screen security when an AI assistant attempts to access the screen, rather than applying one screenshot rule across every Android distribution. People can disable the protection to retain screenshots, though Signal warns that doing so can expose their own and their contacts’ content and break its privacy guarantees.

Signal’s concern is at the endpoint, where private content becomes visible on a screen. Operating-system agents can scan that visible information to answer questions or carry out tasks. Signal indicates the resulting captures can be stored in a local database or on a remote server used by the agent, outside its control, potentially exposing every participant in a conversation. Application encryption therefore cannot determine what happens to content after the operating system captures it.

Apple remarked on September 14, 2026 that Siri AI was beginning to roll out in English beta with its 2027 software releases, including onscreen awareness to answer questions or take actions related to content on a user’s screen. Google’s Gemini documentation says screen actions can upload information visible on the screen or in a file for context, while Intelligent Screen Context can use right now visible content to answer a chat request in English.

Recent findings suggest that signal’s Android design reflects differences across vendor distributions. On many of them, the manufacturer cannot reliably detect a screenshot attempt when screenshots are already disabled. It chose assistant-access detection to avoid screenshots simply stopping without explanation, but that approach also leaves some Android devices without coverage.

Industry observers note that blocking screenshots leaves other routes open as well, including retrieval of content already present on a device through the filesystem. The gap is larger on macOS 27: Signal cannot reliably block screenshots there and cannot apply the available continuous-capture protections to the screenshots most agentic systems use.

It has been revealed that for macOS 27, Signal recommends adding the app under System Settings > Siri > Excluded Apps to protect message content from proactive access by Siri AI. On iPhones, the Electronic Frontier Foundation documented Apple’s iOS 27.2 Excluded Apps control on October 28, 2026. Excluding an app prevents Siri AI from accessing its contents but also disables features such as onscreen awareness for that app. That feature loss illustrates the trade-off behind Signal’s request for exclusions that do not undermine an app’s core utility.

Signal is asking Apple, Google, and Microsoft for a documented way to opt apps out of AI access and processing across screen reading, filesystem access, notifications, APIs, and other operating-system frameworks without undermining core utility. The request also covers accurate technical documentation of how agents access and process data.

It has been revealed that signal argues that confidential-computing approaches are not a complete answer because providers still control the extent of any privacy guarantees. The same concern applies to third-party agents such as Meta’s Muse when deep setup permissions and accessibility settings intended to help people use apps provide broad access to application data.

According to recent reports, signal has used a version of this defense before. On May 21, 2025, it enabled Screen security by default on Windows 11, using a digital rights management window flag so screenshots of Signal Desktop appear blank and Microsoft Recall cannot capture their contents. The Windows control was local to each computer, required a warning and confirmation to disable, and could interfere with accessibility software such as screen readers and magnification tools.

It has been revealed that signal mentioned it is discussing standardized approaches for privacy-sensitive apps with Google and Apple and is cautiously optimistic about further changes. The result is right now a partial defense: Signal can obstruct screenshot capture in certain environments, but the comprehensive privacy boundary it wants still depends on controls and documentation that operating-system providers have not supplied.

QCon San Francisco 2026: The Future of Apache Iceberg

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (710 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Infoq

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage News QCon San Francisco 2026: The Future of Apache Iceberg.
  • Nov 20, 2026 3 min read.
  • In a recent development, apache Iceberg V4 proposes a redesign of table metadata to improve scalability and support more frequent writes, alongside latest capabilities for data management and schema evolution.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News QCon San Francisco 2026: The Future of Apache Iceberg.

Nov 20, 2026 3 min read.

In a recent development, apache Iceberg V4 proposes a redesign of table metadata to improve scalability and support more frequent writes, alongside latest capabilities for data management and schema evolution. Daniel Weeks, co-creator of Apache Iceberg and member of technical staff at Databricks, presented a session at QCon San Francisco on the fourth version of the Apache Iceberg open table format specification.

Sources indicate that iceberg V4 will address the limitations of managing very large tables while expanding the format to support new data types and workloads. The speaker described the new version as a major reimagining of the table format rather than an incremental step, with changes including a new metadata tree, more efficient commits, typed column statistics, relative file paths, and support for file and vector data types. While earlier versions left most of the metadata structure intact, V4 addresses problems that emerge at large scale and adds support for new use cases. Weeks told the audience in San Francisco:.

According to recent reports, V4 is a major reimagining of a table format. We didn't get everything right in V3 and prior, so now we're taking the opportunity to fix some of the biggest things that are challenges as we scale up to even larger data sets and we bring on latest use cases.

Apache Iceberg is an open table format for managing large analytical datasets across different data processing engines. Originally developed at Netflix in 2017, it was open-sourced in 2018 and became an Apache top-level project in 2020. The main alternatives among open table formats are Delta Lake, created by Databricks and now a Linux Foundation project, Apache Hudi, originally developed at Uber, and Apache Paimon, which grew out of the Flink community and gained adoption for streaming-oriented workloads. However, interoperability tools are increasingly blurring the lines between them.

It has been revealed that in his talk, Weeks covered three areas of the proposed Iceberg V4 changes: metadata and scalability, including the Adaptive Metadata Tree, single-file commits, improved column statistics, relative paths, and column-level updates; latest table features, such as expression-based default values and constraints; and new data types, particularly file and vector types, which support additional workloads such as AI and search. Regarding faster commits, Weeks explained:.

This gets us into use cases where we can stream data much faster. We can do commits at the 2nd level or subsecond level, where right now we largely recommend that you don't do commits under 2 minutes.

In V3, adding a data file requires at least four I/O operations, including manifest creation and rewriting. V4 simplifies this process by allowing the metadata tree's root to point directly to data files, reducing the operation to a single metadata write. According to Weeks, this could enable commits every second or even at subsecond intervals, compared with the current recommendation of at least two minutes between commits. Iceberg V3, introduced in 2024, added deletion vectors, row lineage, new data types, encryption, and default values.

According to recent reports, V4 replaces V3's binary column statistics with structured, typed statistics, improving projection and schema evolution. Furthermore, V4 introduces expression-based default values, check, unique, and primary key constraints, and statistics-only fields that support partitioning, sorting, and filtering without storing additional data. It will also track constraint validation status, allowing engines to determine when further checks are needed.

In August, Weeks started an initial V4 scope discussion on the Apache Iceberg developer mailing list, with Steven Wu suggesting adding monotonic snapshot and row-level upgrade timestamps, while Manu Zhang discussed efficient column updates and the removal of equality deletes.

During the Q&A, Weeks explicitly confirmed that V4 metadata will not be backward compatible with older readers. Existing V3 metadata can remain in place during an upgrade, but older readers cannot consume the newly introduced representation.

Dharma Field Extractor: Any Document In, Structured Fields in JSON Out

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1306 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A 2-billion-parameter model that extracts exactly the fields you ask for, from any document type, outperforming every frontier LLM we tested, at a fraction of the cost.
  • In April, we released DharmaOCR-LITE, a model specialized for OCR across a wide range of documents, from contracts and court filings to invoices, IDs and forms.
  • In a recent development, OCR gives you the text on a page, faithful to the original formatting.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A 2-billion-parameter model that extracts exactly the fields you ask for, from any document type, outperforming every frontier LLM we tested, at a fraction of the cost.

In April, we released DharmaOCR-LITE, a model specialized for OCR across a wide range of documents, from contracts and court filings to invoices, IDs and forms. The paper behind it made a narrow, well-measured case for domain specialization: a smaller model trained closer to its task beating general-purpose frontier APIs on that task.

In a recent development, OCR gives you the text on a page, faithful to the original formatting. That's exactly what you want when the job is the whole document, like a contract you'll read end to end or a manuscript you're digitizing.

However, there's a different use case: you don't want the page, you want specific fields out of it, in a shape a system downstream can consume. Every line item on an invoice, as a list. The patient name, exam type and date from a medical requisition, ready to schedule. The fields off an ID, mapped to the columns of an employee record.

According to recent reports, run that document through OCR and you get back everything printed on it, line by line, with no indication of which string is the exam type, which is the date or which number is the total. Someone still has to write the code that maps each value to the right field before it reaches the database.

In a recent development, A general-purpose LLM can do this work today, with careful prompting. At frontier API pricing and latency, on a task many businesses need to run at high volume, that quickly becomes the expensive way to solve a well-defined problem.

So we built a model for it instead. The Field Extractor takes a document image and either a request for everything it can find, or an exact schema to fill, and returns structured JSON: typed, field by field, nested where the document nests. An invoice comes back with every line item as an ordered list, each with its own quantity and value, alongside the totals. An ID comes back as the fields you'll store, under the names your system already uses for them. The same checkpoint handles all of it, with no per-type fine-tuning.

Say a batch of supplier invoices lands every morning, and you need four things off each one to push into your system: the supplier, the invoice number, the due date, the total. Same story for medical requisitions going into a scheduler, or contracts feeding a compliance system, where what matters is the parties, the term, the penalties and the fine amounts. You don't need the page, you need certain fields. With the Field Extractor there are two ways to ask for them:.

Industry observers note that the choice comes down to what you already know. Send an open request when you don't know what the document holds. Send a schema when the output has to match a shape that already exists somewhere else.

Either way, what comes back is JSON: the fields as keys, the values typed as requested, and null where the document didn't have what you asked for. When you send a schema, the output follows it exactly, with the same keys and no extra fields, so it can go straight into the next system.

Recent findings suggest that the base model is DharmaOCR-LITE v1.1, a upcoming 2-billion-parameter version optimized from the one in the paper and already specialized for OCR through supervised fine-tuning and DPO. On top of that checkpoint we trained a LoRA adapter on 43,384 training examples covering both request modes.

The data is organized into three streams:.

Recent findings suggest that all three streams are annotated at the field level. The mix is deliberately multi-domain: receipts, commercial invoices, forms, bank statements, ID documents and synthetic documents, rather than one filing type.

It has been revealed that the full benchmark covers 546 documents across three request scenarios, for 1,638 total cases: extracting every field with no schema, a partial schema naming only real fields, and a schema that also includes deliberately nonexistent fields. The score is field-level F1 (matched by path, including position inside a table), multiplied by the Levenshtein similarity on the values that matched and by the share of outputs that come back as valid JSON.

We ran the same benchmark against four general-purpose frontier configurations.

Against general-purpose LLMs, the quality gap runs from 1.8 points (Claude Opus 5, the closest) to 9.3 points (GPT-5.6 Luna, the widest).

Industry observers note that cost runs from roughly 6 times lower (GPT-5.6 Luna) to roughly 147 times lower (GPT-5.6 Sol). The two sides are priced differently. The frontier figures come from measured average input and output tokens per page, reasoning tokens included, against each provider's published list pricing. Every frontier model ran with reasoning set to low; Claude Opus 5 used adaptive effort, which can skip reasoning on simpler pages while staying at the low level. Ours isn't billed per token: the model runs self-hosted, so the figure is GPU time on a single L40S at $2.24 per hour.

In a recent development, this is not a sales price. Self-hosted cost depends on the hardware, the volume and the latency each deployment needs. The comparison is here to show that a sovereign SSLM, deployed on your own infrastructure, is a real alternative to frontier APIs.

It has been revealed that SROIE and FUNSD are two public datasets in our benchmark, not used in training. Below is one example from each.

On a SROIE receipt, we asked for all 18 fields printed on it, with no phantom fields this time, and every one comes back correct: the multi-line, unlabeled billing address captured as a single field, the two blank fields (salesperson and ref) correctly returned as null, and every number on the receipt matching to the cent.

Sources indicate that on a FUNSD photocopying variance form, a checklist of twelve boolean fields with one nested group of five sub-options, the model marks exactly the one box that's checked (poor quality original, with a handwritten "faded" note beside it) as true, and the other eleven as false, matching the form exactly. It also reads the handwritten Bates ID off the page correctly, and returns null for the two fields left blank.

Industry observers note that A 2-billion-parameter model scored 0.834, above every frontier configuration we tested, from Claude Opus 5 at 0.816 to GPT-5.6 Luna at 0.741, while running on a single L40S at a lower cost per extraction than every API in the comparison. Higher quality and lower cost, measured on the same benchmark, in the same run.

Industry observers note that this isn't the first time we've measured it. Our OCR paper put the first DharmaOCR-LITE, a 3-billion-parameter model, above every commercial frontier API tested on Brazilian Portuguese; three months later, newer and better-resourced models arrived, and the gap held. Now a 2-billion-parameter model does it on field extraction. Each result adds evidence for the thesis we started Dharma-AI with: on a bounded task, a small model trained close to that task beats a frontier model asked to do the same thing in general. In this benchmark, it also cost 6 to 147 times less to run.

It has been revealed that parameter count sets the ceiling; training decides how much of it a model reaches on your task. Your business doesn't need the biggest model available. It needs one trained for your problem.

In a recent development, try it on your own documents here. To learn more about Dharma-AI and the specialized models we build, visit dharma-ai.com.

Latest Update: ARCS∙ai Opens Shared ARPI Center for Physical AI Training

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (770 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Advanced Research in Computational Sciences and Artificial Intelligence (ARCS∙ai) announced the launch of the ARPI Center in Yerevan on November 20, 2026.
  • ARPI stands for Armenian Robotics & Physical Intelligence.
  • Industry observers note that the formal presentation at Digitec took place at Yerevan’s Meridian Exhibition Center with NVIDIA’s Rev Lebaredian, vice president of physical AI simulation, representatives of the participating universities and live robot demonstrations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Advanced Research in Computational Sciences and Artificial Intelligence (ARCS∙ai) announced the launch of the ARPI Center in Yerevan on November 20, 2026. The shared robotics and Physical AI center has a stated goal of graduating 50 specialized engineers annually by combining faculty, students and equipment from three Armenian universities.

ARPI stands for Armenian Robotics & Physical Intelligence. Its focus is Physical AI, which the announcement describes as the convergence of robotics and artificial intelligence. The center’s national-lab model pools resources across the American University of Armenia (AUA), Yerevan State University (YSU) and the National Polytechnic University of Armenia instead of having each institution build separate robotics capacity.

Industry observers note that the formal presentation at Digitec took place at Yerevan’s Meridian Exhibition Center with NVIDIA’s Rev Lebaredian, vice president of physical AI simulation, representatives of the participating universities and live robot demonstrations. Beyond the presentation, the center already has an undergraduate cohort and courses in progress.

Thirty students are enrolled in the first semester of a three-semester Physical AI minor offered within AUA’s Engineering program and YSU’s Data Science program. Nine courses are being delivered across those two universities, spanning robot mechanics, control and estimation, reinforcement learning, digital twins, and the ethics and governance of Physical AI.

The course catalog reveals how classroom topics connect to hardware. Its dynamical systems, control and estimation course combines modeling and controller design with experiments on single-degree-of-freedom mechanisms and multi-rotor aerial robots. The simulation, digital twins and differentiable physics course requires prior study in deep learning, robot mechanics, and control and estimation, placing advanced simulation work after those foundations.

In a recent development, A Physical AI master’s program is scheduled to launch at AUA in 2027. The catalog’s planned capstone has teams build a complete system through simulation, data collection, policy training, transfer from simulation to real hardware, deployment and evaluation. It also brings mechanical design, sensor suites and a safety envelope into that end-to-end project, extending the training pathway beyond the undergraduate minor.

Fourteen faculty members are engaged, including eight recruited from institutions in the United States and Europe, such as the University of Southern California, TU Delft and the Rutherford Appleton Laboratory. Astghik Hakobyan has become the first ARCS∙ai Fellow under a three-year joint appointment between AUA and ARCS∙ai.

It has been revealed that AUA and ARCS∙ai have signed a memorandum of understanding governing their collaboration, while a similar YSU agreement remains in development. That distinction matters for a center built around shared staff and equipment: one university partnership is formalized, while another is still being negotiated.

Industry observers note that the center’s physical base is a fresh robotics laboratory representing a $500,000 investment. It contains robotic manipulator arms, ground robots, virtual-reality headsets, a machine shop and a large drone flight area with motion tracking. On-site NVIDIA GPUs will support AI training and robot simulation. Students and researchers also have access to the Firebird AI initiative’s GPU cluster, which ARCS∙ai describes as one of Europe’s five largest.

Best Supporting Agent: Why Agentic AI in the Contact Centre Still Needs a Human Lead

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1365 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, agentic AI is moving fast from answering customer questions to taking action on their behalf.
  • In a recent development, but giving software permission to act also raises the question of what happens when a customer needs an exception, or when an automated decision is technically correct but plainly unfair.
  • Industry observers note that the opportunity is substantial, provided contact centres are deliberate about which decisions AI can make and when human lead is required.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, agentic AI is moving fast from answering customer questions to taking action on their behalf. It can retrieve account records and move a request forward without waiting for an agent’s input. For contact centres under pressure to handle more conversations with limited resources, that is an appealing prospect.

In a recent development, but giving software permission to act also raises the question of what happens when a customer needs an exception, or when an automated decision is technically correct but plainly unfair. These are everyday realities of customer service, and also moments when trust is won or lost.

Industry observers note that the opportunity is substantial, provided contact centres are deliberate about which decisions AI can make and when human lead is required. A strong option for contact centres is to use automation for routine tasks while giving agents the authority to resolve complex customer problems.

Traditional contact-centre automation could only do so much. Customers were often stuck navigating phone menus or choosing from a limited set of options, and anything more complicated usually meant waiting to speak with an agent. Agentic systems can go further, and given the right permissions, they can follow a customer’s request across multiple systems and carry out approved steps. A request to change an appointment, for example, might involve checking eligibility and updating the booking.

Recent findings suggest that that changes the role of the human agent. Instead of spending the first few minutes hunting for information, an agent can enter the conversation with a clear picture of what has already happened. A well-designed assistant can surface and summarize previous interactions before the agent has to ask another question.

In a recent development, AI can make a real difference in customer service. A study on customer support agents involving more than 5,000 workers found that agents using AI assistance resolved about 15% more customer issues per hour. The biggest improvements came from less experienced agents, who benefited from having helpful suggestions available while handling customer requests.

These findings are encouraging, but there’s an important detail to be considered. The AI was helping agents do their jobs, with people still making the decisions. That leaves an important question for contact centres exploring agentic AI: how much responsibility should these systems have when working directly with customers?

In a recent development, speed is certainly part of good service, but customers also expect accurate answers and fair treatment. An AI agent might resolve a billing inquiry in seconds, but if it misunderstands the customer’s situation or applies the wrong policy, that quick resolution could turn into another complaint. Contact centres need to look beyond how quickly an issue is closed and consider whether the customer actually received the help they needed.

Industry observers note that even with access to customer records, AI doesn’t always have the full picture. Take a billing dispute, for example. The AI checks the account and confirms that a charge matches the contract. However, the customer was previously promised a credit during a service outage, and that information was never added to the billing system. The AI may give an answer based on the available records, but an experienced agent can recognize that something is missing and investigate further.

In 2026, Alibaba’s customer service operations highlighted that AI shortened conversations but received lower customer ratings in AI-eligible interactions. The research also showed that the effectiveness of human intervention depended on when agents stepped in and what had gone wrong. These findings suggest that knowing when to involve a person is just as key as knowing what AI can handle.

According to recent reports, for contact centres, the handoff from an AI agent to a human agent deserves as much attention as the technology itself. Customers shouldn’t have to repeat their concerns every time they’re transferred. Agents need access to previous conversations and the actions AI has already taken so they can pick up where the system left off. A smooth transition can make all the difference, especially when someone is already frustrated and simply wants their problem resolved.

According to recent reports, contact-centre leaders need to think carefully about how much control they give AI. Preparing a refund recommendation, for example, carries less risk than issuing a large credit without approval. Build these limits into the system from the start, with clear rules for when an agent needs to step in.

Contact centres can establish these boundaries by focusing on a few practical measures:.

As AI takes on more responsibilities, these boundaries should be reviewed and adjusted based on how the technology performs in real customer interactions. This allows contact centres to expand automation while maintaining accountability for the decisions being made.

In a recent development, A contact centre can celebrate a lower average handling time while customers lose confidence. If someone calls back the next morning because an AI agent promised a change that never happened, the first conversation was not a success. The reporting should make that visible.

It has been revealed that alongside speed and containment, teams should examine repeat contacts, reopened cases, correction rates, customer complaints and how often a human must reverse an automated action. They should review escalations for missing context and track whether the AI’s recommendations were useful to the people receiving them. These measures are crucial when automated actions affect a customer’s money or access to a service.

Leaders should also ask agents what the system gets wrong. Frontline agents hear the awkward pauses and recognize when a customer has lost patience. Their feedback is a source of operational intelligence. Give them a quick way to flag errors, and show them what changed as a result. If every correction disappears into a generic feedback form, the team will stop bothering.

However, using AI to understand agent experiences also raises questions about how closely workers should be monitored. Some tools claim they can detect emotions through a person’s voice. For example, the EU AI Act generally prohibits using AI to identify agents’ emotions in the workplace, with limited exceptions. The European Commission has even used call centres as an example. Businesses should check the laws in their region before introducing these tools.

Industry observers note that there is a tempting vision of a contact centre where almost every conversation ends without a person. It makes for a neat presentation slide. Actual customers tend to be less tidy. They change their minds, misunderstand instructions, ask for exceptions and bring personal circumstances that a system may not be able to judge fairly.

It has been revealed that as AI takes on more responsibilities, contact-centre leaders need to make sure their teams can recognize mistakes and correct them promptly. Customers shouldn’t have to repeat their problems or deal with the consequences of an automated decision that went wrong.

AI’s success in customer service depends on how well it supports agents in delivering the service customers expect.

Dennis Johns, B.Eng., is President and CEO of TASKE Technology, a Canadian contact centre technology company that helps organizations modernize and optimize their customer service operations. A McGill University graduate with an Honours degree in Engineering and minors in Management and Physics, Dennis has more than 39 years of experience serving contact centre clients. Today, his work focuses on managed services and applied AI solutions for Amazon Connect customers, including cloud migration, AI implementation, analytics, reporting, and ongoing contact centre optimization. TASKE has supported thousands of customers globally and works with organizations across industries including healthcare, financial services, retail, and more. In Canada, TASKE is listed in the Indigenous Business Directory and is affiliated with the Canadian Council for Indigenous Business (CCIB). Outside of his professional work, Dennis supports organizations and causes including the National Arts Centre (NAC), CHEO, and MS charity bike rides.

InfoQ Homepage Presentations Modernising Retail at Scale: Architecting a Cloud‑to‑Edge Platform for a Global Enterprise.

In a recent development, jayesh Bhayani discusses Tesco’s decade-long enterprise transformation from fragmented legacy systems to a unified cloud-edge platform. He explains how aligning system, talent, and process modernizations allowed Tesco to scale mission-critical retail operations to millions of customers, while sharing practical lessons on build vs. buy, cloud cost management, and preparing for agentic commerce.

Recent findings suggest that jayesh Bhayani is Senior Engineering Director at Tesco, playing a central role in leading technology strategy and shaping business direction. His work focuses on creating strategic clarity, architectural direction, and organizational alignment needed for the business to compete at pace in an increasingly disruptive retail environment, driving enterprise scale and agentic commerce readiness.

Industry observers note that software is changing the world. QCon London empowers software development by facilitating the spread of knowledge and innovation in the developer community. A practitioner-driven conference, QCon is designed for technical team leads, architects, engineering directors, and project managers who influence innovation in their teams.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness.

Jayesh Bhayani: I'm going to spend some time in sharing our learnings of transformation at scale at Tesco. That's why modernizing technology at Tesco. How it has changed the culture, not just within the company, along with systems, but enabled the growth for the company. From that perspective, after 10 years being at Tesco, I thought it would be good to share the learnings we had from here and how we are looking at the future.

It has been revealed that I was in California, in Silicon Valley, for about 25 years, when Tesco reached out to me, saying, would you like to work at Tesco? I had got no concept of Tesco, because I had never come to London before that. When I looked at the website, it was a pretty basic website. The outside-in perspective, when you look at the website of a large grocery chain, feels like there is no technology. This went on for a few months. After that, they convinced me to talk to a few people in the technology department. The state that this technology was, and what was needed for growth and the transformation that was needed at scale, was what motivated me and my wife. We were empty nesters already by that time. We decided, why not? Came here. Just around that time, Trump got elected. We felt even better.

It has been revealed that first of all, some context into how large Tesco is. There are about 5,000 stores. Some of them are super. Some of them are medium. Some of them are small. They are across five different countries. We used to be in Asia as well, when I started 10 years back, in Thailand, Malaysia. We divested those businesses. We are still in five countries. We have 20 distribution centers. We have 25 million customers. That's almost one-third of the UK population. That's not small. We have 350,000 colleagues across our stores. Out of that, maybe around 15,000 in head office. Out of that, around 6,000 in technology. Again, it's major. It's big operations, large number of colleagues. We do around 50 million baskets. Not number of transactions, the baskets, which means the orders across our estate in our stores. We do 1.3 million online orders in a week. When COVID came, many companies talk about scale.

When COVID happened, when entire business shifted towards online, our challenge was to double the number of online slots that we can make available for our customers. By that time, for the e-commerce part, our platform was already live. When we doubled it, that's equivalent of putting almost three other competitor companies online in one month. Many companies stopped taking orders. Many companies stopped signing customers. We doubled it in a month. That again demonstrates the scale. Fifty million cases through supply chain, huge. We are not even talking about number of miles the trucks travel and the logistics within the distribution center. We do 4.5 billion calls a day. We have 98% UK coverage when I talk about 25 million customers, but coverage-wise in terms of online business, that can cover the entire geography of UK. We cover almost 98%, which means you can have your home delivery of grocery done in 98% of the UK.

Recent findings suggest that tills, as we call it here in the UK, POS systems, as called in many other countries, almost 50,000. That's just POS devices. We are not talking about all other thousands and tens of thousands of handheld devices that run on the same platform. That's just the context, because that sets a very different tone for the kind of technology, how mission-critical technology becomes. Then driving transformation through that is quite challenging, because I worked at startups. I've worked at mid-size companies. I had my own startup. Being in California and not having a startup is a crime. I tried that, too. I worked at Yahoo for 10 years. I worked at large companies, worked at startups. Tesco is yet another scale. I wanted to reflect here, because it drives quite a lot of complexities in decision-making of what would you do with your transformation and technology choices.

This goes beyond retail. Any industry that has got physical estate, digital, and real-time operations will face these complexities. That's where we learned about being both efficient and effective. Efficient is do things well, fast. Effective, do good things, which are more effective. A slight difference in nuances. You can be doing fast all the things, but if those are not the right things, you are chasing wrong goals. Do the right things and do things the right way, efficiency and effectiveness. I wanted to share here, this is not just about retail. This will apply to many of the industries who operate at that kind of scale and complexity.

In a recent development, let's start as to why. Ten years back, why did we need transformation? It was quite a poor state within technology I'm talking. When they talked about a large grocery company and I was thinking there is no technology inside, there was a lot of technology, but it was very siloed. Multiple technology stacks tied to historical business structures. When I'm talking siloed, this is not just, store had a POS system and e-commerce had something else. I'm talking multiple stacks within online or e-commerce business itself. Grocery, its entire stack. We had marketplace back then, completely different stack. One Microsoft, .NET, one Oracle. F&F, our clothing, Tesco wine. Customers across these, forget having single account, did not even have single login. Jayesh@groceryhomeshopping is different than Jayesh@marketplace, is different than Jayesh@f&f. We had no single customer view, no data platforms, no product management, nothing. It was that fragmented. There was no single identity, as I just explained.

According to recent reports, no single source of truth for stock or pricing. From that perspective, when you have multiple monolithic systems running in private data centers, we were not in public cloud back then. It was not even private data cloud. It was just a bunch of machines. You would be lucky if you asked for a server and you get a server in two months. That was the state. Decades old POS system, 20 years old software running on our POS systems in the stores, completely batch oriented. You couldn't connect to them. The deployments were the engineers would go with the floppy disk and then will deploy the software in the stores. Third-party solutions, not just third-party solutions, they were heavily customized, because when you are at the scale of Tesco, you can demand saying, I need a slightly different thing in your software. Sounds good initially. Then you're locked in with a very customized version of vendor solution for multiple years.

It has been revealed that we had software running from vendor solutions that were at least a decade old. You can't even upgrade them. Then heavily outsourced resources as well. These were where we had lots of consulting firms providing resources for us. Not a good culture, not good quality. You can imagine what the landscape was when we started 10 years back. At the scale of Tesco, that becomes quite complex to say, how do you find your journey through that?

In a recent development, that got us the imperative for change, saying we definitely need omnichannel experience, because customer expectations were moving very fast. The old style of doing business was not working. Technology was not helping business. Business had all the motivation to change. Technology was stuck. We had hit the wall, literally. Global coherence across physical and digital estate, both. Rapid change cycles. Back then, as I noted, if you talked to a vendor and asked for a solution in our POS systems, it would be six months for minor changes. Regression on top of that, so three things would be broken. You do the testing, and they charge you for fixing the bugs again. It would be six to nine months before you could get anything out on our Tills or POS systems in stores. Forget e-commerce. Then along with that, of course, we needed higher reliability, higher capability. We needed omnichannel experience, higher security, everything.

It needed more capability and capacity, both. That led to us chasing from fragmented stacks to unified platforms that could serve all our channels across all our markets and develop a multi-tenant platform. That's what we developed. It was called only platform. Sometimes platform terms are confusing. I'm not talking just the tech platform. I'm talking about the retail platform that runs our business. We'll talk about tech platform as well. That's part of our learning as to how tech platforms are super notable if you don't start early. When we started, it was a retail platform to say, how do we now enable all these businesses and develop the retail platform?

In a recent development, where are we now? All of our entire UK business and Republic of Ireland business runs on this platform, 100%. We are making inroads in our Central European businesses. There are multiple countries there. They all have their nuances. The trust in technology is much higher. Technology strategy is very well integrated with the business strategy. It's not like service-oriented mindset of say, we just need three things. Go ahead and can you build it? That's how the siloed happened long time back. We'll talk about that in our transformation journey. As I noted, the platform is much more scalable but also capable. That's where we are now. We'll talk about how we are looking into the future of agentic commerce from that perspective. Technology has become an integral part of the entire business ecosystem. It's no longer a separate unit that sits in a corner and gets three orders to say, can you develop this for us?

In a recent development, this I describe in my own language. Let's now talk about the journey of transformation. Most companies most people assume that when you talk about transformation, you're talking about system transformation, which is, develop the platforms. We'll talk more about that. That's what I talked about until now. That's not enough. What we had to do along with that was talent transformation. Was very service-oriented mindset, as I mentioned. Most of the development was outsourced. We had to completely change our career paths, the titles within that, the job definitions within that, and completely transform the talent internally. When you want to insource that, that's a huge task. Back then we were only across two different locations, UK and India. As part of this transformation, we started two more, Hungary and Poland, because we had to scale and we needed good talent. The combination of that was required. As I noted, the career frameworks were redefined across product, engineering, and program.

Product did not exist. Product management did not exist back then. It was only program and mostly service engineering. The right org structure is super important as part of that as well. You can have talent, but if they're not set up in the right organization, it does not work. It generally should map the business domains and the business structure. For example, in Tesco, there are four major business units, supply chain and distribution, commercial unit where you decide as to, should we sell potatoes and tomatoes that leads to almost a ranging of 40,000, 100,000 SKUs saying what are we going to sell across our estate? What should be the price of that? What should be the cost of that? What kind of promotion should we run? What kind of store design should be there? How many aisles should be there? Which product goes in which aisle? That's completely very complex business.

According to recent reports, that's all trading decisions. Channels, which is where online and stores where customers actually buy things. Then customer area, which is mostly loyalty programs and stuff like that. We had to mimic that within technology to say we are going to completely map ourselves into how the manufacturer is laid out. You can't run your own ship in a large company and say that we are just different. That doesn't work. Because if you're not sustainable, transformation will not work. That's talent transformation, and we had to change recruitment processes well along with that. The third pillar of this one was process transformation. You can have the right talent, you have the right motivation because you need good challenges for right talent, which is system transformation. If your processes are not conducive, then that fails. The reason why we had silos, not that anything is wrong with program management. We still have hundreds of program managers, but the role of program manager was very different.

Some business person would have a favorite person in technology, as I stated, it was a phone call away. No one knew about technology. They will talk to a program person and say, can you get this done? They will run around, talk to a bunch of service engineers, outsource it, comes back a solution. The silo gets deeper and deeper and deeper. We had to establish that from program led, we are going to be an agile product-driven manufacturer. We develop products, not just solutions. We'll talk more about some of these, mostly in the systems area. I'll refer to a couple other things as needed, because today is just a teaser of the transformation. I'm trying to compress 10 years of our learnings.

Sources indicate that that led to, in the system transformation, what's the strategic framework? One of the very early things we had to decide was build and buy. Build versus buy, many people call it, we call it build and buy. Why? Because while we wanted to insource and build the platform internally with insource resources, you will need to buy many technologies along with that. What we said was, we'll always tend towards building things which are core differentiator for our business. That's how we will win. Something that is not a core differentiator, we'll just buy. Most of the enabling function, as we call it internally, which is back-office applications like people system, finance system, everything, they're not a core differentiator. The retail platform is a core differentiator, including the POS system that runs on every single Tills. You go to Tesco, that's our homegrown system. When you use your scan-as-you-shop device, some of you might be shopping in Tesco, you use those handheld devices, completely synced, runs on the same platform.

According to recent reports, every single device runs on our platform. Cameras runs on our platform. Everything runs on our platform. Those are the core differentiator. Where we buy, platform integration is a must. That's how we say. Platform and domain boundaries. Now, centralization versus decentralization. The reason why I mentioned this here is if you're going through this space, and now even more so, 10 years on it's a different world with the agentic workforce that's coming. You can't centralize things. Gone are the days of change control board, architectural board, queue up in front of those pedestals and get your design reviewed and get your code reviewed and everything. We had to decentralize that. That's where we had to come up with very clear domain boundaries, good set of standards. Freedom within the guardrail, that's how we call it. Freedom within the framework with those guardrails to say how are we going to do it, and then you can decentralize that.

Tech excellence. Tech excellence is not just tech debt. We call it tech excellence, because it's proactive as well. It is not just, do we have a few bugs that we need to do? Or, do we need to patch our operating systems? Of course, yes. How are you taking care that you're not going to face into those challenges on an ongoing basis? Back then, there was no concept of total loss recovery. How do you blueprint for total loss recovery? This is not DR. DR is basic. When you're talking about total loss recovery, it's a completely different ballgame. The kinds of capabilities you need for that, we start to put that into tech excellence. Because it's very easily assumed, even within technology, and I'm not talking outside technology. Of course, business teams don't have that level of understanding. Even within technology, anyone who is not in engineering will assume that this gets done by some engineers who had a good coffee on a good day on the side of their desk.

It doesn't happen that way. You have to dedicate time for that. You have to dedicate focus for that. That requires education. Outside engineering, that requires education. Outside technology, as well, at some point. Where now our business leaders talk about tech excellence saying, are you sure it's built right? It's needed. That's the cultural change we are talking about. That creates the framework for a much faster pace of delivery and clear ownership, as I mentioned, with the clear domain boundaries, and strong and long-term resilience.

It has been revealed that that strategic framework gave us, what are the core tenets of our platform? Only customer is not enough. Yes, we are driven by customer. That drives our business. If you only think about customers, that's not enough. For the size of Tesco, when you've got almost half a million people working for you, colleague experience is equally needed. All the systems that we run in our stores, the operational systems that we run for our business operations, everything needed to be transformed, not just the customer-facing applications. Partners, we had very poor rating from our suppliers back then. We had to establish the trust, but also build the systems to make sure that our suppliers, partners, people who give us potatoes and tomatoes to sell for grocery, I'm referring to those partners, not tech partners, we had to improve experience for that. Reuse across multiple different markets and business units.

Offline operations. When you are talking about thousands of edge devices working in your stores, one of the most critical requirements for us is a network can be flaky. Because if you get in the business of replacing network of your entire thing, you might be spending hundreds of millions. Grocery is a very low margin business, it's around 4%. Some are 3%, some are 4%, some are 4.5%. It's a very low margin business. Every penny that you spend counts, goes in your P&L. Cyber risk and compliance built-in into the platform. Super crucial. This is where we had to innovate across all three public clouds. We did create private cloud, not just a server sitting in our data centers, and edge platform as well. As I was just referring to low margin business, cost is a feature for us, not a constraint. We don't see cost as a constraint.

It has been revealed that it's a very different mindset. As part of one of our learnings, we'll go through the learnings, but since we are talking about that, when we jumped into public cloud, and this now will apply into agentic code development as well, and we are thinking through that. The value that gets created against the cost that you might be spending, you've got to be very careful about that. We were spending upwards of £50 million, £60 million on public cloud. I'm talking four, five years back. It was growing exponentially. If you don't control that, then you've got £50 billion business, which was back then, with 4% margin, you're talking about £2 billion. When you talk £100 million of just cloud cost, I'm not talking our salaries, I'm not talking about entire technology department, this is just cloud cost. You can imagine how much P&L you are impacting at that level. It's the responsibility of the technology department to say, how do you keep cost as a feature, not as a constraint?

According to recent reports, then we came up with good principles for our platform, which, as I mentioned, domain design was very crucial. Create composable services. Data pathways and data quality both matter. You need very clear data pathways as to how data would flow between the various different operating datasets to data lakes, but also data quality across each one of these steps. Security in a layered defense model, all the way from perimeter to built inside. We got tons of different layers of how do you think about security. Multi-tenancy by default, which is, you build the platform once. Even from the physical deployment perspective is the same deployment that works and enables multiple countries for us, multiple different businesses. Build product capabilities, not just solutions, not point solutions. Build products, build capabilities. Then abstractions, all of you will understand that. It's not just for hiding complexity but also when you got mobile applications running across thousands of microservices, running in the data center or in the cloud.

For example, add an item to your shopping cart has got at least 40 different microservices called. Get the identity token, get the product ID, get the customer UUID, get their personalization preferences, get the price, check all that, get the product description. After that, it goes in the basket. Now if you are not creating abstractions that's going all the way from someone's mobile phone all the way to your data center or public cloud, and adding an item if it takes 40 network round trips, you are extremely slow. Yes, it is of course for hiding complexity, but at this scale all that matters. That's what went into our principles because that created cohesion across, as I was saying, digital and physical estate without becoming bottleneck.

It has been revealed that that was one of the lessons learned to say, while you are trying to do that, sometimes it's good to build more centralized capabilities first before you jump into that. It takes a little longer but saves you costly migration. From that perspective, any services that needs true elasticity and scalability we put it in public cloud. Public cloud is a dual-edged sword because when you start using PaaS, Platform as a Service, you get very tightly bound to that public cloud because many of them are very proprietary services. You will never get out of that. You lose your flexibility. As Tesco, at our scale, we like that flexibility. Whether it is when we buy the technologies for our use, deployed or in the cloud, anywhere, we care a lot about saying, does it give us flexibility or not? Because if you're not careful, the license fees keep on increasing exponentially.

If you are locked in, it's a very well-known fact that you will be held hostage. If you don't use PaaS then it's just a compute environment. Why are you in public cloud in the first place? You see, it works both ways. What we try to use is all portable PaaS technologies within the public cloud, that gives us that freedom. It's not perfect. I will not claim that. That does give us an optionality when it's needed. Then, many of our large systems, we are talking about supply chain systems, distribution centers, technologies related to that, we tend to run that into our private cloud. It's almost 80-20, 80% of our presence is in private cloud, 20% is in public cloud. Cost-wise, exact flip of that, 80% of the cost is in public cloud, 20% of the cost is in private cloud. It costs almost 8 to 10 times more for an equivalent setup in public cloud.

It has been revealed that this is where as we are talking about agentic code development and everything, a developer could spend almost £500 a day without realizing or without clarity on what value is getting created. Again, if you step back historically this is where public cloud was almost 10 years back. Easy to jump in, hard to explain what value is getting created. The learnings here that we are talking while the technology will keep on evolving is pretty much where you can reapply.

It has been revealed that then comes the edge part of it. As I was saying, when you are at the scale and you want omni-channel experience, how do I now create a platform that is going to power your edge as well? What we did was, the same platform services, the microservices that run in our cloud, they run in our scaled environment with the right abstractions in our edge devices as well. There is a real consistency of business logic. There is a real consistency from data perspective, because when the network is there it's constantly exchanging data. For whatever reason, if the network is not available, we are able to identify the customer. If you have a club card, we identify your loyalty. We fail in favor of our customer. Let's say you did disable your club card literally last minute and network is chopped off and you are in the store, yes of course, that's a real-time requirement, but we fail in favor of our customers.

We take the payment, not cash, credit card as well. Very lately we have enabled contactless payment as well. That's a huge set of capabilities. It's pretty much, you don't realize the store is running offline. The pricing on the shelf edge, that has to be considered. Now as many companies are talking about electronic shelf edge labels, that's part of our consideration in the platform, saying, what happens when the network is not running. How would you upgrade prices on the shelf edge labels? All this gets very taken for granted. Even I wasn't aware as to what's the level of complexity when you are in a retail business with hundreds of thousands of such devices running across thousands of stores. One part which we made sure was, it's the same team which is responsible for edge platform as well as our retail platform in the cloud. That made sure that consistency was there, that ownership was there.

Industry observers note that in fact, when we were migrating from legacy stack and we were transforming, we made sure it's the same team that owned the legacy platform as well. You cannot compartmentalize and outsource the problem even within the technology department, saying, A team is building latest services and A team will take care of the old services. Never works. You lose motivation very promptly.

This is where we were talking about workload placement. We touched upon this a little bit before, which is, a single team owns that thing. We do use portable PaaS technologies when we are using the public cloud. In public cloud, we generally favor the systems that need scale and they are closer to the customer from that perspective. We, for the private environment in data centers, enabled the cloud as well so that for the developers it's the same experience when you are in the private cloud. We centralized a lot of our shared services. What initially started as, and this is probably a misconception, me being in technology, I'm 35 years in technology, that engineers love doing all these things. Setting up your Cassandra's, setting up your Kafka's, figuring out all the protocols. Yes, all that is true in the beginning part of the transformation. As we started putting more and more production workloads, because early on as part of our talent transformation we decided there is no separate QA team, there is no separate support team.

Of course, first-line support is different, but then pretty soon the call does come to our engineers so they are fully responsible for support of production environment. What started as a good challenge, as a good hobby, learning latest technologies, pretty soon became very onerous. When I talk about creating shared services, so I own the retail platform, I own the tech platform, we'll talk about tech platform at Tesco, and I own the applications as well. It's not as much fun for engineers today to say, I'm going to deploy my own Cassandra, I will do the partitioning, and I will do all these things. It gets very onerous at some point. We invested a lot in shared services to say, how do you now not worry about all these things?

The sequence is very crucial. When we started 10 years back, and we are talking about a company which is 100-plus years old, when we were talking about product development, the misconception in the business teams was, prepared meals in a box is called product. That was the journey when we started. When we started talking about platforms, we had to choose our sequence in the right way. You can never do Big Bang. You cannot ask a 50 billion business to stop and pause and say, we will come back in two years or one year or three years and we'll change everything. Even within that staggered approach, that you see from 2016, this is the real chart. In fact, we stopped counting at 2024, and we had only put significant items here. We had to pick our sequence. Initially it was very far and few in between. We had to develop and create that trust in technology from the business side to say, how are we going to figure this journey out.

According to recent reports, there was a lot of distrust when we started. You have to find the right demand, where the business demand, the customer demand is there, and find the right opportunities to do transformation in small steps early on, and then it gets bigger and bigger. Now we get more demand from the business with more trust, less questions. You say, how can we do it right?

Sources indicate that we have been using AI for a very long time at Tesco. That's nothing latest for us. For example, start with all those business units I was saying, supply chain. One of the biggest challenges is forecasting how much customers would buy. If you go wrong in that one, it either leads to loss in millions or very poor customer experience. For example, if you forecast that you will sell 100kgs of tomatoes. It's in tons generally. I'm just taking an easy number. Except if you go wrong, either your shelves will be empty because customers are buying more and you need more than 100kg, or you will end up buying too much and it goes to waste. Waste is a significant number. We try to control that, and we have done very well on that one. That's a tiny example, but that whole forecasting is dependent upon what's the lead time to getting the products.

Like tomatoes can be supplied four times in a day in our distribution center. Something like jeans might be six months in advance. Then the shelf life could be very different. Tomatoes will get rotten in few days, non-perishable items will stay on the shelf for longer time, so the combination of that. That's the supply chain side. Distribution, how are you going to lay out all that stock? What's the stock management? What's the truck routing algorithms? Because we are talking about hundreds and thousands of miles of trucks traveling every day. How are you going to optimize that? Good for environment, good for company, good for everyone. How do you fill the truck? This is just touching into the supply chain area. Likewise, when you talk about ranging, you talk about customer experience in personalization, you talk about pricing, everything is AI driven. How are we thinking about agentic commerce?

It has been revealed that because that changes the paradigm completely. What I said is agentic commerce is a business decision. Because if you don't participate in agentic commerce, you can be marginalized. Because, let's say most customers are spending time on ChatGPTs and Geminis of the world, and they are going into agentic commerce to say, we can do grocery for you. Of course, they want that. Nothing wrong in it. That's where customers are. If you don't go there, you can be marginalized. If you go there, you can still be marginalized because you're losing the first touch, customer experience. Because now you outsource that experience to someone else. Hence, it's a business decision. It's not just a technology decision. Getting ready requires complete shift. How would you be ready for agentic commerce? Because what used to be the simple SEO and SEM, the metadata and data on your website where the search engines will come and crawl your website and then you appear in the searches, organic search or paid search.

Sources indicate that now the agentic crawlers will come and you need much more machine-readable format of that data so that agents can understand. That's just the AEO, agentic understanding. We'll look at the architecture as to how you will prepare for that kind of integration. You will need the same kind of identity consent and policy frameworks as to how much you can allow the agents to operate on your website or through your APIs. Then multiple protocol interfaces are emerging, UCPs, ACPs. The platform completely evolves from a system of record, that's how it used to be, to a system of delegation. Because now those agents are working with your data, with your services, making decisions for the customer. It's a complete delegation.

Sources indicate that that's the harness, how we are thinking. We are still going to use the platform because the core capabilities are still within our retail platform. If you look at the bottom left, customers, the bottom part is the existing path, existing online channels or stores from that perspective, existing application gateway, existing experience APIs going into our platform, retail platform. When you're talking about the agents on the top, you'll need now the gateways for the agents. How would you allow them? How much would you allow them? Which one would you allow them? The commerce protocol, ACP and UCP, now there are severe regulations in the UK for making payments, not allowed for agents to make payments on behalf of customers. Again, there are differences between the countries and regions to say what is allowed, what is not allowed. Many of these technologies, and I'm talking about both UCP, ACP, we are in direct conversation, are not ready for production scale yet.

Industry observers note that as much as there is marketing, they are not ready. For Tesco scale, again you need very different readiness. We are not even talking about risk and compliance and anything here. I'm just talking pure technology risk here. Then you will have your own sub-agents that might be running, which might be talking to these agents and hence agent-to-agent protocol. You will need MCP for discovery of many of these services, discovery of data. Many of our application experience APIs were built for the applications that we built, like add item to basket, for example. You might need those plus some more for the agentic experience, but going back into the same retail platform. That's how we are looking into the future and thinking how we are going to do that.

According to recent reports, what could have been better is, build central tech platform early. As I noted, we jumped in early into the public cloud and then we realized that everyone had their own version of CI/CD platforms and observability and everything. Now when I was talking to my own teams, say, we got best CI/CD pipelines, and every team was saying that. I don't need 50 CI/CD pipelines, I need one CI/CD pipeline. Portfolio management, we introduced that a bit late, but that where the products are matured when you're talking about 6,000 people in technology and hundreds of products, you need a very good management of where you are going to put your investment, where the value is. The portfolio management becomes very crucial. We use product maturity model for that now to say, our product is mature or not mature, and it can go left and right in the maturity curve.

Location strategy. Most companies, they assume that engineering can be even in-sourced where they are your own teams. They can be in various different locations, but if you're not careful, product management sits somewhere else, engineering sits somewhere else, program sits somewhere else. Try to create self-sufficient teams. I touched on three parts of those transformation, a little bit of each one of them to say what's vital. There are many more in that one. The biggest point was the more you step back and think about it, you will avoid costly re-implementation and migration. That's huge. It spends a lot of time and spend of cost.

Final two slides on what are some of the tips if you are following the transformation at scale. Three pillars, we talked about that. Just system transformation is not enough. Change business processes when required, because they are just organically developed like your technology systems as well. Question that to say, is that really different? Why should four different countries have different operational processes? Simplify operation. Build core capabilities, we just talked about that. Because now we have the tech platform which supports this retail platform for those same CI/CDs, the observabilities, everything, but we could have started that early. Start that early. Throughput is a long game. Today also we get a lot of pressures, and can we go live in two months? Can we go live in two weeks? Can we go live in three weeks? We can do that if the platform capabilities are there. Total throughput is much higher today, but the same thing could have taken us six months long back when we had to develop those capabilities.

If we didn't do that, now we can do 10 such things and we would never have done that because we would have just duplicated it. Evolve continuously. We used to be very horizontally laid. I ran entire engineering of Tesco, all the platforms, all this thing, but product management was separate. Now that platforms are matured, we are going more vertical. I still run the platforms because that we cannot divide. The core platform is still there, but the application domain wise now we are creating more partnership between business and people like me within technology. Evolution is necessary. E-commerce is not just enough. Avoid tech for tech. Communicate value early. It's very hard to understand outside technology for sure. What are you all doing, is the frequent question we get. How come you are so many people? What's going on? It has gone less and less now. Even within technology, it's hard to explain what value we have created for the business.

Recent findings suggest that we talked about the cost, IP and vendor lock-in. We are very careful when we are talking about agentic code development. We are very careful as to what kind of IP leakage could happen. Vendor lock-in, we talked about it. Even when we use many of the SaaS solutions, we ask for those protections from data sharing perspective, from IP perspective, so that we keep that edge of differentiation for Tesco. Then last one is technology will keep evolving, but if you have set the right culture, I mean there was blockchain there, public cloud before that, MapReduce systems, now agentic part. It will keep happening, and the pace has increased. If you don't have the right culture, the right talent, and the right level of trust within the company, it won't work.
