A Closer Look at Phonon TTS. Launching High-Quality On-Device Speech That Tops the Benchmarks.

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1382 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Two weeks ago, we opened up Phonon, our small text-to-speech model that runs on your own device.
  • We've been very happy with the reception so far.
  • According to recent reports, most voice AI lives in the cloud: every sentence makes a round trip to a server.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two weeks ago, we opened up Phonon, our small text-to-speech model that runs on your own device. It needs no server and no network, and what you type stays with you.

We've been very happy with the reception so far. So here's the story of the launch: why we built Phonon, what it can do, the demos that came with it, and how it did on Hugging Face's Open TTS Leaderboard.

According to recent reports, most voice AI lives in the cloud: every sentence makes a round trip to a server. Phonon runs on your own device instead. Your text stays there and the voice works without a network. We’ve also opened the weights. Phonon 31m is Apache 2.0, so you can use it for free, even in a commercial product. The other models are CC BY-NC, so they’re free for non-commercial projects. If you’re building something commercial with those, pricing is based on your number of people, not how much speech you generate.

In a recent development, getting a good voice to run on a small device has always been hard. You could make the model small, but then it didn’t sound great. Or you could make it sound great, but then it wouldn’t fit. We addressed both.

We confirmed Phonon in April and spent the next six months building on it with partners and early owners. Their feedback helped us to shape this release. The models got smaller, and we added more languages and support for custom voices through voice cloning and voice design.

In a recent development, phonon is based on the Pocket TTS lineage and as such uses flow matching to generate the audio which is very different from the modeling techniques used in other TTS systems. This is what allowed us to bring this level of quality to such a small model but it created new challenges while training the models. The training was initially numerically unstable and required several tricks to produce quality results on all five languages.

Sources indicate that phonon comes in two sizes, at about 65 MB and 75 MB. Together they speak English, French, German, Spanish and Portuguese. There are more than 100 built-in voices, and you can create your own in Gradium Studio. Phonon also handles the vital things that most other TTS systems often stumble on, like phone numbers, dates and codes.

It runs on phones, laptops, single-board computers and in a browser tab, so you can hear it right now. Phonon 31m speaks English and is Apache 2.0, so you can build on it freely, including for commercial products. Phonon 40m covers all five languages under a non-commercial license.

Recent findings suggest that the launch came with demos from friends and from our own team. On an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off, Phonon talks you through a coffee brew step by step. On an iPhone with no signal, it counts your reps and keeps you going. A robot called Lamp, from Autonomous, wears a sorting hat and talks in character. In a browser, an offline dino runner becomes a radio show hosted by Rex. There's also a sci-fi game voiced on the player's own machine, and Proust read aloud page by page.

The Hugging Face team built the Transformers integration, so developers could use Phonon in Transformers from day one.

Developers have started building on it too. An ExecuTorch conversion runs Phonon on a visitor's GPU in the browser, Micdrop brings it to Node.js apps, and Spaces like smallest-s2s build on it.

Phonon was downloaded more than 200,000 times in its first two weeks, and it’s still trending on Hugging Face.

In a recent development, the Open TTS Leaderboard is a very newly introduced project from Hugging Face, and we love it. With more than 9,000 TTS models on the Hugging Face Hub, the leaderboard gives developers one place to compare open models and hear them side by side. Across 23 languages, models are evaluated on intelligibility (word error rate of the outputs), speed (inverse real-time factor and time-to-first audio), and naturalness (UTMOS for English and KOMOS for Korean). Fixed-voice and voice cloning are evaluated, with an additional speaker similarity metric for the latter. The leaderboard also has a Listen tab, where you can conveniently compare TTS outputs yourself and vote for the ones you like the most.

On intelligibility, Phonon ranks first in German and Spanish, and in the top three in every language we evaluated, next to models up to 100 times its size.

Speed is where we see Phonon truly shine, as the models top the CPU streaming benchmark on time-to-first audio.

Sources indicate that we built a new inference framework, ptts, specifically for Phonon. The goal of ptts is to get the best performance on a wide variety of devices and as such supports more than 10 backends: CPU (Intel, Arm, WebAssembly), GPU (CUDA, Vulkan, Metal, WebGPU), and NPU (Apple Core ML, Snapdragon®).

Phonon is also available in 🤗 Transformers, from v5.21, as its reference PyTorch implementation. Where ptts runs a single stream on device, Transformers targets GPU throughput: batched generation, full-graph torch.compile, e.g., for synthesizing speech datasets at scale. Being native PyTorch, it is a base to build upon, whether to integrate Phonon into your own stack or to study the model itself.

Recent findings suggest that it belongs to the Pocket TTS lineage, so we first added Pocket TTS to Transformers. Phonon sits on top as a modular model: about 200 lines describing only what differs.

It has been revealed that phonon generates audio latents autoregressively: each step outputs a latent that is fed back as the next input, and the training loss is computed on them. Latents are the model's inputs, outputs and targets, as text tokens are for a language model, so the codec mapping audio to latents plays the role of a tokenizer. Transformers ships it as such: an audio tokenizer, held by the processor next to the text tokenizer:.

Recent findings suggest that A voice is not a recording but a tensor of speaker latents. Phonon never encodes audio directly with its audio tokenizer, which ships decoder-only, and voices come precomputed: gradium/phonon-voices.

According to recent reports, the prompt layout (voice positions, text, then a token opening the audio) ships with the checkpoint as a chat template, as for other multimodal models in Transformers. You write a standard conversation, with an empty audio item where the voice goes, and your code stays the same across checkpoints. The processor then expands the voice placeholder to one position per frame, normalizes and tokenizes the text, and batches the inputs:.

generate returns latents, which the processor decodes to audio:.

Sources indicate that phonon can speak with any voice. Clone one from a short recording with the speaker’s consent, or describe a new one in plain text in Gradium Studio. Then download the voice file, load it in Phonon, and it runs fully on the device.

Sources indicate that we also train custom Phonon models with design partners. If your memory budget is tight, we can make the model smaller. If you need Korean, Arabic or Japanese, we can train for that too. And if your product has its own vocabulary, we can fine-tune on it. Get in touch and tell us what you need.

Thank you to the Hugging Face team, and to everyone who tried Phonon in its first two weeks.

Phonon is our first open release. Try it out and tell us what you build.

Recent findings suggest that congrats on the launch — running this cleanly on an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off is genuinely impressive. As a German speaker I'm happy to see it top the intelligibility ranking in German; the compounding is unforgiving to TTS, so that's not a small win.

One line in "what's next" I keep coming back to: Korean, Arabic and Japanese get offered as custom-training requests. That framing quietly shows where the field's centre of gravity still sits — a handful of languages are first-class citizens, and everything else is a sales conversation. The Open TTS Leaderboard covering 23 languages is a great step, but the long tail of the world's languages is still waiting. Would love to see lower-resource languages get first-class leaderboard slots rather than a custom quote.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Danaher declared a strategic partnership with Microsoft on November 20, 2026, to develop a shared agentic platform for scientific instrument control and insight generation, with initial commercial applications expected in 2026 and additional agent-enabled instruments planned for 2027.

The platform is built on Microsoft Azure for secure, compliant cloud infrastructure and Microsoft Foundry for AI agents that interpret results and guide instrument control. Danaher’s goal is to give specialized products a reusable foundation while keeping the system open to agents and digital solutions in multi-vendor laboratories. That architecture links reuse across Danaher’s technologies with interoperability in laboratories that combine multiple suppliers. For those laboratories, the stated openness extends the interoperability goal beyond any single Danaher product or business.

Sources indicate that one initial application is MetaXpress Acquire AI Assistant, Molecular Devices’ software for its high-content cellular imaging systems, designed to provide product support. The companies are continuing to develop the wider platform. That first example sits at the product-support end of the roadmap; the planned instruments are intended to extend into experimental setup, execution and analysis.

The instruments are being designed to translate scientific intent into experimental plans, instrument setup and methods. They would guide execution and troubleshooting while controlling hardware within defined safety boundaries and with user oversight. The design also includes interpreting results and identifying quality concerns in real time, then recommending corrective actions and next experiments for scientist review.

Recent findings suggest that together, those functions would extend software assistance across the experimental cycle. The oversight model applies different constraints at different steps: instruments can operate hardware within set limits, while scientists assess the recommended corrections and subsequent experiments.

According to recent reports, in preliminary internal testing, Danaher reported, novice scientists conducting an AI-assisted experiment on a Leica microscope took up to 83% less time and up to 68% fewer steps to complete it than a novice working without the assistant. The assisted novices also produced high-quality data and completed the experiment in a time comparable to an expert. The reductions come from the novice-versus-novice comparison; the expert comparison concerns completion time.

Julie Sawyer Montgomery, Danaher’s president and CEO, said: “With Microsoft, we are building a common foundation, so our instruments and laboratories work together consistently, as one connected Danaher. Through context and learning, that foundation can continuously inform the next experiment and the best analysis.”.

According to recent reports, the partnership sits within Danaher’s broader AI and autonomous-science strategy, connecting intelligence at the instrument with data, laboratory workflows and physical experiment execution. Intelligent instruments are the first step. As instruments and laboratory systems become more connected and interoperable, Danaher expects experimental results to help scientists determine what to do next, supporting increasingly connected and autonomous workflows under scientific oversight.

The planned instrument rollout will test whether one shared foundation can support reuse within Danaher and openness across multi-vendor laboratories while preserving the safety boundaries and scientist review built into the design.

As more accents join, we’ll split the Outer and Expanding Circles.

Liva AI collects multimodal interaction data through consumer products used by real people. Because Liva owns both the collection environment and distribution, it can design products around specific model gaps across domains, industries, languages, modalities, and interaction types. This gives it access to natural, high-context behavior that emerges through real product use, rather than artificially elicited or task-based interactions.

Alphabet Raises C$6B Across Four Fixed-Rate Canadian Note Series

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (662 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that alphabet priced C$6 billion of Canadian-dollar senior unsecured notes on November 19, 2026, and filed the final pricing terms with the U.S.
  • The pricing divides the debt into four fixed-rate tranches, with higher coupons and yields on the longer maturities:.
  • Sources indicate that the pricing sheet lists Moody’s Aa2 and S&P AA+ ratings, both with stable outlooks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that alphabet priced C$6 billion of Canadian-dollar senior unsecured notes on November 19, 2026, and filed the final pricing terms with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission on November 20, 2026. Settlement is scheduled for November 24, 2026.

The pricing divides the debt into four fixed-rate tranches, with higher coupons and yields on the longer maturities:.

Sources indicate that the pricing sheet lists Moody’s Aa2 and S&P AA+ ratings, both with stable outlooks. RBC Dominion Securities, Scotia Capital and TD Securities are joint book-running managers, with CIBC World Markets as co-manager.

Sources indicate that alphabet designated the proceeds for general corporate purposes, which may include repayment of outstanding debt; it did not earmark them for AI. The AI significance comes instead from the business growth and capital requirements surrounding the financing.

Alphabet reported third-quarter 2026 Google Cloud revenue of $30.7 billion, up 103% year over year, led by enterprise AI infrastructure, enterprise AI solutions and core Google Cloud Platform services. Sales of Tensor Processing Unit systems were also a meaningful contributor to revenue growth.

Sources indicate that across Alphabet, capital spending is running ahead of operating cash generation. Third-quarter purchases of property and equipment were $51.4 billion, above $42.3 billion of operating cash flow, leaving negative free cash flow of $9.1 billion under Alphabet’s definition of operating cash flow minus capital expenditures.

For the first nine months of 2026, property-and-equipment purchases totaled $132.0 billion, compared with $63.6 billion in the same period of 2025. Those figures place the Canadian borrowing alongside a substantial increase in investment across the company.

According to recent reports, alphabet separately disclosed $28.7 billion of net proceeds from senior unsecured notes issued in the third quarter. For the first nine months of 2026, proceeds from debt issuance, net of costs, were $85.2 billion, showing that substantial borrowing preceded the Canadian offering.

Industry observers note that long-term debt stood at $125.1 billion on September 30, 2026, up from $46.5 billion at December 31, 2025. Cash, cash equivalents and marketable securities totaled $265.1 billion, making the new notes an addition to funding capacity within a large investment program rather than an emergency liquidity raise.

The prospectus also points to substantial infrastructure commitments beyond those already recorded. Alphabet’s preliminary prospectus supplement disclosed $130.5 billion of future payments under leases primarily related to data centers that had not commenced as of September 30, 2026. Those leases were not yet recorded on the consolidated balance sheet, and a portion will represent finance lease obligations.

The Canadian notes add long-dated funding without creating a dedicated AI pool. The central issue for subsequent results is whether operating cash generation catches up with capital spending and the coming data-center commitments, or whether debt and other external financing take on a still larger role in Alphabet’s AI expansion.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde used a November 20, 2026 keynote in Frankfurt to propose European public-private partnerships for chip plants and data centers in which public money, including EU budget funds, would absorb initial losses and attract private capital to an AI buildout estimated at €1.3 trillion.

According to recent reports, the recommendation, delivered at the 36th Frankfurt European Banking Congress, is a policy proposal, not an adopted EU funding program. It came in Lagarde’s eighth and final address to the congress as ECB president and illustrated her broader argument for stronger European institutions when a challenge requires a European solution.

Industry observers note that the estimate came from A Transformative AI Strategy for Europe, an independent project written by experts in their personal capacities. It examines what would be required to raise Europe’s share of global AI computing capacity from around 5% to 15% by 2030.

Recent findings suggest that the strategy translates that goal into 45 gigawatts (GW) of AI compute on EU soil, measured as total facility power, up from less than 2 GW at its 2026 baseline and assuming global supply reaches 300 GW. Compute here means the specialized chips and data-center infrastructure used to train and deploy models. Its investment estimate assumes $34.4 billion of capital expenditure for each GW of that facility power.

The strategy assigns governments a central role in attracting private capital rather than funding the entire buildout. Its recommended €100 billion public contribution would de-risk strategically key investment and increase European-only AI compute, defined as capacity owned and operated by European organizations. Of that amount, €25 billion would come at EU level through loan guarantees and advance purchase commitments, with €75 billion across member states through those instruments and potentially equity investment.

Lagarde argued that continued access to foreign computing providers and frontier AI models makes the upfront investment harder to justify politically. Yet lost industries are difficult to rebuild, and by the time a dependency is turned against Europe, its sovereignty has already been compromised. Ready availability lowers the immediate pressure to build European capacity without removing the vulnerability she described.

Lagarde framed AI infrastructure as a slow-moving risk: the investment is due immediately, the benefits are distant and the costs of inaction accumulate without a single moment forcing a decision, unlike crises such as the pandemic and Ukraine where the price of delay became plainly visible.

Recent findings suggest that lagarde attributed the ECB’s ability to commit early to its euro-area mandate, long horizon and Governing Council majority voting, and recommended stronger European institutions where challenges require European solutions. National governments must instead weigh concentrated domestic opposition against benefits spread across Europe while negotiating with partners facing similar constraints. Her parallel examples were an effective European capital-markets supervisor and European-level public-private partnerships for large technology projects.

Sources indicate that the cited strategy identifies lengthy data-center approval and grid-connection processes, rather than a lack of potential sites or investor interest, as the principal obstacle, and recommends reducing “time to power” through accelerated permitting and prioritized grid connections. The term describes how long a data center takes to connect to the grid.

The strategy also recommends guaranteeing host municipalities a share of local business-tax revenue based on installed facility power, facilitating developer investment in local infrastructure and requiring large operators to compensate for incremental electricity-system costs caused by their projects rather than spreading those costs across households and local businesses.

First-loss public capital could make large projects more attractive to private investors, but the cited strategy places grid access, permitting and local community benefits alongside financing as part of the same buildout challenge. Lagarde’s proposal therefore leaves governments weighing an explicit fiscal risk now against a technological dependency that becomes harder to reverse over time.

Agents with the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) on Thursday arrested an executive at a Canadian cybersecurity firm in connection with an investigation into the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently relieved the FBI of sensitive data on thousands of agents, multiple sources tell KrebsOnSecurity.

Industry observers note that the Fresh York Times reported today that the FBI has arrested a Canadian man in Pennsylvania on suspicion of assisting ShinyHunters. The Times story did not identify the man, nor did a statement on Twitter/X about the arrest from FBI Director Kash Patel.

It has been revealed that one source close to the investigation told KrebsOnSecurity the Canadian person arrested this week was visiting Pennsylvania for a cyber insurance conference, and that the suspect’s company specialized in handling ransomware negotiations with cybercrime groups. Another shared that control over the ShinyHunters investigation has been centralized at an FBI field office in Texas.

An online search reveals the Cyber Risk Summit was held at the Loews Philadelphia Hotel between Oct. 5 and Oct. 7. The conference had several sponsors, but according to the summit’s website its biggest sponsor was a Canadian security tech giant called Cypfer.

According to LinkedIn, one of Cypfer’s “ex-founders” was Edward Dubrovsky, who is now associated with another Canadian security firm and sponsor called CyberSteward. In a post to LinkedIn approximately one month ago, Dubrovsky said he had looks to attend the Cyber Risk Summit with the rest of the CyberSteward team.

According to recent reports, [Update: Oct. 10, 9:58 a.m. ET: A spokesperson for Cypfer said Dubrovsky was not a founder or co-founder as his LinkedIn profile claims, but instead served as a managing director before resigning in December 2025].

Edward Dubrovsky’s LinkedIn profile.

“Looking forward to continuing conversations around strategy & compliant driven coercive (ransomware, extortion) advisory, negotiations and settlement services that are global and truly agnostic,” Dubrovsky wrote.

Sources indicate that federal court records show that on October 8, an Edward Dobrovsky (note the slight misspelling of the last name) was arrested in Pennsylvania on cyber extortion and conspiracy charges. Several of those documents — including the core complaint — are now sealed. But a handful of them were indexed at Courtlistener.com, including a summary of the complaint, which charges the defendant with “conspiracy to threaten to impair the confidentiality of information with the intent to extort money,” and “interference with commerce by threats.”.

The inmate locator at the U.S. Bureau of Prisons website reports that a 54-year-old Edward Dubrovsky is presently being held at a federal facility in Philadelphia. But the court records indexed by CourtListener include a notice filed on October 9 that moved the case to the Eastern District of Texas, which sources say is now the epicenter of the FBI’s ShinyHunters investigation. The FBI declined to comment for this story.

Dubrovsky’s LinkedIn profile states he is the author of Cyber Extortion Strategic Response, a 252-page book that promises to “take readers beyond the ransom note and into the decisions that determine how an organization responds, recovers, and protects what matters.”.

Edward Dubrovsky’s book, which centers on the intricacies of ransomware negotiations.

“At the heart of the book is a critical distinction: communicating with a criminal is not the same as negotiating a payment, and negotiating is not a commitment to pay,” reads an excerpt from the book’s listing on Amazon. “Engagement can serve other objectives, including testing claims, gathering information, creating time, and preserving options while the organization evaluates its next move.”.

In a recent development, mr. Dubrovsky could not be immediately reached for comment. KrebsOnSecurity also sought comment from other executives at CyberSteward, and will enhancement this post in the event they respond. The available court records in Dubrovsky’s case show that he does not currently have an attorney and has yet to be appointed a public defender by the courts.

ShinyHunters typically uses phishing and stolen credentials to siphon data from corporate accounts at software-as-a-service companies, and then threatens to publish the stolen data online unless a ransom demand is paid. According to the FBI, the group has extorted more than $70 million from victims so far this year.

Sources tell KrebsOnSecurity the FBI has been poring over devices that were seized last month when the Dutch police arrested the convicted cybercriminal Pepijn van der Stap in connection with the ShinyHunters investigation, and that charges against principals at other companies that specialize in ransomware negotiation may be forthcoming.

Immediately after Van der Stap’s arrest, another member of ShinyHunters named “Rey” assumed control over the group and began taunting the FBI over data the group stole from the agency’s online recruitment portal, which included each’s person’s unit and specialization, as well as medical and psychiatric records.

In a recent development, last week, Reuters reported that Rey — identified as a teenager named Saif Al-din Khader — had been detained and was cooperating with FBI investigators. On October 7, we detailed how Rey was apprehended as the cybercrime group allegedly sought to extort a navigation and digital aviation unit that was divested by Boeing in late 2025.

This is likely to be a fast-moving story. Updates will be noted along with timestamps.

Your Experts Have Partners. There's HOPE for Keeping Them Together

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1957 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have enabled state-of-the-art LLMs to be scaled to hundreds of billions of parameters, but they come with a fundamental and costly caveat: every expert MLP must occupy memory at inference time, even though the vast majority are idle for any given token.
  • In a recent development, expert pruning is one of the most direct fixes to this memory bottleneck.
  • According to recent reports, existing pruning methods score each expert independently, assigning every expert a scalar importance score (based on a calibration dataset), and cutting out the least notable experts (in each layer independently).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have enabled state-of-the-art LLMs to be scaled to hundreds of billions of parameters, but they come with a fundamental and costly caveat: every expert MLP must occupy memory at inference time, even though the vast majority are idle for any given token. For example, Qwen3.5-122B has 256 experts in each of its 48 MoE layers, and 95% of its ~250 GB parameter memory footprint is taken up entirely by these expert MLPs alone. However, for any given token, only 8 experts in each layer are actually used.

In a recent development, expert pruning is one of the most direct fixes to this memory bottleneck. That is, permanently delete the least useful experts. Pruning avoids the latency complications which make dynamic loading/off-loading of experts impractical; it does not require any training; and it composes with quantization. Given these attractive benefits and the simplicity of the idea, it's easy to see why expert pruning has become a go-to approach for shrinking MoEs. The difficulty lies in deciding which experts are safest to remove.

According to recent reports, existing pruning methods score each expert independently, assigning every expert a scalar importance score (based on a calibration dataset), and cutting out the least notable experts (in each layer independently). These are first-order methods, because they assume each expert's contribution is independent of all others. In reality, experts form cooperative groups. We observe consistent clusters of co-activated experts in our own experiments, and independent work has shown that expert cooperation is a stable property of MoEs and is important for model performance. Ignoring these interactions leads to suboptimal pruning, especially at aggressive rates.

Sources indicate that our newest paper derives HOPE (Higher-Order Pruning of Experts), a second-order method that accounts for pairwise expert interactions. At 50% pruning, HOPE achieves the best average rank of any method, with gains of up to +6.1% on agentic coding tasks over the next-best pruning method.

Industry observers note that in this post, we explain how HOPE works, show where it outperforms existing methods, and walk through how to use it for your own models. For readers unfamiliar with MoE architectures, see Mixture of Experts (MoEs) in Transformers.

In a standard MoE, each layer has EEE experts, and each input token xxx is routed independently to KKK such experts ( K=8 K = 8 K=8 is a typical choice). Routing is performed by a single layer which produces softmax-normalized gate weights gk(x)g_{k}(x)gk​(x) for each expert kkk, wherein the KKK experts with the highest gate weights are selected to form the active set of experts, T(x)⊂{1,..,E}T(x) \subset\{1,..,E\}T(x)⊂{1,..,E}. The output of the layer is then ∑k∈T(x)gk(x)fk(x)\sum\limits_{k\in T(x)}g_{k}(x)f_{k}(x)k∈T(x)∑​gk​(x)fk​(x), where fk(x)f_{k}(x)fk​(x) is the output of expert kkk for token xxx.

Left: typical MoE layer, where each token is routed to the top-K experts. Right: first-order methods rank and delete experts based on a scalar importance score, but the best pruning decisions will also consider the strength of interactions between experts.

Recent findings suggest that importantly, experts in the selected set T(x)T(x)T(x) are not independent. Experts form stable cooperative groups that get consistently co-activated together. This has been observed before in the literature, as well: expert co-selection patterns emerge early in training and stabilize throughout.

This means that when we prune experts from an MoE layer, pruning decisions need to consider the higher-order effects between these experts. Removing expert A might seem fine on its own, but if expert B—which frequently cooperates with and relies on A—is highly vital, then removing A would dismantle a cooperative group just through a single deletion. First-order methods miss this entirely, because they score A and B separately.

Sources indicate that this effect compounds at high pruning rates. When we remove up to 50% of experts, we risk breaking many cooperative links. This is where second-order pruning is most advantageous.

(See Appendix A in our corresponding paper for the full derivation of the HOPE objective).

When we delete a set of PPP experts from some MoE layer, the selected set of experts T(x)T(x)T(x) (for any token xxx) can change. The pruned experts that would have been selected are replaced by the experts with the next-highest gate weights. The resulting change in layer output is the pruning error. Our goal is to find the prune-set PPP (of some predefined pruning budget ∣P∣\vert P\vert∣P∣) that minimizes the resulting pruning error (over tokens xxx from our calibration set).

It has been revealed that unfortunately, minimizing the pruning error over PPP directly is intractable. The pruning error depends on the identities of the replacement experts, which in turn depend on the prune-set PPP itself. HOPE sidesteps this by defining a tractable surrogate ZZZ, which strictly upper-bounds the dominant component of the pruning error:.

Z=[∑j∈P∩T(x)gj(x)∥fj(x)∥2]2≥true errorZ = \bigl[\sum\limits_{j \in P\cap T(x)} g_{j}(x)\Vert f_j(x)\Vert_{2}\bigr]^{2} \geq \text{true error}Z=[j∈P∩T(x)∑​gj​(x)∥fj​(x)∥2​]2≥true error.

Because ZZZ is a squared sum, expanding it naturally produces cross-terms gi(x)gj(x)∥fi(x)∥2∥fj(x)∥2g_{i}(x)g_{j}(x)\Vert f_{i}(x)\Vert_{2}\Vert f_{j}(x)\Vert_{2}gi​(x)gj​(x)∥fi​(x)∥2​∥fj​(x)∥2​ between pairs of experts. These are the interaction terms that first-order methods discard.

To find the optimal prune-set, HOPE minimizes E[Z]\mathbb{E}[Z]E[Z] over the calibration set, which can be reformulated as the following quadratic program:.

where F∈RE×EF\in\mathbb{R}^{E\times E}F∈RE×E is defined as:.

This F-matrix is collected on the calibration dataset, and the optimal prune-set is obtained by solving the resulting quadratic program (QP) with a continuous relaxation (then rounding to binary solutions). Each entry Fi,jF_{i,j}Fi,j​ captures the average gate-weighted output product of experts iii and jjj, across tokens where both are co-activated. Whereas the diagonal Fk,kF_{k,k}Fk,k​ measures individual expert importance, the off-diagonal entries ( Fi,jF_{i,j}Fi,j​ for i≠ji\neq ji=j) measure pairwise cooperative contribution.

It has been revealed that what does FFF look like in practice? It highlights the structure of expert cooperation, which depends on layer:.

Visualization of the interaction matrix F for GLM-4.5-Air (128 experts per layer, 106B parameters total) at three representative layers (early, middle, late). Experts have been clustered to reveal block structure. Bright blocks along the diagonal indicate groups of experts with strong pairwise interaction scores.

In terms of practical cost, HOPE requires the same calibration pass as any other expert-pruning method (one forward pass over calibration data). The only addition is solving the quadratic program, which is non-convex, but can be solved efficiently via a standard QP solver (1–2 seconds each layer). The total additional overhead is negligible compared to first-order methods, as the time for calibration dominates.

Notably, HOPE has a strong connection to Router-weighted Expert Activation Pruning (REAP), a state-of-the-art first-order expert-pruning method. HOPE's F-matrix encodes individual expert importance scores on the diagonal, and this diagonal effectively recovers the scores used by REAP to independently rank experts for pruning (differing only by the variance of expert contributions). The diagonal of FFF recovers REAP's expert rankings almost perfectly (Spearman ρ=0.988\rho = 0.988ρ=0.988). Thus, any improvement HOPE achieves over REAP is attributable to the second-order interaction terms in the off-diagonal entries of the FFF-matrix.

According to recent reports, we evaluated HOPE as an expert pruning method using 3 models (Qwen3.5-122B, Qwen3.5-35B, and GLM-4.5-Air), with 2 calibration datasets (Evol-CodeAlpaca and SWE-Bench Verified trajectories). We used the Tulu3 suite and SWE-Bench Pro (agentic coding) to test the resulting pruned models, comparing HOPE to 4 first-order baselines (REAP, MAN, EAN, and Frequency) across pruning rates spanning from 10% to 50%.

Recent findings suggest that HOPE achieves the best overall rank across conditions and dominates at aggressive pruning rates. Left: average rank (lower = better) across all models, calibration sets, and benchmarks. Right: SWE-Bench Pro performance on Qwen3.5-35B.

Industry observers note that across all conditions, HOPE achieved the best average rank (2.07 out of 5 methods), with the highest rate of top-1 finishes (39% of conditions) and top-2 finishes (67%). In a head-to-head comparison, HOPE beats every other baseline in the majority of conditions.

As expected, HOPE's advantage grows at higher pruning rates. As more experts are removed, more cooperative links are broken, and the off-diagonal terms of FFF become more notable. At 50% pruning, HOPE's average rank improves to 1.58 (vs. 2.42 for the next-best method, REAP). This is also the most deployment-relevant setting, where memory savings are large enough to accommodate longer contexts, deeper reasoning, and more tool calls.

HOPE's advantage is most pronounced on SWE-Bench Pro, an agentic coding benchmark where models must solve real GitHub complications autonomously. These problems involve compositionally diverse tasks (e.g. coding, tool calls, reasoning, etc.) over many turns and likely exercise diverse expert combinations—exactly the regime where preserving cooperative structure matters most. On Qwen3.5-35B-A3B at 50% pruning, HOPE achieved 42.3 on SWE-Bench Pro, matching the unpruned model's 41.8 (while REAP dropped to 36.2, a 13% regression).

In a recent development, notably, pruned models can occasionally match or exceed the unpruned baseline, likely because the removal of low-relevance experts reduces noise on the target tasks. This effect is not unique to HOPE and has been observed across pruning methods. Furthermore, our experiments highlighted that code-focused calibration with any pruning method (including HOPE) did not severely degrade non-coding benchmarks, and HOPE performed well across the Tulu3 suite regardless of calibration set.

Average strength of cooperation (measured by F-matrix value) with retained experts, split by experts on which HOPE and REAP disagree.

HOPE's advantage stems from optimizing over the entire interaction matrix FFF. To understand how this affects pruning decisions in practice, we examine the experts where HOPE and REAP disagree. For each disputed expert, we compute its cooperative score (i.e. its average F-value with other retained experts). Experts retained only by HOPE consistently have higher cooperative scores than experts retained only by REAP. In other words, as part of the QP optimization, HOPE sacrifices some individually high-scoring experts in favor of preserving cooperative clusters. The gains in benchmark performance (shown above) validate that this trade-off is advantageous.

Sources indicate that we created a basic package to run HOPE. It has three steps: 1) calibrate; 2) solve; 3) prune. Our package has been tested on Qwen3, Qwen3-Next, Qwen3.5, and GLM-4.5.

In a recent development, the calibration step runs a single forward pass over calibration data, whether it be agentic rollouts or single-turn traces. This uses HuggingFace transformers to hook into the forward pass of each individual MoE layer. For each token, this records which experts are selected, their gate weights, output norms, and pairwise co-activation statistics. The output of this step is the F-matrix, stored in an HDF5 file.

This command materializes the F-matrix and solves the binary quadratic program via a continuous relaxation. This takes a few seconds per layer, and the output is a JSON file which contains the prune-set. This is technically the final output of the HOPE algorithm.

To complete the pipeline, we run this command to actually create the smaller model checkpoint from the prune-set. The pruned model is a standard HuggingFace checkpoint which is smaller on disk and in memory (no changes to vLLM or SGLang model definitions needed).

We also released a more compact Python API:.

According to recent reports, HOPE's advantage is most pronounced at higher pruning rates (40–50%). At lower pruning rates (10–20%), first-order methods like REAP and MAN are sometimes competitive, and HOPE's advantage shrinks. Additionally, as with most expert-pruning algorithms, HOPE prunes each layer independently and does not account for cross-layer interactions. In our paper, we presented a theoretical framework for cross-layer HOPE, but the results remain preliminary. Finally, HOPE captures pairwise interactions, but even higher-order interactions (triplets and beyond) could provide additional signal, although they are combinatorially difficult to estimate.

For more information, see our corresponding paper and codebase.

Code: https://github.com/awslabs/HOPE.

InfoQ Homepage News Google Donates Agent Substrate and gVisor to the CNCF to Secure AI Agents at Scale.

Nov 20, 2026 2 min read.

It has been revealed that google has confirmed it is donating Agent Substrate and gVisor to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF), placing two crucial components of its AI agent infrastructure under vendor-neutral open-source governance. The move is intended to address two emerging challenges in running autonomous agents at scale: securely executing untrusted, AI-generated code and managing the substantial compute overhead created by agents that frequently pause and resume.

According to recent reports, the announcement also includes OpenRL, Google's open-source reinforcement learning orchestration project. Together, the projects target different layers of agent infrastructure, from isolated code execution to managing agent lifecycles and coordinating large-scale training workloads. The goal is to establish an open foundation for agentic applications, much as Kubernetes helped standardise container orchestration.

Google argues that conventional Kubernetes workloads and AI agents have fundamentally different execution patterns.

A traditional application typically starts, serves requests, and continues running. An AI agent, however, may execute a tool or code for a few seconds before waiting for model inference, an external API, or human approval. Google estimates that agents can spend 90-95% of their time idle while still holding important state, including memory, files, repositories, and active sessions.

Sources indicate that keeping every agent in a dedicated Pod wastes resources, while scaling to zero introduces delays when environments must be reconstructed. At the other extreme, large-scale agent evaluations can overwhelm Kubernetes control planes when thousands of short-lived execution environments are repeatedly created and destroyed.

Google developed Agent Substrate to address these limitations by separating agent state (actors) from the compute resources (workers) used to execute it.

Actors represent individual agent sessions and retain their state, including filesystem contents, memory, and execution context. Workers provide reusable, pre-warmed execution environments drawn from shared Kubernetes pools.

When an agent needs to resume, Substrate assigns it to an available Worker and restores its previous state. When the agent becomes idle, its state can be saved and the underlying compute resource released.

According to Google, this approach lets agents resume in under 500 milliseconds without creating a newly introduced Kubernetes Pod for every execution. It also reduces pressure on the Kubernetes control plane by managing agent lifecycles independently of individual Pod objects.

It has been revealed that the second major challenge is security. AI agents routinely execute generated shell commands, install packages, and interact with external tools. Treating this code as trusted creates significant risks, particularly when multiple agents share infrastructure.

It has been revealed that google's gVisor provides an additional isolation boundary through a user-space application kernel. Instead of letting containerised applications interact directly with the host Linux kernel, gVisor intercepts system calls and handles them within its own isolated environment.

This reduces the exposure of the underlying host while retaining much of the efficiency associated with container-based execution.

Agent Substrate also supports Cloud Hypervisor microVMs for workloads requiring hardware-level virtualisation. This gives platform teams flexibility to select an appropriate isolation boundary without changing the overall agent lifecycle model.

It has been revealed that the announcement reflects a broader shift in cloud-native infrastructure. Kubernetes was designed around long-running applications and relatively stable workloads. Agentic systems introduce more dynamic execution patterns, where environments must be created, suspended, restored, and isolated at much greater frequency.

Recent findings suggest that other providers are addressing similar challenges through technologies such as Kata Containers, Firecracker, and dedicated sandboxing platforms. Google's contribution is to combine secure execution with an agent-aware orchestration model and place the resulting technologies within an open ecosystem.

Sources indicate that the wider implication is that AI agents need more than an orchestration framework and access to tools; they need their own secure, stateful, and efficiently managed execution infrastructure. By donating these projects to the CNCF, Google is helping establish the foundations for that next layer of cloud-native computing.

AI in 2027: Memory Will Become the Next Test of Machine Intelligence

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2237 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that an assistant remembers that Maya owns the project.
  • Sources indicate that memory is useful only when a system can decide what still applies, what deserves retrieval and what should be revised or forgotten.
  • Memory is already present in several forms.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that an assistant remembers that Maya owns the project. Then Maya hands it to someone else. The next day, the assistant confidently assigns her another task. It has retained a fact and lost track of the world. That small failure captures a much larger problem for machine intelligence.

Sources indicate that memory is useful only when a system can decide what still applies, what deserves retrieval and what should be revised or forgotten. In 2027, those decisions will become a sharper test of capability than the amount of history a model can hold.

Memory is already present in several forms. MemGPT explored hierarchical context management. Titans introduced a neural memory module updated at test time. Google’s Gemini personalization controls and Microsoft’s Copilot memory controls describe user-facing persistence and choices about it. These mechanisms should not be collapsed into one capability: retrieving a saved record, maintaining context, and updating learned parameters create different opportunities and failure modes.

The predictions below concern observable progress within those mechanisms. They do not attach an AGI arrival date to a memory score or infer consciousness from a system’s ability to retain information.

Recent findings suggest that remembering yesterday's answer is easy to celebrate until yesterday's answer becomes wrong. New memory evaluations in 2027 will put correction, appropriate abstention and the use of earlier experience into the same test. The system will need to do more than retrieve a sentence that resembles the question. It will need to recognize when the past is relevant—and when relying on it would make the present answer worse.

Temporal reasoning is more demanding than finding the right phrase. A customer may have received a refund, a policy may have expired or an exception may have applied to only one case. The assistant has to reconstruct which state matters now. That requires evaluations with contradictory updates, explicit time boundaries and questions the available record cannot answer.

Recent findings suggest that longMemEval already evaluates abilities including temporal reasoning, knowledge updates, and abstention. It is therefore inaccurate to describe all earlier memory evaluation as simple recall. LongMemEval-V2, introduced in 2026, extends the discussion toward environment-specific experience: workflows, changing state, and recurring operational details. Its 451 curated questions illustrate the difference between remembering a conversation and becoming useful in a particular working environment.

According to recent reports, loCoMo offers another important reference point, using long conversations with human verification and editing. Its construction also highlights a methodological issue: generated conversation histories can impose a cleaner structure than the contradictory, incomplete records of ordinary work. Passing a benchmark built from those histories does not establish dependable memory in every deployment.

My forecast is for stronger combinations of these requirements. An agent should remember that a workflow failed, recognize why that experience matters to a later task, and avoid applying the lesson when its conditions no longer hold. That requires testing the relationship between retained information and a subsequent decision, rather than rewarding the reproduction of a phrase somewhere in the record.

Sources indicate that look for memory evaluations that test what an agent does after a fact changes, when the available record is incomplete, or when an earlier lesson becomes relevant to a new task. Public tasks and scoring methods will make progress easier to assess. Higher recall scores alone would provide limited evidence of dependable continuity across sessions.

According to recent reports, teams evaluating persistent assistants should build tests from the changes that occur in their own work: revised policies, reassigned owners, expired preferences, and incomplete records. Check whether the agent updates its behavior and acknowledges uncertainty. Those cases can reveal operational weaknesses that a demonstration of remembering names or preferences would leave hidden.

According to recent reports, more history can create more opportunities for confusion. An obsolete instruction, a repeated anecdote and a useful observation can all compete for attention inside a long context. In controlled 2027 evaluations, I expect selected, structured memory to beat an undifferentiated full history by a meaningful margin. Holding the underlying model and available information constant will make the result especially interesting: the gain would come from organizing experience, rather than simply supplying a more powerful model.

Sources indicate that the intuition is that useful memory performs selection and organization. It can distinguish a current fact from a retired one, preserve the evidence for a decision, or retrieve a workflow lesson at the moment it matters. The complete transcript makes every detail available but also leaves the model to reconstruct the relevant state for each new question.

That intuition is not a guarantee. A summarizer can delete the only detail needed later. A retrieval system can fail to fetch a relevant event. An indexing process can treat a model’s own conjecture as a confirmed fact. Full context may be the stronger baseline when the answer depends on a subtle detail that the memory writer discarded.

The design space is already visible in the LongMemEval paper, which examines indexing, retrieval, and reading choices. MemGPT’s hierarchy offers an earlier systems-level approach to managing what fits in the active context. These are research contributions about evaluated designs. Their existence does not establish the 10-point advantage or the independent replication required by my forecast.

Industry observers note that the most revealing cases will involve updates and temporal constraints. If a customer changed an address twice, a correct answer may need the latest authorized value and a record of when it became valid. A carefully maintained state representation can make that distinction explicit. A flat history can still contain every fact while giving the model more opportunities to select the wrong one.

Watch for comparisons that give structured memory and full-history context access to the same information through the same base model. The strongest results will use unseen questions and expose memory-writing costs as well as answer accuracy. Gains that depend on truncating the comparison history or selecting evidence with advance knowledge of the answer would be less persuasive.

Evaluate memory design as part of the application architecture. Compare retrieval, summaries, structured state, and longer context on representative tasks, including corrections and contradictory records. Account for the cost of maintaining memory and repairing errors. A larger context allowance may help, but the team still needs evidence that the system retrieves and applies the right information.

An assistant that remembers something about you should be able to show where it came from and let you correct it. That expectation sounds ordinary until a memory has been inferred from several conversations and reused in different settings. In 2027, major assistant products will make some of those relationships more inspectable. The practical advance will be a memory the user can question, edit or remove with a clear understanding of where it may be used.

A memory entry is more useful when the user can ask where it came from and what depends on it. A preference stated in one conversation has a different status from a fact inferred from several documents. A mistaken inference should be correctable without requiring the user to discover every later answer it may have influenced.

In a recent development, important controls already exist. Microsoft’s privacy documentation distinguishes memory settings from conversation history and other personalization choices. Google’s temporary-chat and personalization announcement describes choices about using previous conversations. Google’s 2026 chat and memory import announcement also reveals how persistent context is becoming a portability feature. The forecast is for a stronger combined control surface, rather than the arrival of a delete button.

In a recent development, provenance has to be specific enough to inspect. “Based on your history” identifies a data category, not the evidence for a particular claim. A source link or dated record can let the user distinguish an explicit instruction from an interpretation. A scope statement can explain whether the memory applies to future chats, a particular workspace, or actions taken through connected tools.

Deletion needs similarly careful language. Removing an entry from a product’s active memory store is not automatically equivalent to deleting the originating conversation, purging backups, or unlearning information from model weights. The product should explain the operation it actually performs. My forecast requires observable product controls and documentation, not a claim of perfect erasure from every storage layer.

Recent findings suggest that the reason for expecting progress is practical as much as ethical. An assistant cannot become a dependable long-term collaborator if its user cannot repair the state on which it acts. Corrections are part of operating the system. A polished interface that displays memories while leaving their origins and downstream use unexplained would meet only a portion of that need.

In a recent development, watch for memory interfaces that connect a retained entry to an inspectable source, allow correction or deletion, and explain where the information may be reused. These capabilities should work together for an individual entry. A general memory summary or a whole-history delete control would leave crucial questions about provenance and scope unresolved.

Before deploying persistent assistants, establish how employees can inspect and correct what the system retains. Ask suppliers to distinguish active memory, source conversations, and other retained records, and explain the scope of each control. Those answers will help the business assign responsibility for maintaining accurate context as people, projects, and working relationships change.

According to recent reports, learning something new should not quietly erase something useful. That is the difficult bargain behind persistent parameter updates and neural memory. I expect bounded 2027 progress on substantial models: a clear gain on new knowledge while performance on established evaluations remains largely intact. Such a result would be interesting precisely because it preserves the constraint. Removing the old tests would make improvement easier to claim and much less meaningful.

This is a narrower claim than a system learning every task indefinitely. Updating a model with newly introduced experience can interfere with capabilities it already has. A convincing result has to measure both acquisition and retention across repeated updates, with the compute required to perform those updates made visible.

Industry observers note that the Titans paper studies neural long-term memory and test-time memorization. MIRAS frames a family of sequence models through choices about associative memory, learning objectives, retention, and optimization. Google’s research explanation makes clear that this work concerns particular architectures and memory mechanisms. It should not be presented as evidence that every deployed language model continuously changes its core knowledge.

The more recent sleep-framework announcement, published October 27, 2026, describes alternating active processing with offline consolidation into pre-allocated memory components. It reports a research approach to acquiring information while mitigating forgetting. The name is a computational analogy; the framework operates through a fixed architecture and specified update rules.

Industry observers note that these directions make the forecast plausible, but the evidence remains early and strongly dependent on experimental design. A system can appear to learn because its evaluation questions resemble its update examples. It can preserve an average score while losing a small but key capability. It can also spend so much additional compute consolidating experience that the gain is unattractive for a real deployment. Independent reproduction and separate reporting of old and latest performance are essential.

In a recent development, follow independently reproducible experiments that report latest learning and retained capabilities separately across repeated updates. Compute costs, contamination checks, and performance on older tasks will be essential context. Improvements on newly taught material accompanied by losses elsewhere would show that the acquisition-and-retention trade-off remains substantial, even if the headline learning score rises.

Sources indicate that R&D teams and model vendors should distinguish a promising learning mechanism from a deployment-ready enhancement process. Any pilot needs regression tests, controlled update data, version tracking, and a way to recover an earlier state. Product plans should depend on demonstrated acquisition, retention, and operating costs rather than an assumption that continuous adaptation will work reliably across all customer tasks.

Recent findings suggest that A useful memory system has to be selective enough to avoid drowning in experience and revisable enough to survive a changing world. Its mistakes will often look mundane: an old preference, the wrong owner, a remembered exception applied too broadly. Those are revealing failures. They show whether an assistant can turn a history of interactions into sound judgment about the next one.

Sources indicate that unite.AI may receive compensation when you use links to products we review. This does not influence our editorial evaluations. Read our affiliate disclosure.

A team can leave a workshop with a wall full of ideas and still have no usable record of what it decided. Miro and Notion help at different points in that journey. Miro is our choice for visual thinking and facilitated collaboration. Notion is our recommendation for keeping decisions, documents, and ongoing aims useful after the meeting.

It has been revealed that both feature in our best AI collaboration tools guide. The crucial choice is whether your team needs a shared canvas to develop its thinking or a structured workspace to preserve and use it.

Miro gives a group a shared surface on which to make a problem visible. A customer journey can sit beside research notes, a process map, and competing proposals. The arrangement matters: colleagues can see relationships that would be harder to follow across separate documents. That makes Miro especially useful before the answer is settled.

Industry observers note that its diagramming tools support flowcharts and technical diagrams, while presentation and facilitation features help a group work through material together. Miro also includes Docs, Tables, timelines, and Kanban formats on the canvas. It can carry a workshop into a plan without requiring every result to be exported immediately.

Official Miro guide to using its AI canvas.

In a recent development, we recommend Miro for product discovery, design workshops, process improvement, and technical discussions where seeing the system helps people understand it. The tradeoff is the freedom of the canvas. A sprawling board needs clear frames, ownership, and a useful conclusion; otherwise colleagues return to a large collection of objects without knowing where to start.

According to recent reports, notion starts with a page rather than a canvas. That page can hold a proposal, a decision, an onboarding guide, or a database view showing the tasks connected to it. The result suits work that people need to read, update, and find again. A well-maintained product brief stays useful long after the discussion that created it.

Recent findings suggest that the strength is the connection between explanation and structure. A research database can link to a roadmap; a roadmap item can link to its specification and meeting notes. Notion’s wiki tools add a stronger home for shared knowledge, including page ownership and verification. Its project features also include subtasks, dependencies, and timelines.

Official Notion introduction to projects and tasks.

Sources indicate that we prefer Notion for a firm handbook, an editorial operation, or a product team that wants its reasoning beside its initiative. Someone still needs to maintain the organization. Its flexible pages work best when there is an agreed home for key information and a clear owner for keeping it reliable.

Consider a product team trying to improve its first-week customer experience. It has interview notes, a rough journey map, several proposed changes, and a deadline for choosing what to build. Here is how we would use each tool for the same project.

In a recent development, our choice: Miro. Arrange the customer journey, interview observations, and friction points on one board. Keep the original notes beside the proposed themes so colleagues can inspect the evidence behind a suggestion. This is a stronger working surface when the group needs to move ideas around, spot relationships, and compare alternatives together.

Recent findings suggest that in Notion, we would organize the interview notes in a research database and write a synthesis page. That is a good fit for an asynchronous review, especially when colleagues primarily need to read the findings rather than rearrange them in a workshop.

Our choice: Notion. Give the agreed change a brief containing the customer problem, selected approach, evidence, and owner. Link it to tasks with a status and deadline. A upcoming collaborator should be able to understand both what the team chose and why it chose it.

Miro can also keep the proposal on its canvas using Docs, Tables, and timelines. We would stay there when the map remains the team’s main working surface. We would prefer Notion when the result becomes an ongoing specification, operating guide, or searchable record that colleagues maintain between meetings.

Industry observers note that if the team uses both products, put the exploration in Miro and the approved brief in Notion. Link the board from the brief, name the decision owner, and agree which task list is authoritative. The benefit comes from preserving the thinking without maintaining two competing versions of the delivery plan.

Industry observers note that for a service-design workshop, a visual map lets participants place observations beside the stage of the customer experience they describe. They can group related problems, trace dependencies, and vote on priorities. Miro’s Starter plan includes a timer, voting, and private mode, which are useful tools for running that session rather than merely recording its notes.

Notion is better suited to the brief before the session and the agreed decisions afterward. It can host collaborative notes and embed supporting material, but we would choose Miro when the exercise depends on arranging, connecting, and discussing objects across an open surface.

A workshop output becomes more valuable when it has an owner, a next action, and a dependable home. Notion makes that transition natural: a decision can become a page with context, linked tasks, and a place for later revisions. Database views help people see the part of the strategy relevant to them.

Miro’s Tables and Docs make it a more capable ongoing workspace than a simple whiteboard. We would keep a visually complex roadmap there when the surrounding maps remain essential. For policies, research libraries, and specifications that colleagues primarily read and search, Notion is our clearer recommendation.

In a recent development, miro’s Create with AI tools can use selected board content to generate output, turn sticky notes into a document, and group notes by keyword or sentiment. This is useful after a workshop: a facilitator can turn a crowded board into an initial summary while preserving the visual material that produced it.

It has been revealed that that context has boundaries. Miro’s AI overview explains that canvas-visible material is central to its processing. An embedded tool does not automatically give the assistant unrestricted access to everything behind it. Miro AI also uses credits, with consumption depending on the feature.

Notion AI is the better fit when the useful context lives in pages and databases. Its agent can help create and edit that workspace, while search and meeting notes support finding information and capturing discussion. We recommend Miro for synthesizing visual discovery and Notion for producing work from maintained team knowledge.

According to recent reports, in Miro, we would select the onboarding observations and ask for a summary of the main friction points, with related notes grouped into themes. The useful result is a clearer discussion surface: the facilitator can see which observations support each theme and whether an important exception has been lost in the grouping.

According to recent reports, in Notion, the next request would be: “Draft an onboarding improvement brief using these research pages, link the evidence, and organize the agreed actions in our task database.” Its agent can create and edit pages and databases within the user’s access. That is the more useful direction when the output should become maintained documentation and structured follow-through.

Our preference is Miro for making sense of workshop material and Notion for turning maintained knowledge into a reusable work product. Neither output establishes that a proposed improvement will help customers; the team still owns the decision and the implementation.

Notion is our default choice for a lasting team workspace. It provides a more natural home for the documents, decisions, and linked aims that people need between meetings. For most teams choosing only one system of record, that ongoing usefulness gives Notion the edge.

It has been revealed that miro can hold documents and organized information, but we recommend Notion for a wiki that colleagues primarily read, search, and maintain over time. Miro is stronger when the relationships on the canvas are the main value.
