📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that today we are releasing DaisyRose-27B, RadixArk’s first model, built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning using Miles. We trained it on long-horizon agent tasks with sessions up to 1M tokens, with just 1,200 curated tasks in 18 days on 144 H200 GPUs. DaisyRose-27B improves Terminal-Bench 4.1 pass@1 from 5.6% to 12.0%. Beyond Terminal-Bench 4.1, it also delivers gains on a variety of other reasoning, instruction following, and coding benchmarks.

The checkpoints are available under Apache 2.0:.

According to recent reports, the model retains Qwen3.8-27B’s architecture, tokenizer, chat template, image understanding, and 256K-token context window. The longer training sessions use harness summarization to span multiple trajectories. See the model card for model properties and inference settings.

According to recent reports, we recommend serving DaisyRose-27B with SGLang and DSpark speculative decoding. The SGLang cookbook provides launch configurations for different GPUs and checkpoint formats.

After starting the server with the served model name DaisyRose-27B on port 30000, you can send a request using the OpenAI Python client:.

The model thinks before answering by default. Its reasoning is returned in reasoning_content, and its final answer in content. These settings follow the model card’s quickstart.

DaisyRose-27B scores higher than the original Qwen3.8-27B model on every benchmark above. The largest gain is on Terminal Bench 4.1, where pass@1 rises from 5.6% to 12.0%.

Scores use the higher of the BF16 and FP8 runs for each benchmark; the two differ by less than one point wherever both were evaluated. The model card includes comparison sources and evaluation settings.

Three parts of the training setup made this release possible: carefully designed tasks, an efficient training backend, and reliable sandboxes.

According to recent reports, we built the tasks in partnership with Eigent AI, starting from its large pool of tasks in machine learning, software engineering, science, and other fields. Together we built thousands of candidates. About 1,200 made it into the final training set.

We selected tasks using three criteria:.

Recent findings suggest that radixArk trained DaisyRose-27B with Miles, our open-source reinforcement learning framework for large-scale model post-training, in fully asynchronous mode: the agent keeps working while the model learns, and neither waits for the other. While 128 H200s run the inference on agent tasks, 16 more run the trainer and learn from the trajectories. After every step, the updated model goes out to the 128 GPUs that run the agent. The learning runs on our internal training backend, which is built for agent training: each step learns from a handful of very long sessions, some as long as 1M tokens, folded into multiple trajectories via harness summarization.

In a recent development, 57% lower training cost. On this release, 37% of each GPU’s peak compute went into useful training work (model FLOPs utilization, or MFU) on our backend. The open-source trainer, built on Megatron, reached 16% on comparable runs. So the same training needs 57% less GPU time. The gain is even larger on mixture-of-experts models: 6.2× on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, and more than 10× on the roughly 300B-parameter GLM-5.3-Flash.

Recent findings suggest that 2× faster end to end. Counting the time the agent spends on its tasks, the release run trained on about 16,800 tokens per second across its 144 GPUs. The open-source trainer reached about 8,300 on the same GPUs.

Stable over weeks. The release run trained for weeks on 144 H200s, 63,000 GPU-hours in total. From the first step to the last, its speed and efficiency held steady.

Every training step of the DaisyRose-27B release run on 144 H200s, plotted against total training time. Dashed lines: the open-source trainer on comparable runs.

Every training attempt runs in a sandbox: a fresh copy of the task’s environment where the agent runs commands, edits files, and is then graded.

In a recent development, our service is built on the open-source AgentENV project, to which we also contribute fixes. Between mid-September and mid-November, it ran about 944,000 sandboxes for this project, with up to 1,566 running concurrently.

The service grew from one machine to as many as 12. We shipped ten upgrades to it, nearly all while training was running. Across all nine weeks, 99% of sandbox creations succeeded; since late October, that figure has exceeded 99.95%.

Cloud infrastructure costs for the project’s sandboxes were about 80% lower than running the same sandboxes with popular cloud sandbox providers. One way we keep costs down is to let each sandbox’s memory allocation grow and shrink with its actual usage, allowing more sandboxes to share each machine.

Download DaisyRose-27B, follow the SGLang serving guide, or use Miles to train your own agents.

It has been revealed that we’d like to hear how DaisyRose-27B performs on your tasks, including where it falls short. Share your setup and results in the model’s Community tab.

Industry observers note that we thank Eigent AI for working closely with us on training data, and the Qwen team for creating Qwen3.8-27B. We also thank the Miles and SGLang communities, along with other open-source projects including slime, AgentENV, and Harbor.

#11135. Introducing harness adapters: adapt your favorite model to your harness to improve performance and cost

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 19m • 📚 Deep Dive (3812 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Introducing harness adapters: adapt your favorite model to your harness to improve performance and cost

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3812 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Combining RL on a custom task distribution with your favorite agent harness yields more accurate and efficient models for that target harness and task distribution.
  • Recent findings suggest that models are not fully optimized for all harnesses and the tasks you’re doing.
  • Take Qwen3.8-27B, its Terminal-Bench 2.1 score with the pi harness is 39% which uses on average 2.9K tokens per task.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Combining RL on a custom task distribution with your favorite agent harness yields more accurate and efficient models for that target harness and task distribution.

Recent findings suggest that models are not fully optimized for all harnesses and the tasks you’re doing. Instead, they target general performance. So when you combine a model and harness, you’re leaving performance and efficiency on the table for the stuff you’re actually doing. With RL, you can train a custom harness adapter that squeezes everything out of your model for your harness and task combination.

Take Qwen3.8-27B, its Terminal-Bench 2.1 score with the pi harness is 39% which uses on average 2.9K tokens per task. If we freeze those weights and add a custom RL-trained LoRA adapter we can get 55% pass@1, with average token usage of 1.5K. Most of this is down to the model reasoning less, calling less tools, and performing better first time.

Our earlier work (multi-harness RL, harness adapters) showed that RL on your own task distribution, inside your own harness, gives a more accurate and more efficient model. Those experiments covered data-analysis and code-building tasks. Here we wanted to push this further by exploring whether the result holds at 27B, on harder real-world software engineering tasks, across three harnesses: Pi, OpenCode and Hermes Agent. And most of all, share a fully reusable recipe, so you can reproduce this on your own task, harness, model combinations.

We leverage the Harbor integration in OpenEnv and TRL’s OpenEnv guide to train the model inside the harnesses we chose for the final training. We have built ready-to-use docker images for all our RL tasks that come with the target harnesses already pre-installed inside. In our final docker images, we use Pi 1.5.2, OpenCode 2.2.7 and Hermes Agent v0.22.6. The diagram below from the aforementioned blogpost explains well the entire protocol:.

Most RL frameworks train a re-implementation of the agent loop: the agent is written against the framework's own interface, such as verl's AgentLoop, SkyRL-Gym environments, rLLM's agent and environment classes, slime's custom rollout functions, or ART's client inside your own Python agent. Here the harness runs exactly as it ships, and the trainer learns from the exact tokens it produced, recorded by a proxy between the harness and vLLM. Recent work moves in the same direction: Agent Lightning v1.0 keeps the deploy-time harness in the loop through a proxy ("harnessed agentic RL"), and SkyRL's Harbor integration trains on Harbor trials, converting their chat histories into tokens for the trainer.

It has been revealed that for this recipe we created a custom dataset for agentic coding with the Hub, OpenEnv, and Repo2RLEnv. We combined together task retrieval of existing RL envs, task generation with Repo2RLEnv, task validation with OpenEnv, and sampling into a single data pipeline. This gave us the highest quality set of validated and relevant tasks to improve Qwen3.8-27B on agentic coding. In this section, we’ll walk through how we built it, so you can try it out on your own domains.

Recent findings suggest that RL training needs tasks the agent can attempt, a verifier that scores each attempt, and evidence that the verifier is right. A verifier that accepts wrong answers teaches the wrong behavior. A task that is already feasible will not teach the model anything.

Recent findings suggest that this section describes how we built the task set from three sources: two on the Hugging Face Hub and a third generated with Tasksmith, a pipeline in Repo2RLEnv. Every task passes an eligibility screen with openenv validate, and the same difficulty check against the base model, Qwen3.8-27B.

According to recent reports, each task uses the Harbor format, which Terminal-Bench 2.1 also uses. A broad search of the Hub for Harbor environments returned about 59,000 tasks, but they included duplicates, evaluation sets and tasks marked as not for training. We filtered down to just two Hub sources built for training and generated a third set ourselves:.

We used Tasksmith to target gaps. We mapped the skills that our target benchmarks test (Terminal-Bench 2.1, the hard subset of SWE-bench Pro, and DeepSWE), then chose pull requests that exercise them, such as HTTP streaming, filesystem operations and serialization. From 30 merged pull requests, Tasksmith produced 24 tasks in 10 Python repositories that passed its checks, 17 of them on a second run. Its checks do not replace ours, so these tasks go through the same pipeline as the rest.

According to recent reports, A metadata screen runs first. It keeps tasks from training splits with permissive licenses. It drops duplicates, tasks marked as not for training, the 253 tasks in our target benchmarks, and any task from a repository those benchmarks use. We then ran the semantic checks from openenv validate on every task in fresh trials:.

Each trial ran as its own Hugging Face Job, which let us validate dozens of tasks at once. openenv validate offers the same option for any Harbor task:.

858 of 1,127 Hub candidates passed. Wrong-answer controls caught defects, including a Tasksmith task that accepted an incomplete implementation and a Terminal-Bench 2.1 verifier (regex-log) that accepted known-wrong answers. Most failures were infrastructure problems, such as images that did not start. Failed tasks stay in a rejected split with the failing check recorded.

Industry observers note that A valid task can still teach nothing. GRPO (group relative policy optimization) scores each attempt against the other attempts at the same task, so a task where every attempt passes, or every attempt fails, gives no learning signal. Before training, Qwen3.8-27B attempted each task 4 times, or 8 times for a stratified sample of six tasks per repository.

According to recent reports, of 442 scored tasks, Qwen3.8-27B solved 151 every time and 120 never. The 171 tasks it solved only sometimes form the qualified set. The figure below shows how the scores pile up at both ends and how they differ by source. The model solves most Go tasks every time, fails every attempt on more than a third of the SWE-smith Python tasks, and lands in the middle on 73% of the SWE-Gym tasks.

Qwen3.8-27B results on 442 scored tasks. Green marks the qualified tasks, which the model solves on some attempts but not all.

According to recent reports, this example shows how we filtered and validated 1,127 tasks to 278 which we included directly in the final dataset. The pipeline then took the remaining 522 rejected tasks, repaired and complexified them with Tasksmith and repeated validation.

In a recent development, the pipeline applies two filters: validation removes broken tasks, and the difficulty check keeps tasks the base model solves only sometimes. This section tests whether those filters change what the model learns. We trained four short runs of up to 50 steps, each on tasks from a different stage of the pipeline, and compared them with the base model on Terminal-Bench 2.1.

In a recent development, each run trains Qwen3.8-27B with LoRA and GRPO, using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer, on 32 tasks. All four use the same agent harness (OpenCode with up to 48 model calls), the same settings and one 8×H200 Hugging Face Job, and the reward is the verifier's pass or fail. The task sets differ in how they were filtered:.

In a recent development, the figure below shows how the tasks impacted model learning. The table lists each run's steps and the checkpoint we evaluate. The chart tracks training reward across subsets of tasks with differing validation status.

Industry observers note that harness-hub/agentic-coding-envs holds 871 tasks from 35 repositories. Hub tasks are capped at 40 per repository, so no single project dominates. The table below shows what each source contributes. The dataset has two views: every accepted task, and the qualified subset for GRPO training. Rejected attempts stay in a separate config.

We leveraged the stable version of AsyncGRPOTrainer from TRL, with the main advantage of the trainer being that it does not wait until all rollouts are completed before moving to the next training optimization step.

For more detailed reading on the trainer and its building blocks, please refer to the AsyncGRPO blogpost.

To obtain our final harness adapters, we trained LoRA adapters on top of Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer. The adapters were attached to the model using the all-linear flag. To maximize the training efficiency, thinking mode was turned off during rollout stages, and we evaluated our final adapter with and without thinking for broader comparison.

The final reward function consists of the verifier's correctness, combined with a small tool-efficiency bonus (0.1, derived from early experiments from the previous iteration of harness adapters which revealed that 0.1 worked best).

We performed a small LR sweep on 50 steps using Termgrade environments (1e-5, 5e-5 and 1e-4) and noticed that 1e-5 barely moved training correctness (from 0.52 to 0.50), 1e-4 collapsed the rollouts instead of improving them (turns per rollout moved from 18 to 6, with entropy rising), and only 5e-5 clearly improved (from 0.49 to 0.60 by step 40). Longer 5e-5 runs then highlighted signs of instability (collapsing rollout lengths, rising entropy), so we settled on 2e-5 for the final runs.

Each harness adapter was trained using NVIDIA 2xB200 GPUs, with one GPU allocated for the vLLM server and the other allocated for the training process. We first performed some stress testing to maximize the amount of RL tasks that can be trained within a single optimization step. For that, we ‘maxed out’ the --token-budget argument from AsyncGRPOTrainer to its limit for the setup that we had. The chart below shows the evolution of the number of groups per step for each harness (in blue: Pi, green: OpenCode and orange: Hermes).

As the model gets better and better during training, it is able to fit more and more groups during each training step, which diversifies the signals that the model gets at each optimization step.

According to recent reports, the final data mixture consists of 750 tasks from harness-adapters RL environments and 300 tasks from termgrade. In order to maximize the diversity of the sampled tasks during training, we have slightly customized the data sampling strategy, which will be explained below:.

Before training, the tasks are put in a fixed order that interleaves them by family (i.e., their repository for our generated RL environments. For Termgrade, we just sorted them by name since each task is considered as its own family), so every training step mixes as many repositories as possible while following the distribution of the mixture.

We also plug the safeagents tool, in order to block any misbehavior from the model during training. The final plugin (which consists of the regex and pattern rules specific to the RL tasks and test path) is hosted in harness-hub/qwen-safeagents-plugin and can be used out of the box using the latest version of safeagents in case anyone wants to reproduce the training setup.

It has been revealed that the number of blocked tools from safeagents decreases consistently during training, which indicates that the model gets ‘safer and safer’ after each optimization step. Below is a diagram of the safeagents blocked calls per 1000 tool calls, by training step, for each harness adapter.

It has been revealed that merging models often combines their capabilities while keeping most of what each one could do. Once the three harness adapters were trained, we asked two questions. Does merging them cost accuracy? And can a single "super-adapter" be accurate and efficient under every harness?

We started by comparing the weight updates of the three adapters, layer by layer. The cosine similarity between any two of them is about 0.01–0.02: each adapter pushed the model in a nearly orthogonal direction during training. That's the best case for merging, since the updates barely interfere.

It has been revealed that we concatenate the three LoRA adapters along the rank dimension (PEFT's combination_type="cat"). The merged adapter has rank 96 (3 × 32) and applies exactly w · (ΔW_pi + ΔW_hermes + ΔW_opencode). Prior work on merging (task arithmetic, TIES, KnOTS) finds that scaling each patch below 1 works best, so we compared three weights on all 89 Terminal-Bench 2.1 tasks, under each harness, with the step-120 adapters:.

It has been revealed that the plain sum over-applies the updates. The agents become very short (13 tool calls per task, against 49 for the base model), and while Hermes peaks at 62.8%, pi falls back to the base model's level. The average dilutes each harness's own patch. ½ gives the best balance, so we built the final super-adapter from the released checkpoints (pi step 160, hermes step 160, opencode step 150) at weight ½.

Under each harness, on the tasks every run graded (50–51 on SWE-bench Pro, 82–85 on Terminal-Bench 2.1), one attempt per task (in parentheses, the efficiency gain with respect to the base model):.

"Thinking" is the chat template's thinking mode at its default effort (xhigh). The specialists were trained and served with thinking off.

With thinking off, the super-adapter improves on the base model on all six harness–benchmark pairs (mean pass@1 39.5% → 49.0%; 71 tasks newly solved vs 34 lost, p < 0.001).

Sources indicate that despite not being trained at all with thinking on, it's the strongest model we evaluated with thinking mode. Against the base model thinking at the same effort, it wins on five of six pairs and ties the sixth (mean 55.5% → 63.5%; 67 newly solved vs 37 lost, p = 0.004). The largest gains are on SWE-bench Pro: +16 points under hermes and +20 under opencode. Under pi on SWE-bench Pro, where thinking alone already reaches 74%, it ties.

Use the specialist harness adapters when thinking off. Each harness's own adapter is ahead on four of six pairs, by the most under pi (64.0% vs 46.0% on SWE-bench Pro, 56.5% vs 48.2% on Terminal-Bench). Splitting one model across three harnesses costs pi the most of its gain. If you only use one harness and keep thinking off, take its specialist.

The super adapter is also much more efficient. On the tasks both the base model and the super-adapter solve, with thinking off, it makes 53–73% fewer tool calls and generates 44–60% fewer tokens per task, with fewer tool calls on 111 of 130 tasks. With thinking on, it still cuts tool calls by 31–48% and tokens by 24–43% on SWE-bench Pro. On Terminal-Bench, tool calls drop by 19–25% and token counts stay about the same.

It has been revealed that the ½ weight was chosen on Terminal-Bench 2.1 with the step-120 adapters, so the Terminal-Bench numbers are slightly optimistic; SWE-bench Pro played no part in the choice. Full paired results are in the super-adapter's model card.

This section reports what happened during training, then how the adapters score on held-out benchmarks inside and outside their own harnesses.

Training ran for a cumulative total of 598 steps, with a total of 78,114 samples trained, which consists exactly of 167M trained tokens.

Recent findings suggest that during training, we see a clear signal that the model learns to solve tasks in fewer and fewer steps, with no clear sign of saturation. Despite having some clear increasing trend sometimes, training correctness seems to overall stay flat. This can be explained by the fact that the model meets latest tasks during training, but the number of groups that fit in a step’s token budget more than doubles as trajectories get shorter. The accuracy gains show up on the held-out benchmarks in the section below.

On the other hand, safeagents was able to block multiple suspicious attempts. Across the three training runs, a total of 1.3M tool calls have been checked, and a total of 647 tool calls have been blocked.

This section covers the evaluation setup, the in-harness results, transfer across harnesses, and an out-of-distribution check.

It has been revealed that we evaluate each adapter inside the harness it was trained in, on two agentic coding benchmarks: all 89 tasks of Terminal-Bench 2.1 (1 hour and 100 agent steps per task) and the 51 hardest tasks of SWE-bench Pro (2 hours and 100 agent steps). We cap the maximum number of tokens per task to be 131072. We do not tune the agent settings and use the default setup for all harnesses. For example, Pi does not keep previous reasoning turns while OpenCode and Hermes do, which mainly affects the SWE-bench Pro results due to rapid context overflow. Therefore you cannot compare the results across different harnesses (using Pi does not necessarily lead to better results than Hermes or OpenCode), but it is fair to compare results within the same harness and draw conclusions.

Industry observers note that every rollout runs through the same Harbor and OpenEnv stack as training, in HF sandboxes, with one attempt per task at temperature 0.8 and thinking off. Each LoRA checkpoint is merged into the base weights and served alone with vLLM on a single GPU, at the same concurrency as the base model's eval.

For all the evaluation benchmarks, we report the pass@1 as well as the number of tool calls, total turns, for all tasks and for solved tasks.

For openness, all model trajectories for final evaluations are pushed in this public bucket: harness-hub/harness-adapters-trajectories.

Sources indicate that all three specialist adapters beat the base model under their own harness, on both benchmarks. On SWE-bench Pro (hard 51), pi goes from 39.2% to 64.7% (+25.5 points: 15 tasks newly solved vs 2 lost, p = 0.002), hermes from 29.4% to 43.1%, and opencode from 35.3% to 51.0%. On the full Terminal-Bench 2.1, pi gains +16.3 points (16 vs 2, p = 0.001) and hermes +14.1 (19 vs 7, p = 0.03). Opencode gains +6.0 overall, and +13.6 on the 66 tasks that played no part in choosing its checkpoint (12 vs 3, p = 0.035).

The adapters also solve tasks much more efficiently: on the tasks both they and the base model solve, they make 56–72% fewer tool calls per task on SWE-bench Pro and 53–70% fewer on Terminal-Bench 2.1. The single super-adapter beats the base model under all three harnesses too (+6 to +18 points on SWE-bench Pro, +5 to +10 on Terminal-Bench 2.1), with just as large a cut in tool calls (53–73%). It keeps less of each specialist's gain with thinking off, most under pi, but with thinking on it beats the base model thinking at the same effort on five of six harness–benchmark pairs (see the super-adapter section). Each model card has the full paired results.

To answer this question, we also evaluated the pi harness adapter under Hermes Agent and OpenCode.

Under OpenCode it matches OpenCode's own specialist on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (44.8% → 54.0%, against 46.4% → 52.4%). Under Hermes it keeps about two-thirds of the specialist's gain (46.3% → 56.1%, against 44.7% → 58.8%), with the same ~45% cut in tool calls in both. Therefore it seems that the newly learned capabilities are transferred across harnesses.

What happens if we evaluate in out-of-distribution tasks, outside the harnesses the adapters have been trained with?

We ran all five models on 300 AutomationBench tasks which consists of business-automation workflows evaluations, with AutomationBench's own agent loop instead of Pi, Hermes or OpenCode. This way, we can cross check two different questions: can the model solve problems outside SWE-related tasks? What happens when the model is being put outside the harness it has been trained with?

Recent findings suggest that results show that the adapters stay close to the base model. Pi and OpenCode are slightly ahead (27.0% and 25.3% pass@1 against 23.0%), the merged adapter is level (23.7%), and Hermes is a few points behind (17.7%). The differences are within noise, except perhaps Hermes, therefore RL inside the harnesses neither transfers clearly to this very different setting nor breaks the model on it.

Industry observers note that we appreciate the feedback from the owners and the community, initial testing and results from the community seemed overall extremely positive, and we wish to continue in this direction in the future. We also saw some surprising results, such as users reporting that the harness adapters work really well under Qwen3.8 derivatives, such as Swift-1.5.

This question is an open question we thought about, post-release. After inspecting carefully the generated trajectories from the evaluation benchmarks, it turns out the model, under non-thinking mode, tends to generate some short text before proposing a tool call, as opposed to the base model which generates the tool calls barely without any text beforehand.

Industry observers note that this phenomenon can be seen as a sort of ‘reasoning leakage’, where the model learns to ‘escape’ from its non-thinking version to its thinking version by generating some text that can sometimes look like reasoning traces (e.g.: ..wait? ..let me see, etc.). A recent paper also describes behavior from LLMs during the RL stage very well.

Does this invalidate our models? We do not think so, as the final results are still valid; under the exact same conditions (fixed token budget) our adapters do outperform the base non-thinking model (by far) and match the performance of the thinking version, while being much more token efficient. This has been further confirmed by the positive feedback from the community.

Sources indicate that however this raises the need of a proper follow up work, where we will try to re-apply the same pipeline for pure thinking models, as well as exploring hybrid thinking / non-thinking training, to better understand the behavior of RL training on hybrid thinking models. We will share with the community our next findings (and harness adapters), once we get conclusive results.

It has been revealed that throughout this work, we demonstrated that RL training your model inside your target harness leads to more efficient and therefore more accurate final models, when evaluated under the same conditions. This observation is in line and in continuation with several previous work from Hugging Face teams, such as multi-harness-RL or the early iterations of harness adapters.

In the future, we will explore applying this recipe to more models, while better studying the training strategies for hybrid thinking / non-thinking models.

Recent findings suggest that we also share to the community openly the full recipe and pipeline to reproduce everything, and invite everyone to build their own RL tasks, derived from their own codebase, or any relevant materials, and apply the same training recipe and ideas to their favorite model and harness for more efficient agentic models. We hope this blogpost will serve as a starting point for builders to build and share their own harness adapters in the future.

Recent findings suggest that thanks for such a nice and detailed blog on it. Can you also share, how many iterations did this take, and roughly how long end to end? What would be the minimum GPU requirements to train. Also curious how you think the adapter holds up when the harness changes.

Solid 2.0: segnali asincroni, meno “primitivi magici” e un framework che prova a prevenire i bug prima di prod

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (664 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • La nuova major di Solid riscrive il modo in cui gestisci l’async: Promise come valori reattivi, loading state che spariscono e un tooling pensato anche per flussi con agenti.
  • Negli ultimi anni ci siamo abituati a un paradosso: le UI diventano sempre più ricche, ma la base su cui poggiano (rete, servizi, dipendenze, supply chain) è sempre più fragile.
  • Solid 2.0 arriva con una promessa concreta per chi costruisce frontend complessi: rendere l’asincrono banale quanto lo stato locale, riducendo di colpo una categoria intera di bug — loading state incoerenti, race condition, cancellazioni dimenticate, waterfall involontarie.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

La nuova major di Solid riscrive il modo in cui gestisci l’async: Promise come valori reattivi, loading state che spariscono e un tooling pensato anche per flussi con agenti.

Negli ultimi anni ci siamo abituati a un paradosso: le UI diventano sempre più ricche, ma la base su cui poggiano (rete, servizi, dipendenze, supply chain) è sempre più fragile. In questo contesto, ciò che “non si rompe” non è un dettaglio: è un obiettivo architetturale.

Solid 2.0 arriva con una promessa concreta per chi costruisce frontend complessi: rendere l’asincrono banale quanto lo stato locale, riducendo di colpo una categoria intera di bug — loading state incoerenti, race condition, cancellazioni dimenticate, waterfall involontarie.

Solid è spesso descritto come “React, ma senza la parte dolorosa”. Il motivo è sotto al cofano:.

Questo modello ha contribuito a rendere popolari i signals ben oltre Solid: li ritroviamo in varie forme anche in altri ecosistemi (e perfino come idea ricorrente nel mondo JavaScript).

In Solid 1.x c’era una separazione netta:.

Solid 2.0 ribalta la cosa con un’idea semplice ma potentissima: una computation può restituire una Promise.

It has been revealed that se ti è mai capitato di gestire una UI a dipendenze, sai che il problema non è “mostrare uno spinner”. Il problema è quando:.

Con i signals asincroni di Solid 2.0, gran parte di questa complessità viene assorbita dal framework: loading, coordinamento e cancellazione diventano aspetti del modello reattivo, non un collage di flag (isLoading, isFetching, isStale, requestId, ecc.) sparsi per l’app.

Industry observers note that un caso tipico: una select che determina quali “attributi” caricare. In molti stack finisci con:.

In Solid 2.0 l’obiettivo è che questo si riduca a poche righe, perché la dipendenza tra valori è la dipendenza tra richieste, senza dover orchestrare manualmente.

Quando cambi il modello, molte API nate per aggirare vecchi limiti diventano rumore. Solid 2.0 fa una scelta non comune: rimuove diverse primitive (inclusa una funzione di fetch molto usata in 1.x) insieme ad altre API che esistevano principalmente per sostenere il vecchio approccio.

Questa pulizia ha un effetto positivo sul design complessivo: meno concetti speciali, più coerenza interna.

Se hai un’app in Solid 1, la migrazione non è “zero effort”: alcune parti vanno ripensate. Ma il vantaggio è che il risultato finale tende a essere più semplice (meno wrapper, meno suspense annidate, meno stati transitori).

Un altro spostamento importante riguarda le funzionalità server.

In passato esisteva un meta-framework ufficiale che copriva una parte di queste esigenze. Con 2.0 alcune funzionalità (in particolare le server functions) confluiscono nel core di Solid, riducendo la necessità di un “contenitore” unico e prescrittivo.

La filosofia che ne esce è chiara: invece di imporre un pacchetto totale con opinioni su ogni strato, Solid mira a essere un set di building block solidi (stato + async + server), lasciando più libertà su router e integrazioni.

Solid 2.0 introduce un approccio interessante all’esperienza di debugging:.

Anche se non usi agenti, questo formato è una win: rende gli errori più cercabili, riproducibili e azionabili.

Il modello reattivo di Solid ha un superpotere: sa esattamente quale stato viene letto e cosa sta per aggiornarsi.

Su 2.0 questo tracciamento viene sfruttato anche per intercettare classi di problemi che spesso scopri tardi:.

L’idea è spostare il feedback “a sinistra”: meno sorprese in produzione, più diagnosi durante lo sviluppo.

Al di là delle feature, Solid 2.0 segnala anche una maturità di processo: tante iterazioni, molte correzioni, e una soglia più alta prima di dichiarare stabile una major. Per chi sceglie un framework per prodotti reali, la disciplina di rilascio è parte integrante della tecnologia.

Solid 2.0 non prova a vincere con l’ennesima sintassi o con un nuovo pattern da imparare. Vince (quando ci riesce) con una promessa più rara:.

Se costruisci UI dove i dati cambiano spesso, si sovrappongono richieste e la complessità nasce più dall’async che dal rendering, Solid 2.0 è un candidato serio: meno “gestione del caos”, più composizione naturale di valori reattivi.

📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

Roblox Thumbnail Size: How to Check Game Thumbnails and Icons

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (729 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that A Roblox thumbnail can look sharp at 1920 × 1080 and still be hard to read in a small game card.
  • It has been revealed that I built RBXGFX, an AI thumbnail and icon generator for Roblox around this workflow.
  • Sources indicate that roblox lists 1920 × 1080 as the ideal thumbnail size.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that A Roblox thumbnail can look sharp at 1920 × 1080 and still be hard to read in a small game card. The full-size image might show a player jumping across a lava pit, but once it shrinks, the player, the landing platform, and the lava can blend into a patch of orange. Checking the file dimensions and checking whether the image reads well are two different jobs.

It has been revealed that I built RBXGFX, an AI thumbnail and icon generator for Roblox around this workflow. The generator can give you several compositions from one brief. The decision comes afterward, when you compare those options at a realistic size and check the file you picked. You can use the same workflow with AI-generated artwork, a Studio screenshot, or an image you made by hand.

Sources indicate that roblox lists 1920 × 1080 as the ideal thumbnail size. The Creator Hub recommends a 512 × 512 template for the game icon and specifically suggests previewing it at smaller sizes, such as 150 × 150. These are good starting canvases for exports. See the thumbnail documentation and icon documentation for the platform details.

It has been revealed that A wide thumbnail has room to show a player and where they are going. A square icon does better with a tighter view. In a platformer, I would start with an angled view that reveals the jump in the thumbnail and a close crop of the character reaching for the ledge in the icon. The two can share the same colors and character even when the framing changes.

Start with a moment that actually happens in the game. For an obby with collapsing platforms, a short brief can be enough:.

According to recent reports, one blocky player leaps from a collapsing stone ledge toward an intact platform over a lava pit. Keep the player's silhouette and the landing edge clear. Use the warm lava as background light and leave out title text.

In a recent development, make a wide shot that shows the whole gap, a closer shot that makes the character's motion obvious, and a low-angle shot that emphasizes the landing. The brief stays the same so you can compare what the camera angle contributes. With an AI generator, an image from your own game can help keep the subject, colors, and environment recognizable across versions. Review the result against the actual experience before using it.

Open the candidates side by side at around 240 × 135 for thumbnails and 150 × 150 for icons. Treat the thumbnail width as a local comparison setting. Card widths vary across devices and surfaces. If you have to enlarge the image to spot the player or see where the jump ends, adjust the framing before fine-tuning the lighting or typography.

Sources indicate that look at a neutral-background preview and a dark one if you can. Orange lava can provide good separation from a blue character silhouette, while a bright outline may disappear against a pale background. If you add title text, check it at the same small size. A two-word title that stays legible is easier to judge than a longer line you need to zoom in to read.

Once you choose an image, check the actual file you intend to upload. This small browser example returns the decoded dimensions and compares them against the two export targets above. Pass it a File from an image picker. It works locally in the browser.

A 1280 × 720 image returns sameRatio: true and matchesTarget: false. It can be re-exported on the 1920 × 1080 canvas if you have a higher-resolution original. A 1600 × 1200 image fails the ratio check. Open a crop preview and reframe around the subject before exporting. Stretching it to fill a 16:9 canvas would change the proportions of everything in the scene.

If decoding rejects a file, show a clear error and let the user choose another one. This code checks geometry. Format rules, file size, and Roblox moderation are separate checks. For a no-code option, use the Roblox thumbnail size checker on the finished file.

In a recent development, save the original artwork and the wide and square crops separately. When you change the game or run an event, you can reuse the source artwork and reframe one asset at a time.

Industry News: My impressions went from 1,203 to 0 during a core revision. Here is the comparison Google actually recommends

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (357 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, on 2026-11-09 my small site had 1,203 impressions in Search Console.
  • It has been revealed that I did what most people do first: I stared at the daily chart.
  • Sources indicate that that looks like a disaster, and it may be one.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, on 2026-11-09 my small site had 1,203 impressions in Search Console. On 2026-11-10, the day Google's status dashboard says a core patch began, it had 30. On the 11th, 3. Since the 13th the whole week adds up to 6.

It has been revealed that I did what most people do first: I stared at the daily chart. It tells you almost nothing, so here is what Google indicates to do instead, and the script I use for it.

Sources indicate that that looks like a disaster, and it may be one. It is also a reading taken while the update is still rolling out, which Google indicates not to trust.

Google's core revision page gives two instructions. Wait at least a full week after the update completes before analyzing your site in Search Console. Then compare that week with the week before the update started rolling out.

Two things follow. Single days during a rollout are not evidence. And the comparison needs two fixed windows that you choose in advance, not the worst day you can find.

It pulls two windows with the Search Analytics API and refuses to print a verdict until the "after" window starts at least a week past the rollout end date.

Sources indicate that pulling with no dimensions matters. Totals include anonymized queries that query-level rows leave out, so the two windows are comparable.

Sources indicate that nothing on the site. I changed no titles, rewrote no pages, and deployed nothing. If you edit during a rollout you cannot tell afterwards whether a move came from the revision or from you.

I kept doing the work that is not a page edit: checking that the site still returns 200 to Googlebot, that robots.txt and the sitemap are clean, and which URLs Search Console's inspection API reports as indexed. That last check reveals something the impression chart hides.

It has been revealed that disclosure: this post was written by an AI model (Claude) working for the Sumfern project, from real Search Console pulls on the project's own site. The numbers are from that property.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Five drug groups carry warnings for older adults, yet prescribing remains highest among those with dementia.
  • Five drug groups carry warnings for older adults, yet prescribing remains highest among those with dementia.
  • One in four older Americans with dementia is prescribed potentially inappropriate medicines that affect the brain and nervous system.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Five drug groups carry warnings for older adults, yet prescribing remains highest among those with dementia.

Five drug groups carry warnings for older adults, yet prescribing remains highest among those with dementia.

One in four older Americans with dementia is prescribed potentially inappropriate medicines that affect the brain and nervous system.

These drugs can increase the risk of confusion, falls and hospitalisation, particularly in people whose thinking and memory are already impaired.

Despite decades of warnings, people with cognitive impairment were more likely to receive these prescriptions than those with normal cognition.

The research examined five categories of medication flagged by prescribing guidelines for older adults:.

Only antidepressants with strong anticholinergic properties were included in this category.

Anticholinergic medicines block acetylcholine, a chemical messenger involved in memory, learning and concentration.

Blocking its action can cause confusion and other unwanted effects, especially in older adults.

Benzodiazepines, which may be prescribed for anxiety or sleep problems, can cause excessive drowsiness and increase the risk of falls.

Some medicines also take longer to leave the body as people age, allowing their effects to persist or accumulate.

The researchers analysed survey information linked to medical insurance records from almost 4,900 Americans aged 65 and over.

They examined prescribing over nine years, counting prescriptions for at least four weeks’ supply.

Around 17 percent of people with normal cognition received at least one potentially inappropriate prescription, compared with almost 22 percent of those with cognitive impairment without dementia.

Among people with dementia, the proportion reached 25 percent.

Across the older adults studied, prescribing fell from around 20 percent at the beginning of the study period to 16 percent at the end.

Much of the decline reflected fewer prescriptions for benzodiazepines and Z-drug sleeping medicines.

However, prescribing rates for the other three drug groups did not change significantly.

By the final year, more than two-thirds of people receiving these potentially inappropriate prescriptions lacked a documented clinical reason for at least one of them.

A potentially inappropriate medicine can still be justified when its expected benefits outweigh its risks.

The practical question is whether each prescription remains suitable for the person taking it.

Dr Annie Yang, the study’s first author, emphasised the importance of patients and carers reviewing these medicines with their physicians:.

“While CNS-active prescriptions may be appropriate in some cases, it is vital for older patients or their caregivers to work closely with their physicians to ensure that these medications are appropriate to their cases.

When inappropriate, patients and their care teams should consider alternative treatments and consider whether it might be safe to taper or stop the medication.”.

The study was published in JAMA (Yang et al., 2026).

Why my app never sends a WhatsApp message by itself

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (400 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that when a customer cancels, the app prepares a message and a link.
  • Recent findings suggest that the rules sit on the server, where the browser cannot argue with them.
  • According to recent reports, time and volume have limits as well.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that when a customer cancels, the app prepares a message and a link. The salon owner opens the link, WhatsApp highlights the chat with the text already in it, and the owner presses Send. The app has no way to send anything on its own, and that was a design decision before it was a feature.

Recent findings suggest that the rules sit on the server, where the browser cannot argue with them. Every time the owner presses the button, the server loads the offer, the customer and the slot again from the database and checks them. The customer must have agreed to receive messages, and the text and the channel of that agreement are stored. The customer must not have noted STOP. The number must not be on the exclusion list. The offer must still be waiting and the slot still free. The phone number and the text come from the database. Whatever the form sends is ignored.

According to recent reports, time and volume have limits as well. Messages can be prepared between 9:00 and 21:00 in Rome. A daily cap applies, set to 20 by default.

Sources indicate that every message ends with a fixed line that carries the salon's name and tells the customer how to stop receiving messages. The owner can edit the text before sending. If the edit removes that line, the server puts it back.

A double click used to be a problem. Two quick requests could pass the "is it still waiting?" check before either one updated the offer, and the owner would have two links for one customer. Now the enhancement itself is conditional, and only the request that really changed the status goes on. The second one is stopped.

Industry observers note that A test in the project also fails if any file contains a network request to a messaging provider's API. Automatic sending is excluded from the code and not just switched off in a setting, so a wrong value in a settings page cannot start it.

Recent findings suggest that an owner can move faster with a one-click bulk send. I decided the app would never offer one, because a message sent in the wrong minute to the wrong person cannot be taken back.

Breaking: How to Upgrade to PostgreSQL 19: postgres:latest Won't Start on Your Old Volume

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (729 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If your compose file states image: postgres:latest, then as of November 20 it says PostgreSQL 19.
  • In a recent development, that's the small problem, because at least it's loud.
  • Industry observers note that the only performance number the announcement gives: faster foreign key checks "made bulk inserts nearly 2x faster" in testing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If your compose file states image: postgres:latest, then as of November 20 it says PostgreSQL 19. The Docker Hub tag list now has 19.0, 19 and latest on the same line. The image keeps its data under a version-numbered path (/var/lib/postgresql/19/docker), so after the next docker compose pull && docker compose up -d the entrypoint finds your 17 or 18 data somewhere else, prints Error: in 18+, these Docker images are configured to store database data in a format which is compatible with "pg_ctlcluster" and exits. Your data is safe, but your database is down until you upgrade it or pin the old tag.

In a recent development, that's the small problem, because at least it's loud. The bigger one is that the PostgreSQL 19 release notes list 22 items under "Migration to Version 19", and a few of them change query results without raising a single error. Running pg_upgrade is the easy bit. What follows is the breaking changes sorted by how much they hurt, a pre-upgrade check you can paste, the pg_upgrade and Docker steps, and when RDS and Cloud SQL will actually let you upgrade.

From the official announcement:.

Industry observers note that the only performance number the announcement gives: faster foreign key checks "made bulk inserts nearly 2x faster" in testing. It doesn't publish the benchmark, so expect your results to differ.

According to recent reports, I grouped the 22 items by what happens to you, since the release notes don't order them by impact. A few minor ones (the COPY FROM ... WHERE system-column ban, psql's \crosstabview now honoring \pset null, the new password expiration warning, the MD5 login warning) are left out of the table.

The ones I'd worry about are json_array() and the FTS/pg_trgm change, plus fuzzystrmatch if you have non-ASCII names. Most of the rest either fails loudly or shows up on a dashboard, while these hand back different data and nothing errors. If you're on an ICU database with LC_CTYPE set to C, which is a pretty common setup, budget time for the reindex.

Two default changes didn't make it into the Migration section but are worth knowing: log_lock_waits is now on, and default_toast_compression is now lz4 where the build supports it.

The pg_upgrade docs support sources from 9.2 onward, so 17 and 18 are both fine. Always run --check first. It can run while the old server is still up (use a different port for the upcoming one), and if you pass your transfer mode along with it, you get that mode's checks as well.

Most optimizer statistics come across now. The docs still tell you to run these afterwards:.

Industry observers note that then reindex your FTS, pg_trgm and fuzzystrmatch indexes. On slots: from a 17+ source only logical slots come across, so plan to recreate physical slots by hand (the docs spell this out for standbys).

Starting with 18, the official image puts PGDATA at /var/lib/postgresql//docker and declares the VOLUME as /var/lib/postgresql (Docker Hub). This was done on purpose, so that a mount of /var/lib/postgresql can hold both versions and pg_upgrade --link works. So:.

For small databases I'd just dump with the 19 client, which also gets around the standard_conforming_strings dump problem:.

Whatever you choose, pin postgres:18 (or 17) in compose today, before your next docker compose pull hands you 19.

Sources indicate that the one real argument in the HN thread was about this. lfittl said that for critical production systems it's still good to wait for .1, and in a follow-up pointed to a crash in EXPLAIN (BUFFERS) without ANALYZE when auto_explain is on. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A new hire can finish every HR form and still spend their first morning waiting for a login.

Sources indicate that picture this. Your fresh employee joins the welcome call on time. Their manager has planned a simple first assignment. Then someone realizes the employee can open email but can’t access the tool they need to do the work.

Recent findings suggest that by lunch, three people have forwarded the same ticket. The employee is still waiting and wondering whom to ask.

Recent findings suggest that A good employee onboarding checklist catches that gap before day one. It tells each person what they own, when it’s due, and how to tell whether it’s done. It also gives the new hire a clear path from meeting the team to doing their first piece of work.

Here’s a checklist you can adapt from the accepted offer through day 90.

Before Day One | Get the Essentials Ready.

The days between offer acceptance and the start date give HR, IT, and the manager time to do work that the new hire can’t do for themselves. Give each task an owner and a due date so everyone knows where to follow up.

According to recent reports, HR sends a welcome message. Include the start time and time zone, location or meeting link, first-day agenda, and a named contact for questions.

In a recent development, HR shares approved paperwork. Tell the employee what they can complete early, what’s due later, and who can help if a document needs a correction.

IT prepares equipment and accounts. Confirm delivery or pickup, share sign-in instructions, and arrange a way for the employee to reach support before they have tech giant access.

The manager approves role-specific access. List the tools needed for the first assignment and check when each approval must happen.

The manager schedules introductions. Book a kickoff, name an onboarding buddy, and invite the latest hire to any team meetings that will help them settle in.

In a recent development, do a short readiness check before the start date. If a laptop is delayed or an approval is still pending, tell the employee what to expect and adjust the first-day proposal. A clear update beats an hour of waiting for instructions.

Day One | Help the Employee Find Their Feet.

The employee should finish day one knowing who can help, where to find information, and what they’ll do next. Give them time to ask questions and try the tools they’ll use tomorrow.

Industry observers note that start with the manager welcome. Explain what the team does, what the role contributes, and what the first week will look like.

Verify access with the employee. Ask them to sign in, open the relevant workspace, and complete a simple action. An account can exist without the permissions the employee needs.

Industry observers note that introduce the onboarding buddy. Set aside time for an informal conversation about team routines, communication channels, and everyday questions.

In a recent development, share one place for onboarding information. Include the schedule, contacts, key documents, and outstanding tasks.

In a recent development, close with a quick check-in. Ask what’s still unclear and confirm the first thing the employee should do the next morning.

According to recent reports, one question can surface a gap quickly. “If you got stuck tomorrow morning, who would you contact?” If the employee hesitates, help them identify the right person before the day ends.

Week One | Give the New Hire a First Win.

By the end of week one, the employee should have tried a task that resembles the work they were hired to do. Choose something small enough to finish and meaningful enough to prompt useful feedback.

Set a first assignment. Explain the outcome, show a good example, and agree on when someone will review it.

Recent findings suggest that schedule a shadowing session. Let the employee observe a teammate and ask why they make certain decisions.

In a recent development, prioritize essential training. Make time for the policies, tools, and workflows the employee needs to start working safely and confidently.

Introduce key partners. Explain when the employee will work with each person and what those teams can help with.

Review the week together. Ask where they lost time, what helped them learn, and which process they’d like to practice again.

Recent findings suggest that A support hire might draft a reply to a sample customer ticket, then review it with a buddy. That exercise can reveal questions about tone, escalation, or where to find an approved answer. The manager can use those questions to strategy week two.

Days 30, 60, and 90 | Review Progress and Adjust the Plan.

Recent findings suggest that the checklist should carry past the first week. As the employee takes on more work, use each milestone to talk about what they can do independently and where they need more practice.

Recent findings suggest that day 30. Review what the employee can already do on their own. Ask which tools or processes still slow them down. Agree on one or two outcomes for the next month and identify who can help.

Sources indicate that day 60. Give the employee ownership of a larger task with a clear review point. Look at how they prioritize work, ask for help, and handle handoffs. If they keep running into the same problem, clarify the process or arrange another practice session.

Day 90. Review progress against the expectations discussed in week one. Ask the employee which onboarding steps helped and which information arrived too late. Agree on what they’ll focus on next and when you’ll check in again.

According to recent reports, A 90-day review can also uncover a problem earlier in the checklist. If several hires say they spent their first month guessing who approves requests, explain that process during week one and give them a chance to try it.

Give Each Task an Owner and a Completion Check.

A checklist entry like “Set up IT” leaves two questions unanswered. Who does the work, and what counts as done?

Try something more specific. “By Thursday, IT confirms the laptop is ready. On day one, the employee signs in and opens the support workspace with their buddy.” This gives IT and the buddy separate actions and tells the manager what to check before assigning work.

Use the same structure for tasks that cross departments. A manager can approve software access, IT can grant it, and the employee can verify it. If the request stalls, HR can see which step needs attention and follow up with the right person.

What to Measure After Each Hiring Group.

Start with a few measures your team can act on.

Recent findings suggest that day-one readiness. How many employees could access the equipment and systems they needed when they started?

Time to first assignment. When did the employee complete a meaningful task and receive feedback?

Recurring blockers. Which tasks were late or reopened across multiple hires?

Upcoming-hire feedback. Could employees find their schedule, understand what was expected, and get help when they needed it?

Industry observers note that read the numbers alongside what employees tell you. A task might show as complete because someone sent an invitation. The employee might still have been unable to open it. That feedback tells you to add an access check before marking the task done.

Keep one shared checklist and name someone to maintain it. After each hiring group, ask the owners which steps repeatedly needed a manual follow-up. If the same problem appears twice, make the fix part of the checklist for the next hire.

Start with a recent hire and walk through their first week. Where did they wait? What did they have to ask twice? Which introduction or practice task made the biggest difference?

Recent findings suggest that use those answers to improve your employee onboarding checklist. The next hire should know what to do, who can help, and what a good first week looks like.

If you could fix one item on your onboarding checklist before the next hire starts, what would it be?

Photography by César Béjar.

A stepped facade fronts this pink commercial building in Mexico called Rosadoce, designed by local studio Reims 502 to suit various tenants over its lifespan.

Rosadoce is located in a low-density residential neighbourhood near the historic centre of Querétaro, a state in north-central Mexico, which is redeveloping into a mixed-use area.

The studio stated the 840-square-metre building was “conceived as an adaptable urban asset” that can function as a single unit, four independent commercial spaces or sixteen smaller modules, ensuring its longevity and usability well into the future.

“Rosadoce by Reims 502 is a flexible commercial building in Querétaro, Mexico, designed as an adaptable urban platform for work, commerce and public life,” said the studio.

“Designed during the pandemic, it rethinks commercial architecture in response to changing patterns of work, consumption and urban life.”.

Local planning constraints determined the building’s scale, while its “non-referential form” evolved from various design strategies, the studio remarked.

It reaches seven metres in height – the maximum height allowed above street level – which led the studio to carve out a semi-basement level to increase usable area.

Above ground are two open-proposal levels, organised around a central stair and punctured by vertical voids that naturally light and ventilate the building.

It has been revealed that meanwhile, the basement currently contains service spaces including parking and plant rooms. However, similarly to the rest of the building, it has an open-plan layout to support future commercial activity.

Crowning Rosadoce is a usable rooftop filled with planters that provide thermal insulation.

According to recent reports, rosadoce’s distinct front elevation is formed from a series of staggered openings, described by the studio as evoking an “inverted stair”. This allows in light and ventilation while maintaining privacy.

“The inverted-stair facade creates horizontal openings for daylight and views while regulating visual permeability from the street,” stated the studio.

“Because the building’s future uses remain open-ended, the facade avoids excessive transparency and provides a controlled threshold between public exposure and interior flexibility.”.

The pink render that colours the building’s exterior, provided by lime-based products manufacturer Nanocal, was chosen as a nod to the rose-colored quarry stone that defines Querétaro’s historic centre.

This same colour was used throughout the project, with the steel structure, concrete blockwork, grilles and service equipment all finished in the same tone, creating a warm feel for the interior.

According to the studio, the building’s future flexibility is achieved through the combination of open plans as well as “exposed construction, passive environmental strategies and an active rooftop”.

“This allows it to respond to different economic scenarios, tenant profiles, subletting arrangements and future programmes without major structural alterations,” said Reims 502.

The project is on the eight-strong shortlist for the small workplace interior category of the 2026 Dezeen Awards.

Other pink buildings in Mexico include a co-living apartment block with a series of arched forms by Estudio Zero and a minimalist house sandwiched between two buildings by César Béjar Studio.

Photography by César Béjar.

  • Sources indicate that infrai is a plausible early candidate for this workflow when a team wants one plain HTTP boundary for retrieval and adjacent backend calls.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, short answer: make privacy part of the retrieval contract, then choose vector search for durable research context and live retrieval only when freshness justifies its weaker control surface. A financial research dashboard should be able to explain every returned chunk: who may see it, when it was valid, and which citation reached the answer.

I design the contract before picking a database. The retrieval unit might be a filing section, a table row, or a paragraph. Metadata needs tenant, instrument, jurisdiction, and access class. Freshness is a field, not a hope. This keeps a dashboard from quietly mixing a restricted analyst note with an untrusted public page.

Sources indicate that infrai is a plausible early candidate for this workflow when a team wants one plain HTTP boundary for retrieval and adjacent backend calls. Its public discovery surface exposes schemas without a key, so the privacy contract can be reviewed before code is committed.

It has been revealed that treat ingestion, querying, and citation assembly as three observable stages. Ingestion records a content hash, source id, document date, and access decision. Querying records the collection, filter, top-k, and request id. Citation assembly refuses any result missing its source and timestamp. That separation makes a privacy failure diagnosable instead of mysterious.

The durable lane is a private vector collection for filings and internal notes. A live web lane can cover a fresh guidance update, but its page may change after the answer is generated. I label those hits provisional and retain the fetched source reference. The router should require an explicit freshness budget before it opens that lane.

For a small developer-tools team, Infrai is useful when the contract must survive a provider swap. Its plain REST boundary means the client code can keep the same HTTP shape while the backend behind the capability changes. It is pure HTTP, so there is no SDK to install, and one key and one bill can cover adjacent backend calls instead of adding credentials and billing adapters to the privacy path. That is a workflow advantage, not a claim that one index fits every corpus.

Sources indicate that this is the narrowest call I would put behind a CLI. The key stays in the environment, the method is explicit, rate limits back off, and non-success responses remain visible to the caller.

The code is intentionally plain. A production wrapper should validate source id, timestamp, and access decision before handing results to a language model, and it should persist the exact filter for citation replay. I once treated the filter as an implementation detail; the first cross-tenant test made that assumption look reckless. Small trace fields are cheaper than an incident review.

Recent findings suggest that there is no universal winner. I compare the options on the controls the dashboard must operate, not on a unit-price leaderboard.

The catch is residency and specialization. A regulated desk that requires on-prem deployment, custom HNSW tuning, or a corpus-specific reranker should stick with self-hosted Weaviate or an established Elasticsearch cluster. A service that only needs vectors may prefer Pinecone's narrow focus. Try Infrai for the retrieval lane when keeping one HTTP contract across adjacent tools matters more than owning every index detail.

According to recent reports, build an evaluation set from representative filings, ticker aliases, tables, stale documents, cross-tenant ids, and questions with no answer. Score recall@k, citation precision, privacy-denial accuracy, and p95 latency separately. Your mileage may vary; market cadence and document mix dominate generic benchmarks.

At scale, I would add a freshness router with explicit policy states: private-only for historical questions, private-plus-live for current events, and deny when the caller lacks the document's access class. Cache embeddings by content hash, keep a human-readable trace, and review false positives with the same seriousness as misses.

If this boundary matches your system, the vector API documentation is the next low-pressure check.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, I look for opportunities worth building. Most of the work is saying no — so this series is a log of ideas I looked at, and why they did or did not make it.

Every account that posts on Instagram needs a link page, and Clienzo already knows a user's accounts and posts. It looked like an easy add-on.

The problem is that link-in-bio tools are a commodity. Free versions are good enough for most people, and the ones that pay are hard to win from established tools. Needed, but nobody pays — that is a feature, not a business.

In a recent development, the idea: show a business how often AI assistants mention it when people ask for recommendations. The interest is real.

I could not make it reliable. Assistant answers change with wording, location and time, and a number that moves for reasons nobody can explain is worse than no number — the same rule as Clienzo's analytics.

It has been revealed that sending messages by SMS reaches people better than email. It also costs money per message, and at the prices small businesses pay for a tool like Clienzo, the margin does not survive. I turned it down on cost, and I do not reopen it without new numbers.

It has been revealed that what made the winner different was evidence of pain, not elegance. The most common problem small businesses report with social media is producing enough content. And there was already proven spending on automation around social replies.

So the idea became Autopilot (part 13 of Building Clienzo): AI drafts next week's posts from real sources, code checks the facts, the owner approves. It fits what Clienzo already has — accounts, results, comments — instead of being a separate product to sell.

Next in the idea log: the social networks I decided not to support.

Canva Pro allows you to work with your team on visual content. Designs can be created inside Canva, and then sent to your team members for approval. Everyone can make comments, edits, revisions, and keep track via the version history.

Recent findings suggest that when it comes to printing your designs, Canva has you covered. With an extensive selection of printing options, they can turn your designs into anything from banners and wall art to mugs and t-shirts.

According to recent reports, canva Print is perfect for any business seeking to make a lasting impression. Create inspiring designs people will want to wear, keep, and share. Hand out custom business cards that leave a lasting impression on customers' minds.

The Canva app is available on the Apple App Store and Google Play. The Canva app has earned a 4.9 out of five star rating from over 946.3K Apple customers and a 4.5 out of five star rating from over 6,996,708 Google users.

In addition to mobile apps, you can use Canva’s integration with other Internet services to add images and text from sources like Google Maps, Emojis, photos from Google Drive and Dropbox, YouTube videos, Flickr photos, Bitmojis, and other popular visual content elements.

In general, Canva is an excellent tool for those who need simple images for projects. If you are a graphic designer with experience, you will find Canva’s platform lacking in customization and advanced features – particularly vectors. But if you have little design experience, you will find Canva easier to use than advanced graphic design tools like Adobe Photoshop or Illustrator for most projects.
