# I Spent 6 Months Building an AI Coding Memory Layer to Reduce Token Waste

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1174 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • AI coding agents are getting better at writing code, navigating codebases and handling increasingly complex tasks.
  • But as projects grow, another problem becomes harder to ignore: agents repeatedly spend tokens rediscovering information they have already encountered.
  • They explore the same files, reconstruct previous decisions and investigate problems that were already understood in earlier sessions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI coding agents are getting better at writing code, navigating codebases and handling increasingly complex tasks.

But as projects grow, another problem becomes harder to ignore: agents repeatedly spend tokens rediscovering information they have already encountered.

They explore the same files, reconstruct previous decisions and investigate problems that were already understood in earlier sessions.

I spent the last six months building OpenLotus, an independent memory layer designed to address this problem.

While working on a project, an AI coding agent accumulates valuable knowledge.

It learns the architecture, identifies technical constraints, makes implementation decisions, discovers failed approaches and tracks what still needs to be done.

The problem is that much of this knowledge exists inside the agent's conversation.

And conversations are not reliable long term storage.

Consider what happens in a few common situations:.

Session resets: A newly introduced session may not have access to the previous conversation or the reasoning accumulated during it.

Industry observers note that context compaction: When a conversation approaches the context window limit, an agent may compress its history into a shorter summary. This helps it continue working, but notable details can be lost in the process.

Context window pressure: Repeatedly loading instructions, conversation history and previously explored information consumes tokens that could otherwise be used for implementation.

Switching agents: Moving from Claude Code to OpenCode or another coding environment does not automatically transfer everything the previous agent learned about the project.

This creates a familiar experience.

It has been revealed that you ask an agent to continue working, and it starts investigating something you already investigated. It revisits architectural decisions, reads previously explored files or reconstructs context from scratch.

The model may be perfectly capable of understanding the project. The problem is that the knowledge it acquired has no reliable, independent place to live.

Repeated exploration has a cost.

Every unnecessary file read, reconstructed decision, repeated investigation and replayed conversation consumes additional tokens.

It also puts pressure on the available context window, leaving less room for the actual task.

Research into memory and retrieval systems suggests that this problem can be addressed more efficiently than simply providing agents with more conversation history.

For example, a ContextSniper study referenced in the OpenLotus research collection reports token reductions of 51.5% for OpenClaw and 38.9% for Claude Code under its tested conditions.

A separate Mem0 comparison reports 166 prompt tokens for retrieval based memory compared with 594 for naive history, at equal answer quality.

According to recent reports, these are findings from external research, not OpenLotus benchmarks. I have deliberately kept that distinction clear.

The underlying idea is straightforward: an agent does not always need more context. It needs access to the relevant information without repeatedly reconstructing it.

Research: https://www.openlotus.io/research.

Existing approaches provide useful pieces of persistent context.

Sources indicate that instruction files such as CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md help establish project rules. Built in memory systems can preserve selected information. Conversation summaries help agents continue previous work.

But I wanted to address a broader problem.

What if project knowledge belonged to the project itself, rather than a particular agent, conversation or development environment?

A shared record that could preserve decisions, constraints, discoveries and implementation progress, and remain accessible regardless of which coding agent was being used.

OpenLotus is an independent project memory and state layer for AI coding agents.

It has been revealed that at its centre is a shared data structure called ProgressMap. It provides a persistent representation of a project's evolving state that compatible agents can access and update through the CLI and MCP.

Instead of storing another copy of the entire conversation, OpenLotus organises project knowledge into structured information:.

The goal is not to preserve every interaction.

It is to preserve the information that makes future development more informed and less repetitive.

OpenLotus has three main components.

A local repository can be paired with an OpenLotus project using:.

The CLI handles project pairing, while MCP gives compatible coding agents access to the shared project state.

This means project memory is not tied to one coding environment. Different agents can work with the same underlying record rather than maintaining isolated versions of project knowledge.

ProgressMap is the central representation of project knowledge.

It brings together plans, decisions, actions, changes, lessons and other information that describes the project's evolving state.

When a new session begins, an agent can retrieve relevant project information instead of reconstructing everything from previous conversations.

It also provides a basis for comparing declared project intent with observed repository reality.

OpenLotus exposes the shared project record through three interfaces:.

The crucial part is that the human and the agent work from the same underlying project record.

Sources indicate that context compaction is useful. It allows an agent to continue working when its conversation becomes too large for the available context window.

However, a compressed conversation is not necessarily a complete record of the project.

An architectural decision might be reduced to a short statement without its original reasoning. A failed approach might disappear from the summary. An unresolved constraint might lose the detail needed to avoid repeating an earlier mistake.

OpenLotus addresses a different layer of the problem.

According to recent reports, important decisions, constraints, lessons and project progress can be maintained independently of the conversation. When another session starts, the agent can retrieve that information again.

A context window is working space.

Compaction manages that working space.

OpenLotus maintains the project record that future working sessions can return to.

According to recent reports, it does not eliminate context windows or replace compaction. It provides a more durable source of project knowledge alongside them.

I want to be careful about token savings.

According to recent reports, external research supports the idea that structured memory and retrieval can reduce unnecessary context consumption. But I have not yet established a reliable percentage of token savings attributable specifically to OpenLotus through controlled benchmarks.

That requires testing identical repositories and tasks with and without OpenLotus, while measuring token consumption and task success.

Reducing token usage by making an agent perform worse would defeat the purpose.

The objective is to reduce unnecessary exploration and context reconstruction without sacrificing implementation quality.

That is the standard I want OpenLotus to meet.

I believe AI coding infrastructure needs to evolve beyond individual agent sessions.

As developers work with multiple agents, longer running projects and increasingly autonomous workflows, the project itself needs a durable source of truth.

OpenLotus aims to preserve the context behind those changes: why decisions were made, what constraints exist, what has been learned and where implementation stands.

That is what I have spent the last six months building.

You can explore OpenLotus at https://www.openlotus.io/.

It presently supports Claude Code, OpenCode, Codex, Cursor and other MCP compatible clients.

I would like to hear how other developers approach this problem.

How do you preserve project knowledge across context compaction and session resets?

And if you work with multiple coding agents, how do you keep them aligned on the same decisions?

I am particularly interested in the technical approaches people are using.

#11115. AI, Machine Learning, and ChatGPT Are Not the Same Thing — A Beginner's Map

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (943 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

AI, Machine Learning, and ChatGPT Are Not the Same Thing — A Beginner's Map

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (943 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ask a first-year student what artificial intelligence is, and you will probably hear "ChatGPT." Ask what machine learning is, and you will probably hear "also ChatGPT." That is not the student's fault.
  • Think of them as three nested layers.
  • Artificial intelligence is the goal of getting machines to perform tasks that usually require human judgment — recognizing a face, translating a sentence, recommending the next video to watch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ask a first-year student what artificial intelligence is, and you will probably hear "ChatGPT." Ask what machine learning is, and you will probably hear "also ChatGPT." That is not the student's fault. The three terms are used interchangeably in headlines, advertisements, and casual conversation — but they are not the same thing, and confusing them is the fastest way to misunderstand the entire field.

Think of them as three nested layers. AI is the broadest: the field. Machine learning is one method inside that field. ChatGPT is a single product built on top of that method. Keep the layers apart, and everything else starts to make sense.

Artificial intelligence is the goal of getting machines to perform tasks that usually require human judgment — recognizing a face, translating a sentence, recommending the next video to watch. The key word is "usually." These are tasks where the inputs are messy and the rules are hard to write down. Nobody can write a complete set of if-then rules for recognizing your grandmother's face in a crowd. Whenever a task is too fuzzy for explicit rules, you are probably looking at a job for AI.

It has been revealed that that definition matters because it draws a line. A calculator is not AI: its rules are exact and complete. A chess engine from the 1990s was arguably AI, because it had to search and evaluate positions no human could fully enumerate. The boundary moves as technology improves, but the idea stays the same: AI is the field that studies how machines can handle tasks we cannot fully specify in advance.

Machine learning is how most modern AI actually works — and it is a method, not a synonym for the field. The classic approach to AI was to write rules by hand. The machine learning approach is the opposite: instead of writing rules, you show the system many examples and let it find the patterns.

Sources indicate that A spam filter is the textbook case. Nobody wrote a rule for every possible spam email. The filter was trained on millions of labeled messages — this one is spam, this one is not — and it learned which signals matter: certain words, certain senders, certain patterns of links. The same idea sits behind recommendations, voice recognition, and autocomplete. When someone states "the AI learned," what usually happened is that a model adjusted its internal parameters based on data.

That sentence carries the method's biggest implication: no data, no learning — and bad data means bad learning. A model trained on biased or incomplete data will reproduce those biases, confidently. Students who understand this one point are already ahead of most people: they know the machine is not wise, it is statistical.

Sources indicate that it is also worth naming the main families, because the terms come up everywhere. Supervised learning trains on labeled examples, like the spam filter. Unsupervised learning looks for structure in unlabeled data, like grouping customers by behavior. Reinforcement learning learns by trial and error with rewards, like a program learning to play a game. Deep learning is a subfamily that uses large neural networks with many layers — the engine behind most recent breakthroughs, including the one that powers the product in layer three.

Sources indicate that chatGPT is a product: a chatbot built on a large language model, which is itself built with deep learning. A large language model is trained on enormous amounts of text, and its core job is deceptively simple — predict what word is likely to come next. Chained together over thousands of steps, those predictions produce fluent paragraphs, working code, and plausible-sounding explanations.

Fluent is not the same as correct. The model does not check facts against the world; it generates the most likely continuation of the text so far. That is why it can write a beautiful essay about a historical event that never happened, and why it can be confidently wrong about a citation. Used well, it is a remarkable tutor: it can summarize, rephrase, generate practice questions, and explain a concept five different ways until one clicks. Used uncritically, it is a machine for producing confident nonsense.

Recent findings suggest that the practical habit is simple: verify anything that matters. Let the tool draft, then check the draft against a source you trust. Let it quiz you, then check the answers. The students who benefit most from these tools will not be the ones who prompt the fastest. They will be the ones who understand what the machine is actually doing, so they can judge its output instead of copying it.

According to recent reports, three confusions disappear once the layers are clear. First, "AI" is not one technology you either know or do not know; it is a field with many methods, and machine learning is only the most popular one today. Second, machine learning is not magic; it is pattern-finding from data, and its quality is bounded by the data it was fed. Third, ChatGPT is not "the AI" — it is one product, built on one kind of model, trained on one slice of the internet. Newly introduced products will arrive on the same layers, and the map will still hold.

For readers who want the same ideas in plainer language with everyday examples — no math, no jargon — I keep a beginner-friendly explainer of AI, machine learning, and ChatGPT on my blog, written for students meeting these terms for the first time.

Learn the map first, and the tools become what they should have been all along: a patient tutor, not a substitute for thinking.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, on cash-on-delivery stores, most sellers remember only the return charge when a parcel comes back. The real cost is bigger: shipping out, shipping back, packaging, the time spent packing and calling, and sometimes a damaged product. One return can wipe out the profit of several successful orders.

    It has been revealed that this post summarises a new Bangla episode on my channel. The video (7 min) walks through the calculation with a fictional seller, Sumi Apu.

    List everything that left your pocket for one returned parcel: outbound charge, return charge, packaging, time, and the product value if it came back damaged. Counting only the courier fee makes the number look small.

    Divide the cost of one return by the profit you keep on one delivered order. The result is how many successful orders it takes to cover one return.

    Recent findings suggest that A single return looks small; a month of them does not. The formula is simple:.

    According to recent reports, example: 50 orders a day, a 25% return rate and ৳120 per return gives about 375 returns a month, roughly ৳45,000 of loss. (Example numbers; your store will differ.).

    In a recent development, try your own three numbers in the free return-loss calculator (Bangla UI). The result is an educational estimate, not a promise of savings.

    The cheapest place to cut return loss is before the parcel leaves. If an order looks risky, look up the number's courier history (free checker, limited use) and keep the confirmation call. The full call script is in the previous episode: https://youtu.be/RmLMOhzYhHM.

    One notable caveat: a low delivery success ratio does not prove a customer is fake. It is a signal, not a verdict. If in doubt, call or ask for an advance.

    The same three inputs (daily orders, return rate, cost per return) are a quick way to show a client why order verification matters before you talk about features.

    What is your store's return rate: under 10%, 10–20%, or above 20%?

    It has been revealed that sumi Apu is a fictional example. Amounts are examples/estimates. The video's voice and some images are AI-generated.

    Photography by Xiao Tan.

    Local practice Tant A Temps Design aimed to revive the aesthetics of the Tang Dynasty when designing the interiors for cafe Laibei 1087, located in a historical building in Xi’an, China.

    The cafe sits inside the Beilin Museum, originally constructed in 1087 to preserve stone steles inscribed with Confucian philosophy and famous calligraphic works.

    The timber columns and beams of the historic building were preserved, with the same approach extended into the cafe interiors.

    Guided by a “minimum intervention” and “zero damage” renovation strategy, Tant A Temps Design made every newly introduced addition detachable and reversible, which allowed the building’s original features to remain untouched.

    In the cafe, the furniture is suspended from wooden beams or arranged around columns to avoid direct contact with the original structures.

    Tant A Temps Design also created tables, chairs and display cabinets with designs that draw from elements of the ancient building framework, such as the beams, columns and dougong brackets.

    Lightweight and prefabricated materials and modular systems were used throughout the space.

    For the main colour palette, Tant A Temps Design chose light green hues complemented by gold accents.

    “The purpose of choosing this colour scheme is to restore the visual characteristics of Tang architecture – robust, imposing and richly coloured,” the studio explained.

    “Abandoning the rigid replication of ancient architecture, it extracts and reshapes the spiritual core of Tang and Song aesthetics through a restrained colour palette and minimalist structural language, creating a serene and elegant atmosphere that highly matches the cultural temperament of the Stele Forest.”.

    An integrated functional island was designed to function as the central bar counter.

    All modern utility systems, including air conditioning, water, electricity, lighting and exhausts, were concealed and integrated into the top and bottom of the bar counter.

    This is consistent with the studio’s commitment to preserving the heritage building while giving it a contemporary, functional upgrade.

    “This forms a functional system that is both independent of the original building structure and seamlessly integrated into the historical environment, setting a latest paradigm for the adaptive reuse of similar cultural heritage buildings,” noted the studio.

    The cafe is part of a 220-square-metre development that also includes a rest area, a retail zone and a stone-rubbing workshop that serves as a history learning centre.

    According to Tant A Temps Design, the project has transformed a dormant historical building into an accessible and interactive cultural space.

    Led by founder Wei Chen, Tant A Temps Design is an interior design practice based in Xi’an.

    Elsewhere in China, Linehouse has completed the interiors of the Jen hotel in Hangzhou and Keiji Ashizawa designed an “open and inviting retail space” in the historic building in Shanghai.

    Photography by Xiao Tan.

    Breaking: This Breakfast Addition Sharpens Memory Later In The Day

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A simple breakfast addition improved reaction times, but its effects on memory took a more complicated turn.
    • A simple breakfast addition improved reaction times, but its effects on memory took a more complicated turn.
    • Adding walnuts to breakfast could help people respond faster on mental tasks and learn information more effectively later in the day.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A simple breakfast addition improved reaction times, but its effects on memory took a more complicated turn.

    A simple breakfast addition improved reaction times, but its effects on memory took a more complicated turn.

    Adding walnuts to breakfast could help people respond faster on mental tasks and learn information more effectively later in the day.

    A generous handful produced small cognitive benefits over the following six hours, although memory performance varied with the timing of the tests.

    Walnuts may influence how the brain directs attention and obtains the energy needed for demanding mental work.

    Professor Claire Williams, study co-author, mentioned:.

    “A handful of walnuts with breakfast could give young adults a mental edge when they need to perform at the top of their game.”.

    The research involved over 30 healthy young adults aged 18–30, who ate two different breakfasts on separate visits to the laboratory.

    One contained 50 g of crushed walnuts mixed into muesli and vanilla yoghurt, while the other contained no nuts.

    The breakfasts contained almost identical calorie and fat totals, with butter added to the comparison meal to help achieve this match.

    Participants completed tests before breakfast and again two, four and six hours afterwards, while researchers also recorded their brain activity.

    After the walnut breakfast, participants responded faster on tasks involving attention, resisting distractions and switching between different mental rules.

    These abilities form part of executive function, which helps us control our responses and adapt to changing demands.

    The differences were modest, averaging around eight milliseconds on the attention test and 22 milliseconds when switching between rules.

    Whether improvements of this size would make a noticeable difference outside the laboratory remains uncertain.

    The memory findings were more complicated.

    Two hours after eating walnuts, participants performed slightly worse when repeatedly learning and recalling a list of words.

    By six hours, however, the pattern had reversed, with better performance after walnuts than after the comparison breakfast.

    One possibility is that walnuts helped protect learning performance as the testing day wore on.

    Repeated mental effort can make it harder to take in latest information, so preserving the ability to learn could be useful even without improving every aspect of memory.

    However, participants did not report feeling less mentally fatigued after walnuts, leaving this explanation unconfirmed.

    Another possibility is that some benefits emerged gradually as nutrients were absorbed and processed.

    Walnuts contain omega-3 fats, protein and plant compounds called polyphenols, which could contribute individually or together.

    Electrical recordings revealed differences in frontal and parietal brain activity after the two breakfasts.

    These regions contribute to attention, memory and the control of behaviour.

    The changes may indicate that walnuts altered how mental resources were allocated during the tests, although they do not establish precisely why performance improved.

    Blood samples also demonstrated slightly higher glucose availability and lower concentrations of circulating free fatty acids after walnuts.

    Greater glucose availability might help fuel demanding mental work.

    The study was published in the journal Food & Function (Bell et al., 2025).

    Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean.

    You can organize your store by creating your product categories, sorting by any characteristic you choose. Your title, description, and the image will be included on each product page. In this way, customers can immediately evaluate all of your products.     Industry observers note that sellfy is a simple online platform that allows customers to buy your products directly through your store. Sellfy has two payment processing options: PayPal and Stripe. You will receive instant payments with both of these processors, and your customer data is protected by Sellfy's secure (PCI-compliant) payment security measures. In addition to payment security, Sellfy provides anti-fraud tools to help protect your products including PDF stamping, unique download links, and limited download attempts.

    To expand functionality and make your e-commerce store run more efficiently, Sellfy offers several integrations. Google Analytics and Webhooks, as well as integrations with Patreon and Facebook Live Chat, are just a few of the options available. Sellfy allows you to connect to Zapier, which gives you access to hundreds of third-party apps, including tools like Mailchimp, Trello, Salesforce, and more.

    Industry News: Foster + Partners creates Area worktable for today's office

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Foster + Partners Industrial Design aimed to bring expressive and functional workplace design together in its modular Area table system, created with Spanish furniture brand Kettal.
    • Designed to be durable and adaptable, Area combines aluminium columns, a panoply of tabletop options and concealed power.
    • The aluminium columns anchor the design, serving as both structural support and discreet container for power cables and electrical components.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Photography by Salva López.

    Foster + Partners Industrial Design aimed to bring expressive and functional workplace design together in its modular Area table system, created with Spanish furniture brand Kettal.

    Designed to be durable and adaptable, Area combines aluminium columns, a panoply of tabletop options and concealed power.

    The aluminium columns anchor the design, serving as both structural support and discreet container for power cables and electrical components.

    Available in three diameters – 90, 160 or 450 millimetres – and either anodised or powder-coated finishes, they also bring customisable personality to the worktable.

    In a recent development, the tabletops, meanwhile, come in shapes ranging from round to triangular and rhomboid and materials including timber, linoleum, melamine and Fenix. For larger conference or feature tables, terrazzo or marble are also options.

    “Area is a collection of durable, expressive elements that define workstations and gathering points within a space to support both individual and collaborative work,” said Foster + Partners head of industrial design Mike Holland.

    “The development of Area involved finding the right balance between structural performance, flexibility and visual simplicity,” he continued.

    “The system needed to accommodate a wide variety of tabletop configurations and working arrangements, while integrating the technical infrastructure required in contemporary workplaces.”.

    It has been revealed that the Area system can be accessorised with lighting or fabric screen dividers, the infrastructure for which is built into the table. Screen dividers attach magnetically at designed points, with lighting used in combination or mounted independently.

    Cables are hidden underneath the tabletop within a J-profile aluminium beam that also provides structural support, while concealed grommets provide access to plug sockets and USB-C connections.

    Holland told Dezeen that designing these accessories so they could function seamlessly across a range of tabletop configurations was the key challenge of the design process for Area, alongside achieving the desired proportions and textures for the aluminium columns.

    To realise their vision for the expansive system, the design team undertook extensive prototyping, including using both one-to-one and full-scale models and augmented reality (AR).

    “Working with full-scale models, augmented reality and 3D printing allowed us to understand the relationship between the different components and how they would function together in real working environments,” said Holland.

    It has been revealed that “This approach was particularly crucial in refining the columns, assessing their proportions, and adapting the surface texture pattern at full scale. It also allowed us to evolve the design from wider diameters into more elegant and efficient forms.”.

    He said that working with models and AR also allowed manufacturer Kettal to engage in the design process and contribute ideas.

    “Collaboration is at the heart of our approach, and we believe it is fundamental to achieving the highest-quality results,” said Holland.

    Area was designed for the contemporary workplace, said Holland, where flexible and hybrid working have made the office primarily a place for collaboration and connection, and where the table’s modularity and adaptability allow it to evolve as needs change.

    “As designers, we are interested in the points of interaction between people and buildings,” stated Holland. “At the heart of industrial design lies the creation of these touchpoints through which people experience space.”.

    “In the workplace, furniture plays a vital role in shaping how people engage with their environment, influencing how they occupy, navigate and connect with the spaces around them,” Holland concluded.

    Part of the architecture firm Foster + Partners, Foster + Partners Industrial Design started by creating site-specific furniture, fixtures and fittings for the company’s buildings and over the last 50 years have expanded to more stand-alone commercial products.

    Some of its recent designs include the Join plywood furniture collection, Ori bird feeders and Datum porcelain tableware.

    Photography by Salva López.

    • Imagine a world in which you can do transactions and many other things without having to give your personal information.
    • It’s like your computer’s hard drive.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Imagine a world in which you can do transactions and many other things without having to give your personal information. A world in which you don’t need to rely on banks or governments anymore. Sounds amazing, right? That’s exactly what blockchain technology allows us to do.

    It’s like your computer’s hard drive. blockchain is a technology that lets you store data in digital blocks, which are connected together like links in a chain.

    Blockchain technology was originally invented in 1991 by two mathematicians, Stuart Haber and W. Scot Stornetta. They first proposed the system to ensure that timestamps could not be tampered with.

    A few years later, in 1998, software developer Nick Szabo proposed using a similar kind of technology to secure a digital payments system he called “Bit Gold.” However, this innovation was not adopted until Satoshi Nakamoto claimed to have invented the first Blockchain and Bitcoin.

    A blockchain is a distributed database shared between the nodes of a computer network. It saves information in digital format. Many people first heard of blockchain technology when they started to look up information about bitcoin.

    Blockchain is used in cryptocurrency systems to ensure secure, decentralized records of transactions.

    Blockchain allowed people to guarantee the fidelity and security of a record of data without the need for a third party to ensure accuracy.

    To understand how a blockchain works, Consider these basic steps:.

    Let’s get to know more about the blockchain.

    Sources indicate that blockchain records digital information and distributes it across the network without changing it. The information is distributed among many people and stored in an immutable, permanent ledger that can't be changed or destroyed. That's why blockchain is also called "Distributed Ledger Technology" or DLT.

    And that’s the beauty of it! The process may seem complicated, but it’s done in minutes with modern technology. And because technology is advancing rapidly, I expect things to move even more quickly than ever.

    Even though blockchain is integral to cryptocurrency, it has other applications. For example, blockchain can be used for storing reliable data about transactions. Many people confuse blockchain with cryptocurrencies like bitcoin and ethereum.

    In a recent development, blockchain already being adopted by some substantial-name companies, such as Walmart, AIG, Siemens, Pfizer, and Unilever. For example, IBM's Food Trust uses blockchain to track food's journey before reaching its final destination.

    Sources indicate that although some of you may consider this practice excessive, food suppliers and manufacturers adhere to the policy of tracing their products because bacteria such as E. coli and Salmonella have been found in packaged foods. In addition, there have been isolated cases where dangerous allergens such as peanuts have accidentally been introduced into certain products.

    Recent findings suggest that tracing and identifying the sources of an outbreak is a challenging task that can take months or years. Thanks to the Blockchain, however, companies now know exactly where their food has been—so they can trace its location and prevent future outbreaks.

    Blockchain technology allows systems to react much faster in the event of a hazard. It also has many other uses in the modern world.

    Industry observers note that blockchain technology is safe, even if it’s public. People can access the technology using an internet connection.

    Industry observers note that have you ever been in a situation where you had all your data stored at one place and that one secure place got compromised? Wouldn't it be great if there was a way to prevent your data from leaking out even when the security of your storage systems is compromised?

    Blockchain technology provides a way of avoiding this situation by using multiple computers at different locations to store information about transactions. If one computer experiences problems with a transaction, it will not affect the other nodes.

    Sources indicate that instead, other nodes will use the correct information to cross-reference your incorrect node. This is called “Decentralization,” meaning all the information is stored in multiple places.

    In a recent development, blockchain guarantees your data's authenticity—not just its accuracy, but also its irreversibility. It can also be used to store data that are difficult to register, like legal contracts, state identifications, or a company's product inventory.

    Blockchain has many advantages and disadvantages.

    I’ll answer the most frequently asked questions about blockchain in this section.

    Blockchain is not a cryptocurrency but a technology that makes cryptocurrencies possible. It's a digital ledger that records every transaction seamlessly.

    Yes, blockchain can be theoretically hacked, but it is a complicated task to be achieved. A network of consumers constantly reviews it, which makes hacking the blockchain difficult.

    Coinbase Global is presently the biggest blockchain company in the world. The company runs a commendable infrastructure, services, and technology for the digital currency economy.

    Blockchain is a decentralized technology. It’s a chain of distributed ledgers connected with nodes. Each node can be any electronic device. Thus, one owns blockhain.

    Bitcoin is a cryptocurrency, which is powered by Blockchain technology while Blockchain is a distributed ledger of cryptocurrency.

    It has been revealed that generally a database is a collection of data which can be stored and organized using a database management system. The people who have access to the database can view or edit the information stored there. The client-server network architecture is used to implement databases. whereas a blockchain is a growing list of records, called blocks, stored in a distributed system. Each block contains a cryptographic hash of the previous block, timestamp and transaction information. Modification of data is not allowed due to the design of the blockchain. The technology allows decentralized control and eliminates risks of data modification by other parties.

    In a recent development, blockchain has a wide spectrum of applications and, over the next 5-10 years, we will likely see it being integrated into all sorts of industries. From finance to healthcare, blockchain could revolutionize the way we store and share data. Although there is some hesitation to adopt blockchain systems right now, that won't be the case in 2022-2023 (and even less so in 2026). Once people become more comfortable with the technology and understand how it can work for them, owners, CEOs and entrepreneurs alike will be quick to leverage blockchain technology for their own gain.     Pepper & Well designs bathroom that mimics concrete architecture of Paul Couch house

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Melbourne-based studio Pepper & Well took cues from crisscrossing concrete walls and ceiling beams when designing Lumeah, a new en-suite for a house by celebrated architect Paul Couch.
    • Located in Macedon, central Victoria, the linear single-storey house was completed in 2006 by the late Couch, who passed away earlier this year.
    • When newly introduced owners bought the property in 2018, they felt the layout and finishes of the main bathroom didn’t meet the standards of the rest of the house.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Photography by Tom Ross.

    Melbourne-based studio Pepper & Well took cues from crisscrossing concrete walls and ceiling beams when designing Lumeah, a new en-suite for a house by celebrated architect Paul Couch.

    Located in Macedon, central Victoria, the linear single-storey house was completed in 2006 by the late Couch, who passed away earlier this year.

    When newly introduced owners bought the property in 2018, they felt the layout and finishes of the main bathroom didn’t meet the standards of the rest of the house.

    They asked Pepper & Well to upgrade it and make it more accessible.

    “There was an opportunity to make the space more comfortable and practical as they aged,” remarked lead architect Andy Dal Pozzo.

    The previous layout included a WC, an enclosed shower and a step-in plunge pool, all within a space just 3.5 metres long.

    Pepper & Well’s scheme removed the plunge, allowing space for a larger WC and for an open shower to be built in place of the old frosted-glass enclosure.

    The defining move was the addition of a cast-concrete element that partitions the toilet and shower areas.

    This incorporates an informal bench, allowing for seated showers if preferred.

    The geometry of this element clearly references the house’s exposed concrete structure, a rhythmic arrangement of concrete beams over concrete walls.

    “Our approach began with understanding the logic of Paul’s work,” explained Dal Pozzo.

    “We wanted the renovation to share the original architecture’s material honesty and clarity, while remaining recognisable as a fresh contribution,” he noted.

    A change in floor surface marks the junction between old and upcoming.

    While most of the room features the bluestone flooring installed 20 years ago, the toilet and shower have a surface of crazy-paved slate.

    The stone is the same Mintaro Brown Back slate that Couch installed in the bathroom of his own house, Toolern Vale.

    “Laid in crazy paving beside the retained bluestone, it introduces a distinct texture with a direct connection to Paul’s work,” remarked Dal Pozzo.

    “Both materials remain clearly legible.”.

    The rest of the room was left largely intact, including the solid timber doors and the vanity unit spanning the opposite wall.

    Industry observers note that there are subtle correlations between the two sides of the room, so as not to make the latest insertion feel disparate. For instance, a glass screen matches the height of the mirror opposite.

    The shower also includes a stainless-steel handrail that doubles as a towel rail, matching the rest of the bathroom fixtures.

    “The scale of the commission demanded close attention to every decision, from the arrangement of the room to the meeting of two stones,” added Dal Pozzo.

    “By revealing the original fabric, retaining what worked and introducing a few carefully resolved elements, we sought to give the clients a bathroom that would serve them into the future and continue the architectural story of their home.”.

    Lumeah is shortlisted for bathroom of the year in Dezeen Awards 2026.

    Other projects in this category include Kan Atelier’s design for the William King Apartment, a residence in a 1950s block in Athens, which won the public vote.

    Photography by Tom Ross.

    Breaking: What Happier People Tend To Believe About Others

    📅 30 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (644 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Org

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A review involving over 2.5 million people links one social outlook to greater happiness—and the connection runs both ways.
    • A review involving over 2.5 million people links one social outlook to greater happiness—and the connection runs both ways.
    • Trusting others is linked to greater happiness and life satisfaction, a review involving over 2.5 million people finds.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A review involving over 2.5 million people links one social outlook to greater happiness—and the connection runs both ways.

    A review involving over 2.5 million people links one social outlook to greater happiness—and the connection runs both ways.

    Trusting others is linked to greater happiness and life satisfaction, a review involving over 2.5 million people finds.

    Happier people also tend to become more trusting over time.

    The link between trust and happiness is slightly stronger in children, adolescents and older adults, possibly because supportive relationships are especially important at these ages.

    Trust may help meet the need to belong by making it easier to build relationships in which people feel supported and secure.

    The research combined almost 1,000 findings from studies involving people aged six to 84.

    The analysis examined how trust related to everyday emotions, including happiness and sadness, as well as people’s overall satisfaction with their lives.

    Greater trust was consistently associated with better wellbeing.

    The association was somewhat stronger among children and adolescents than among young and middle-aged adults, and stronger among older adults than young adults.

    Trust may matter more at ages when people are building close relationships or becoming more dependent on others.

    For younger people, learning whom to trust is part of building meaningful friendships and supportive social networks.

    In later life, people may prioritise a smaller circle of close relationships and depend more on others for support.

    The researchers distinguished between trust in familiar people, trust in people generally and trust in institutions.

    The first involves confidence in someone known personally, such as a partner, friend or relative.

    General trust involves expectations about people more broadly, including strangers, while institutional trust concerns organisations such as governments, banks and the police.

    All three were associated with better wellbeing, but trust in familiar people revealed the strongest connection.

    Trust may support wellbeing partly because close relationships require a willingness to be vulnerable.

    Expecting someone to respond with care can make it easier to seek help, cooperate and maintain a supportive connection.

    These relationships may satisfy the basic psychological need to feel connected to others and cared for in return.

    Trust could also provide a broader sense of security and predictability, making the social world feel more dependable.

    This may help explain why trust was slightly more closely related to overall life satisfaction than to positive or negative emotions.

    Life satisfaction reflects a broader assessment of how life is going, whereas emotions can fluctuate with immediate experiences.

    The relationship also worked in the other direction, with greater wellbeing predicting more trust later.

    One proposed explanation is that emotions influence how people interpret the world around them.

    Feeling happy may encourage more positive perceptions of other people, while anxiety may draw attention towards threats and uncertainty.

    Trust and wellbeing could therefore reinforce each other, with supportive expectations helping people feel better and positive feelings making trust easier.

    The wider social environment mattered too, with a stronger connection between trust and wellbeing in countries where people were generally more trusting.

    A trusting outlook may be more beneficial when the people around us are dependable.

    Simply encouraging someone to trust more overlooks the behaviour of the people and institutions receiving that trust.

    Professor Catrin Finkenauer, study co-author, said:.

    “But trust can’t be forced—it has to be earned.”.

    The findings therefore highlight the importance of honesty, reliability, transparency and fair treatment in relationships and institutions.

    “When we build trust, we also support mental health and stronger communities.”.

    The study was published in the journal Psychological Bulletin (Bi et al., 2025).

    Recent findings suggest that psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004.     Industry observers note that affiliate marketing is a way to make money by promoting the products and services of other people and companies. You don't need to create your product or service, just promote existing ones. That's why it's so easy to get started with affiliate marketing. You can even get started with no budget at all!

    Recent findings suggest that an affiliate program is a package of information you create for your product, which is then made available to potential publishers. The program will typically include details about the product and its retail value, commission levels, and promotional materials. Many affiliate programs are managed via an affiliate network like ShareASale, which acts as a platform to connect publishers and advertisers, but it is also possible to offer your program directly.

    Affiliate networks connect publishers to advertisers. Affiliate networks make money by charging fees to the merchants who advertise with them; these merchants are known as advertisers. The percentage of each sale that the advertiser pays is negotiated between the merchant and the affiliate network.

    Dropshipping is a method of selling that allows you to run an online store without having to stock products. You advertise the products as if you owned them, but when someone makes an order, you create a duplicate order with the distributor at a reduced price. The distributor takes care of the post and packaging on your behalf. As affiliate marketing is based on referrals and this type of drop shipping requires no investment in inventory when a customer buys through the affiliate link, no money exchanges hands.

    Sources indicate that performance marketing is a method of marketing that pays for performance, like when a sale is made or an ad is clicked This can include methods like PPC (pay-per-click) or display advertising. Affiliate marketing is one form of performance marketing where commissions are paid out to affiliates on a performance basis when they click on their affiliate link and make a purchase or action.

    Smartphones are essentially miniature computers, so publishers can display the same websites and offers that are available on a PC. But mobiles also offer specific tools not available on computers, and these can be used to good effect for publishers. Publishers can optimize their ads for mobile people by making them easy to access by this audience. Publishers can also make good use of text and instant messaging to promote their offers. As the mobile market is predicted to make up 80% of traffic in the future, publishers who do not promote on mobile devices are missing out on a substantial opportunity.

    The best way to find affiliate publishers is on reputable networks like ShareASale Cj(Commission Junction), Awin, and Impact radius. These networks have a strict application process and compliance checks, which means that all affiliates are trustworthy.

    An affiliate disclosure statement discloses to the reader that there may be affiliate links on a website, for which a commission may be paid to the publisher if visitors follow these links and make purchases.

    Industry observers note that publishers promote their programs through a variety of means, including blogs, websites, email marketing, and pay-per-click ads. Social media has a huge interactive audience, making this platform a good source of potential traffic.

    Sources indicate that A super affiliate is an affiliate partner who consistently drives a large majority of sales from any program they promote, compared to other affiliate partners involved in that program. Affiliates make a lot of money from affiliate marketing Pat Flynn earned more than $50000 in 2013 from affiliate marketing.

    It has been revealed that because the Internet is so widespread, affiliate programs can be promoted in any country. Affiliate strategies that are set internationally need to be tailored to the language of the targeted country.

    Affiliate marketing can help you grow your business in the following ways:.

    One of the best ways to work with qualified affiliates is to hire an affiliate marketing agency that works with all the networks. Affiliates are carefully selected and go through a rigorous application process to be included in the network.

    Affiliate marketing is generally associated with websites, but there are other ways to promote your affiliate links, including:.

    It has been revealed that commission rates are typically based on a percentage of the total sale and in some cases can also be a flat fee for each transaction. The rates are set by the merchant.

    Who manages your affiliate program?

    Some merchants run their affiliate programs internally, while others choose to contract out management to a network or an external agency.

    Tech Report: B2 Architecture turns North Korean defector testimonies into Prague exhibition

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (441 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dezeen

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • B2 Architecture has created the Life Behind the Walls exhibition in Prague, using a maze of red timber frames and translucent fabric to explore life in North Korea.
    • The 1,500-square-metre exhibition takes visitors from a bright, interactive installation designed around a children’s book to a darkened gallery featuring portraits and testimonies from North Korean defectors.
    • Sources indicate that B2 Architecture divided the installation into two contrasting environments.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Photography by Radek Šrettr Úlehla.

    B2 Architecture has created the Life Behind the Walls exhibition in Prague, using a maze of red timber frames and translucent fabric to explore life in North Korea.

    The 1,500-square-metre exhibition takes visitors from a bright, interactive installation designed around a children’s book to a darkened gallery featuring portraits and testimonies from North Korean defectors.

    Sources indicate that B2 Architecture divided the installation into two contrasting environments. The first features a grid of red-painted timber beams, with large sheets of red and pink fabric suspended between the frames to create semi-transparent walls.

    The structure forms a maze that visitors can explore, with glimpses of other rooms and activities visible through the fabric.

    Illustrated panels, games and interactive activities are fitted into the structure, while photographs by photographer Michal Huniewicz show North Korea as it is presented to the outside world.

    Children are encouraged to navigate the maze independently and stop to draw, write and complete activities as they move through the installation.

    The displays are based on Tota lítá, a children’s book by North Korean studies scholar and writer Nina Špitálníková, which explains the principles of totalitarianism in language that is accessible to younger readers.

    Recent findings suggest that “Children are often given very little space within exhibition formats,” B2 Architecture told Dezeen. “This project consciously challenges that convention.”.

    The atmosphere changes as visitors pass between two walls displaying photographs of the border between North Korea and China by photographer Tim Franco.

    Beyond this threshold, the playful red maze gives way to a dark gallery. This contains black display structures with portraits and personal accounts of people who escaped North Korea, alongside stories of those who did not survive its regime.

    Tall, translucent fabric panels printed with shadowy human figures were arranged throughout the space, creating silhouettes that overlap with the portraits displayed behind them.

    In a central room, a monumental statue of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un stands on a raised plinth, surrounded by spotlights and theatrical mist.

    The temporary installation was constructed using lightweight, modular timber beams and stretched textiles, allowing it to be assembled and dismantled efficiently.

    The timber structure was retained for use in another project, while the textiles and flooring were passed on to several theatres for reuse.

    Prague-based B2 Architecture was founded by architect Barbara Bencová in 2012 and works across residential and commercial architecture, interiors and public spaces.

    Other projects by the studio featured on Dezeen include the DDB Prague office, which features an anamorphic optical illusion that makes the advertising agency’s logo appear complete from a particular viewpoint.

    Photography by Radek Šrettr Úlehla.

    #11084. Industry News: Eight highlights from this year's Sharjah Architecture Triennial

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1398 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dezeen ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Eight highlights from this year's Sharjah Architecture Triennial

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1398 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, the third Sharjah Architecture Triennial focuses on the myriad ways architecture can be understood through the lens of anthropology.
    • Curated by anthropologist Vyjayanthi Rao, this year’s edition was centred on the theme Architecture Otherwise: Building Civic Infrastructure for Collective Futures.
    • Rao said the 2026 Sharjah Architecture Triennial, which takes place over five months, will invite discourse about the different ways cities and urban life can be imagined.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, the third Sharjah Architecture Triennial focuses on the myriad ways architecture can be understood through the lens of anthropology. Here are our highlights from the event, including installations and exhibitions.

    Curated by anthropologist Vyjayanthi Rao, this year’s edition was centred on the theme Architecture Otherwise: Building Civic Infrastructure for Collective Futures.

    Rao said the 2026 Sharjah Architecture Triennial, which takes place over five months, will invite discourse about the different ways cities and urban life can be imagined.

    “Though I’m not an architect, I’m literally talking to students day in and day out about how they see the world, and how that translates into the practice,” Rao told Dezeen.

    “Being an academic, you’re always asked to define yourself in terms of your discipline,” she continued. “It doesn’t make sense to limit yourself, especially when you are in the practice of life.”.

    “You’re learning from people about the ways in which they live – that’s what I do as an anthropologist, and I think that’s what a lot of architects do because they’re inspired to build for people and the places that they inhabit and thrive in.”.

    Read on for eight highlights from this year’s Sharjah Architecture Triennial.

    Open the School by Curry J Hackett.

    Artist Curry J Hackett created this draping shelter spanning the width of the Old Al Jubail Vegetable Market in homage to the Black community in Virginia’s Prince Edward County, which created improvised learning spaces when schools closed during the Civil Rights Movement.

    Videos play in the former stalls at either end of the fabric enclosure, screening archival images of the period, as well as images of Rosenwald Schools – the community-building initiative that established thousands of schools for Black children in the South.

    According to recent reports, “Rather than integrate, schools closed for five years, and leading up to that, schools were dealing with a lot of overcrowding,” Hackett told Dezeen. “The county begrudgingly funded ‘tar paper shacks’, which were shoddy, demoralising structures, to ease overcrowding, and that’s what you’re seeing interpreted here,” he continued.

    “Interspersed sonically and visually throughout the installation is a mashing up of the local story of my home town in Virginia with the regional story of the Rosenwald Schools in the South – their architectural rethinking of materials and retelling the history.”.

    Research and construction studio Abari showcased a tent-like structure made from a bamboo frame, which was limited in size due to difficulties with material regulations.

    The structure is one module of a larger pavilion that was constructed in Nepal, designed as a travelling venue to host bamboo weaving workshops.

    “We were not able to create an installation here in the UAE, partly because Abari’s work is based on building with bamboo, and the difficulty with this project was that the global supply chain and its regulations could not be met within the timeframe,” remarked Rao.

    “What you see here is one repeatable module of a pavilion that is currently moving within different communities in Nepal – we improvised and decided Sharjah would travel to Nepal, and we’d just have a piece of it here in this exhibition.”.

    Sabeel Negotiated by Samar Halloum.

    Drawing upon her fieldwork in Sharjah, Palestinian architect Samar Halloum designed a brick pavilion that was shaded overhead by a draping fabric canopy.

    In reference to the historical public drinking-water structures in the Gulf region, Sabeel Negotiated features a water fountain and wooden stools for people to gather around.

    According to Rao, the strikes by Iran on countries in the Middle East in February disrupted brick supply in the United Arab Emirates, so Halloum redesigned the pavilion with cloth-filled bricks.

    “One of the shortages was bricks because they come from Saudi Arabia, and the factory stopped producing bricks,” noted Rao. “There were some leftover bales of cloth from another installation, so Halloum used those bales and cast them in resin, so you’ll see some of the bricks in the installation are actually made of cloth.”.

    History as Repair: Documenting Karachi by Kishwar Rizvi.

    This exhibition by art historian Kishwar Rizvi explores how colonised communities in Karachi, Pakistan, took ownership of their urban environment by adapting architectural styles, from European classicism to Mughal-inspired ornament.

    Through maps, photographs, sketches and interviews, it aims to shine a light on an architectural history at risk of being forgotten.

    The exhibition argues for the protection of colonial-era buildings in Karachi, which are under threat of demolition due to neglect.

    Patch-Time by Hiba Bou Akar, Mohamad Hafeda and Nathalie Harb.

    The Patch-Time installation is a collaboration between architect Hiba Bou Akar and artists Mohamad Hafeda and Nathalie Harb that explores the displacement of people in Lebanon, from the 1970s to the present day, through the materials used to protect and repair homes.

    In workshops organised by the Patch-Time team with Lebanese non-profit Ahla Fawda, displaced women crocheted tarpaulin, sand-bag cloth and sheeting into panels that form a canopy displayed in a courtyard at the triennial’s Al Qasimiyah School venue.

    Underneath the canopy, a table made from breeze blocks, wood and a central mirror displays fabric artwork and the stories of women and children affected by war.

    Industry observers note that “We worked on two levels: one that is the collective, and one that is more of the individual, looking at how people shelter their home through war adversity and displacement,” said Harb. “We asked [the women] what their relationship to their home was, and in the pieces, you see how it changes from generation to generation with their relationship to material.”.

    After Night There is Nothing by Mohamad Nahleh and Ozayr Saloojee.

    Architect Mohamad Nahleh and architecture professor Ozayr Saloojee designed a giant globe of the night sky and split it into three parts, which were scattered across different locations at the triennale.

    The outer shells of the curved structures are wrapped in thatch, while the interiors feature vinyl surfaces with designs showing man-made military objects in the sky reimagined as creature-like constellations.

    “This is ‘night sky optimism’ – optimism through catastrophe,” remarked Nahleh. “The night sky we are talking about in this project is not the sky of beautiful stars and constellations, but the contemporary sky filled with drones, satellites, rockets and missiles that are changing the way we understand the sky above us.”.

    According to recent reports, “We have noticed in our research that, especially in geographies witnessing prolonged violence, these objects are producing latest mythical creatures,” he continued. “We think of these creatures as ones that attempt to tame the military brightness that is populating the sky around us.”.

    As the Sun Rests by Badriyah Alsalem.

    Kuwaiti designer Badriyah Alsalem plotted 41 medieval Arabic poetic names for the sun as cut-outs on the astronomical graph that forms a circular canopy over her pavilion, As the Sun Rests.

    Forming patterns of shadow in the sand below, three of the suns were embroidered in red, depicting the sharaq rising sun, saqa’a noon sun and gharab setting sun, while markers on the ground show where these canopy highlights will fall on different dates during the triennial.

    “If you look up, you see the static data visualisation, and if you look down, it is animated by the sun itself, so it becomes an analogue device to read this historical data,” said Alsalem.

    Lalla Alwyia Khalwa by Ziad Jamaleddine, Makram el Kadi, Iheb Guermazi and Beya Othmani.

    Situated on Sharjah’s Al Khan Open Beach, Lalla Alwyia Khalwa is an installation designed as a place for reflection away from the busy city, dedicated to the saint Lalla Alwyia Kasserine.

    Dried plants form a grid of columns on a raised platform for visitors to walk through. Stone slabs on the floor mark places of pause, and a metal stool provides a reflective space to listen to the accompanying sound installation.

    “We chose the beach because it is already a space for retreat, so this is a retreat inside a retreat,” said the design team, Ziad Jamaleddine, Makram el Kadi, Iheb Guermazi and Beya Othmani.

    “We carved a series of spaces – one for prayer, one for sitting, and a courtyard to enjoy the sky.”.

    It has been revealed that sharjah Architecture Triennial 2026 takes place from 14 November 2026 to 14 April 2027 at various locations across Sharjah, UAE. See Dezeen Events Guide for an up-to-date list of architecture and design events taking place around the world.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Could childhood exposure to fluoridated water leave a lasting mark on cognition?
    • Could childhood exposure to fluoridated water leave a lasting mark on cognition?
    • Fluoride in community drinking water is not linked to lower adolescent IQ or poorer thinking skills later in life, a long-running US study finds.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Could childhood exposure to fluoridated water leave a lasting mark on cognition? Decades of data offer clues.

    Could childhood exposure to fluoridated water leave a lasting mark on cognition? Decades of data offer clues.

    Fluoride in community drinking water is not linked to lower adolescent IQ or poorer thinking skills later in life, a long-running US study finds.

    Researchers followed a generation of Wisconsin school-leavers, examining cognitive performance from adolescence into their eighties.

    Those exposed to fluoridated water did not show a consistent disadvantage compared with people whose communities had no fluoridation.

    The findings address concerns that adding fluoride to drinking water to prevent tooth decay could undermine intellectual development.

    Professor John Robert Warren, the study’s first author, remarked:.

    “Utah, Florida and many municipalities have chosen to remove fluoride from drinking water based on flawed studies that considered the IQ effects of exposure to massive doses of fluoride.

    According to recent reports, because levels of fluoride added to municipal drinking water in the U.S. are so much lower, almost all prior evidence from those international studies is not relevant to U.S. public policy debates.”.

    The research draws on the Wisconsin Longitudinal Study, which began with over 10,000 people who graduated from high school in 1957.

    Researchers combined school IQ records with historical information about community water fluoridation and naturally occurring fluoride levels.

    Following participants into old age allowed researchers to examine whether childhood exposure was associated with lasting differences in cognitive performance.

    Comparing communities requires care because their residents can differ in ways that also relate to cognitive performance.

    Once those background differences were taken into account, there was no consistent evidence that exposure was associated with either better or worse performance.

    The same broad pattern appeared when researchers focused on people who had lived in the same county since early childhood, increasing confidence in their estimates of exposure.

    Overall, the findings suggest that growing up with fluoridated community water is not associated with poorer cognitive performance in old age.

    The study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (Warren et al., 2026).
